Breaking: When Everything Has Changed, What Do We Do Next?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I think the most common emoji I’ve seen this year is “Face with Bags Under Eyes” (🫩) and that indicates a lot.
  • Recent findings suggest that technology hyperscalers like Microsoft and Meta, along with AI startups like Open AI and Anthropic have transformed everything about tech and the job we do.
  • It’s not just tech jobs that have transformed either.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been a… year, huh? I think the most common emoji I’ve seen this year is “Face with Bags Under Eyes” (🫩) and that indicates a lot. One thing is for sure: the industry we make a living in is in flux, regardless of the outcomes of the AI bubble. Let’s take a look at how we can try and navigate that situation as best we can. But first….

Recent findings suggest that technology hyperscalers like Microsoft and Meta, along with AI startups like Open AI and Anthropic have transformed everything about tech and the job we do. This is true regardless of if they fail or somehow succeed in their quest to have everyone paying a subscription fee for their Large Language Model (LLM) technology, which is marketed to us as AI. I’ll refer to this technology as AI for the rest of this article for simplicity.

It’s not just tech jobs that have transformed either. Everywhere you go, you will see some slop, somewhere. Be it a flyer, website, a village poster or a food truck menu. Heck, people are even using LLMs to work out what’s special about their own children. The effects of this technology are far-reaching, way beyond our own industry.

Industry observers note that the technology has hit us all in tech especially hard though. Mid-last year, I did some investigating because I suspected that so-called AI mandates were becoming increasingly popular and what I learned from conversations then feels like some sort of utopia compared to now. In the space between that piece being published and now, we went from token maxxing to companies realizing that actually, this technology is extremely expensive and not returning the promised outcomes.

The mandates have cooled, sure, but the demands to use AI to produce more volume, regardless of whether that volume is actually needed or not are still very much there. I’m in a fortunate position to have friendships with people all across the industry, from tech hyperscalers, to tiny little studios, and the stories I have heard from their work life are nothing short of horrifying. No one really seems to be happy with their work either.

This is such a long way away from even a handful of years ago where yes, there was a lot of problematic culture and outcomes from the tech industry, but people were generally quite happy with the work they were doing at least.

The sudden urge to sprint towards AI technologies over the last few years has had a devastating effect in so many places. The technology has encouraged suicide, devastated communities with the data center build-out and of course, displaced thousands of people’s careers. It’s worth noting that I’ve mentioned only a tiny sample of the harms there. If I listed them all, this article would be unbearably long and depressing.

It has been revealed that some harms I do want to touch on though are the effects on our communities in tech. The community spirit of open source and open knowledge was the foundation of the industry’s — especially the web industry’s — rapid success. At the root of everything there was people happy to share knowledge and build everyone up with them. Those people still do exist — myself included — but being one of those people is increasingly difficult.

According to recent reports, as the numbers go up in the AI world, the numbers very much go down for independent educators, publishers and community conferences. There’s a developing and worrying culture of “I don’t need to skill up now because I can use AI for work”, so allow me to break down why that reductive view of your work and your career is harmful in the long term.

And don’t ever forget that! Let’s have a think for a second about what actually makes you a good developer, because typing characters in a text editor certainly isn’t it. What makes us good is experience, knowledge, nuance and above all else, creativity.

According to recent reports, look, I get it, AI really can feel like it’s a miracle machine, but it’s crucial to take a wider view. Along with the published studies on cognitive decline and the widening skills gap, it’s more important than ever to invest in your brain to keep your skills sharp because you’re not getting that repetitive reinforcement that writing code every day gives you anymore if AI tools do everything for you. There’s a reason that I often build most of my teaching around a linear build-along because the tangible nature of repeating patterns you’ve learned really helps that knowledge to sink in.

As always, this article is addressed to everyone, but I want to talk directly to founders (like me), decision makers, and managers for a second. A massive part of our job, in fact, the most important part, is to ensure that our workers are looked after. I’m not just talking about compensation and perks here. I’m talking about our responsibility to ensure that our workers’ skills are kept sharp, their professional curiosities are satisfied and above all else that they are happy in the work they are doing. Our workers are much more than “number go up” vehicles.

In a recent development, you should be giving your developers more time to learn, rather than chasing endless volume. If AI enthusiasts are to be believed, there’s hours upon hours of time efficiencies created by this technology. Don’t fill that time with more volume. Instead, invest that time in developing your worker’s skills. It’s going to avoid burnout which yep, daily LLM use will likely cause in the long term.

According to recent reports, one thing that is increasingly clear is that the health of the AI industry is not good. The bubble has already effectively burst in China and more worryingly for economy enjoyers, the “picks and shovels” — AKA the chips industry in Korea — has seen dramatic downturns. This is not how an “inevitable” outcome is supposed to happen!

Sources indicate that the U.S. AI industry is on very shaky ground too. Circular financing, unbelievable levels of debt and a data center build out that simply cannot keep up with the required power levels to turn profits for hyperscalers and startups, mixed with a genuine hatred of the technology by the general public, creates enough risk in itself. Recent events, such as the Democrats dominating the midterms causing AI stocks to drop and as well as Nvidia’s stock because of its CEO being caught up in a spying scandal shine a light on the fragility of the industry. A healthy industry doesn’t work like this.

Recent findings suggest that with all that in mind, what would be a really silly thing to do? Yeh, you guessed it: put AI at the heart of everything in your business. Sure, there’s open source models — which I think is the logical destination of the technology — but how many companies are going to be willing to maintain their infrastructure needs? Not many. The low barrier of entry of commercial AI technology is the selling point, let’s be honest.

Above everything, people need to be invested in, not pushed aside by technology like AI. As I mentioned earlier, it’s experience, knowledge, nuance, and creativity that sets humans far apart from AI. That technology does indeed keep evolving, but even the most ardent of AI supporters will concede that the rate of frontier model improvement is very much levelling out.

There’s never been a more crucial time to keep human skills sharp, so here’s some ideas on how to do that.

It has been revealed that this is not just directed at individuals but also at founders, decision makers and managers. Our industry has been historically excellent at investing in skilling people up and we need to bring that back.

In a recent development, give staff the time and budget to learn, to develop their skills and to engage with the community at conferences. You already know the positive outcomes that brings, so bring it back to your organization. At the absolute worst case, it’ll make the usage of AI in your organization more efficient and when the token subsidies inevitably end, more cost effective.

Again, token subsidies will inevitably end. So, getting thousands of dollars of worth from a $200 a month subscription will be something you’ll look fondly back on. When hallucinations from AI tools are suddenly costing thousands, does it make sense to force your staff to produce as much volume as possible? Of course not.

According to recent reports, my advice is to re-evaluate those prior decisions and invest saved costs back into developing your workers instead, while there’s still a hope of them not burning out completely. Make sure you include your workers in these decisions and discuss the impacts of mandates on them. It’s crucial for you to understand the impact of these sort of decisions.

This advice is more aimed at developers, but stay paying attention, managers. As I mentioned earlier, repetition (especially typing) reinforces newly introduced learning and existing knowledge. The slower pace also allows your brain to think, which from a quality of output perspective, is imperative. Doing none of that atrophies skills over time.

According to recent reports, I recently read Jenn Schiffer’s great post. She did the Weird Web October challenge and wrote this:.

[…] i encourage anyone who uses ai and/or vibe codes to consider doing an exercise like this without those tools as a way to challenge your brain and you can continue doing your regular work the way you do your regular work.

I think that’s a very good idea, even if it’s messing around with a little side project — if you’ve got the energy from Producing Value all day, of course. Guess what bosses: this is another way you can make your staff happier, by giving them time to do this on the clock.

At the end of the day, you’ll miss the soul when it’s gone. It’s not gone yet though. Far from it. Independents like CSS-Tricks, my publication, Piccalilli, and Smashing Magazine are trying hard to keep the soul of our industry alive by sharing high quality educational content with the community.

Most of this content is free at the point of entry, but it certainly isn’t free to produce. We all pay writers fairly to share their knowledge with the community and we are all tiny organizations. We’re certainly not in this game to make huge profits, that’s for sure.

Sources indicate that all of us could do more though, but funding is the ultimate barrier. For both companies and individuals, purchase courses, join the membership programs, and purchase ad space. With the right financial support, publications like ours can be a real force in pushing the good stuff back into our industry and bringing everyone up with us. That’s what we do it for.

Industry observers note that some course producers I recommend are Miriam, Sara, Mat, Scott, Brad and Ian, Josh, Ahmad, Christine, Vitaly, Ben and of course, myself! All of these will have generous Black Friday deals, so go ahead and ask your boss to invest in you.

Now, share this post with your boss.

Profiling in PyTorch (Part 3): Attention is all you profile

📅 10 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is the third post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:.
  • The series "Profiling in PyTorch" is meant to make you comfortable reading profiler traces and tables.
  • Industry observers note that in Part 2 we wrapped that addition and multiplication into a torch linear layer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the third post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:.

The series "Profiling in PyTorch" is meant to make you comfortable reading profiler traces and tables. In Part 1 we profiled basic math operations like addition and multiplication. We saw how the profiler table uncovers hotspots, and how the profiler trace demonstrates the order in which an algorithm runs over time.

Industry observers note that in Part 2 we wrapped that addition and multiplication into a torch linear layer. We then stacked several linear layers on top of each other (a multilayer perceptron) and profiled that. Along the way we also profiled fused and hand-tuned kernels.

From the perspective of the Transformer architecture, the next logical step for us to profile is yet another fundamental algorithm, attention. While being infamous for its quadratic-time complexity, many clever tricks exist to mitigate that problem and make it fast. Our goal here is not to cover every trick in detail. Instead, we want to see how each one looks different under the profiler.

The scripts for this blog post live here: 04_a_naive_attention.py, 04_b_inplace_ops_attention.py, 04_c_sdpa_attention.py, and 04_d_kernels_attention.py. Like before, it helps to open them in a separate tab and walk through the code as you read. We use an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU to run the scripts. It is really easy to set up a GPU on the Hugging Face infrastructure and experiment with the scripts using Dev Mode with Spaces. One could also run the scripts with the Hugging Face Jobs pipeline.

It has been revealed that attention works with Queries (q), Keys (k), and Values (v). The interaction between them can be written as a short sequence of steps:.

So attention is really a collection of primitive operations. Some of them we already know (the matmuls), and the rest are easy to spot. Let's write a naive attention module in PyTorch and profile it.

Before opening the trace, let's do our usual exercise and guess what we should see. Tracing the forward of this module, we expect:.

Sources indicate that figure 1 indicates the CPU lane of the profile (the GPU lane is folded so it does not overwhelm us). Inside attn_fwd (our annotated forward call) we can see exactly the operations we guessed. The matmul is an old friend by now, and the new operations are easy to spot:.

Now let's unfold the GPU lane and see which kernels were actually introduced.

Figure 2 demonstrates the GPU lane next to the CPU lane. Let's zoom into a single attn_fwd block on the GPU lane to look at the kernels one by one.

Figure 3 lets us read off the individual kernels for one profiler step:.

Five of these are expected. The memory copy is the odd one out, so where does this come from? The clue is that PyTorch has in-place operations. When you operate on a tensor the ordinary (out-of-place) way, PyTorch often makes a copy, applies the requested operation to it, and returns the copy. Following the sequence of operations, the culprit here is our masked_fill.

What if we replaced this with an in-place operation?

All we change is masked_fill to masked_fill_ (note the trailing underscore, PyTorch's convention for in-place operations), and we run the same script.

Let's look at the trace and see if something changed.

The in-place version (Figure 5) wraps far fewer CPU ops inside the masking step than the out-of-place version (Figure 4). This is an encouraging signal. Let's unfold the GPU lane to confirm what happened there.

On the GPU lane the Memcpy kernel is gone for good (Figures 6 and 7). With a one line change we shaved a whole kernel off each forward pass. This may not look like much on its own, but remember this is a single attention operation. In the context of a transformer based large model (LLMs, Diffusion models, etc.), it repeats once per layer, and there are many layers, so the saving adds up rapidly (and if it earns you a raise, sharing at least 10% with us feels only fair).

In a recent development, out-of-place is PyTorch's default for a reason. To compute gradients, autograd has to remember the tensor values it saw on the forward pass, because many backward formulas reuse them. An in-place operation overwrites those values in memory, so the backward pass would read the wrong numbers. Due to the fact that we run forward under torch.no_grad, in-place is safe for us, with no backward pass and nothing to corrupt. It is also noteworthy that in-place operations do not only save time (like we see in our case) but also memory (due to no extra copy) which is great for large tensors like logits!

In a recent development, we just built attention from primitives, and even shaved off a Memcpy. The good news is that the PyTorch team has done all of this for us, and packaged the whole pipeline into a single function:.

Recent findings suggest that this one line replaces our hand written module, and is_causal=True even saves us from building the mask by hand. It is worth pausing to appreciate how much this one call hides. And it hides more than just code lines. Scaled Dot Product Attention (SDPA) does not have a single implementation. Under the hood it dispatches to one of the several backends and picks the fastest one that supports our inputs (dtype, head dimension, mask, hardware, etc.).

The official SDPA tutorial walks us through this selection, and the backends themselves are listed in the torch.nn.attention.SDPBackend enum:.

Industry observers note that normally SDPA chooses for us, but we can pin a specific backend with the torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel context manager. This is what we do in our scripts. This lets us profile each backend on its own and read how differently they show up in the trace. Let's go one at a time.

Before we open anything, let's guess. We have replaced hand written attention (matmul, mul, mask, softmax, matmul) with a single one liner, so we should expect the trace to get simpler and faster. Fewer kernels, less CPU dispatch, maybe even a fused kernel. Let's check the profiler table first.

This is our first surprise, the one liner is 3.7x slower.

Opening the trace (Figure 9) indicates why the alarm bells ring, the math backend releases 20 GPU kernels per forward instead of the 5 launched with our naive attention implementation (Figure 8). This is the opposite of what we guessed. Let's figure out why this happens.

In Part 2 we learned to read a kernel name like a fingerprint. Let's use that habit here:.

The A100s we used to capture these traces ship with Tensor Cores, specialised hardware for accelerated matmuls that is known to be far faster than the ordinary CUDA cores. To see why that matters here, it helps to know what lives inside a GPU. A Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) is the compute unit of a GPU, and each SM has two kinds of arithmetic units, the CUDA cores and the Tensor Cores. CUDA cores are general purpose and process a handful of elements at a time, while Tensor Cores multiply and accumulate a whole small matrix tile in a single instruction. So the question is simple, "Is each backend actually using the fast path?".

Sources indicate that the kernel names answer it. The s16816 in the naive kernel (Figure 10) is the signature of a bfloat16 Tensor Core matmul (the 16x8x16 Tensor Core instruction), so the naive version is on the fast path. sgemm (Figure 11) is the classic single precision (FP32) matmul that runs on the ordinary CUDA cores. In other words, the math backend never touches the Tensor Cores at all: to trade speed for numerical accuracy it upcasts tensors to FP32 (doubling the data moved, even when the inputs are in bf16) and falls back to the slower CUDA cores.

It has been revealed that in the naive version we built the causal mask once and reused it. Here we passed is_causal=True and the math backend materialized one for us, on every single call. You can watch it happen on the CPU lane:.

Here is what we see in Figure 12.

On the GPU this reveals up as a triu_tril_kernel, several where kernels, and an add_. The convenience flag that let us stop thinking about the mask did not remove the work, it just moved it one layer down, where the mask is rebuilt from scratch every forward.

Recent findings suggest that our hand written version called plain aten::softmax. The math backend calls aten::_safe_softmax, and the difference is again visible as extra kernels (Figure 13):.

A row that is fully masked (every entry -inf) would make an ordinary softmax compute exp(-inf)/sum(exp(-inf)) = 0/0 = NaN. _safe_softmax guards against exactly that. Our naive kernel never bothered, and would have quietly produced NaNs in that corner case.

Put together, the math backend is the reference implementation. It is a straightforward, dtype-safe, NaN-safe decomposition of attention into primitive ATen ops. It is essentially the naive attention we wrote by hand, but more careful. That carefulness is exactly what makes it extremely slow.

Its job is not to be fast, but to always work. This makes it the perfect baseline. Every backend we profile next (flash, efficient, cudnn) is trying to collapse the 20 GPU kernels into essentially one fused kernel that stays in bf16 and never materializes the intermediate matrices at all.

Where the math backend launched 20 kernels across one profiler step, the efficient backend debuts only one fmha_cutlassF_bf16_aligned_64x64_rf_sm80 (as seen in Figure 14).

Let's decode the name of the kernel:.

This is the memory efficient attention kernel that grew out of Meta's xformers library and was upstreamed into PyTorch. When people say "the xformers backend," this fmha_cutlassF kernel is what they mean.

The void pytorch_flash kernel (Figure 15) is FlashAttention-2 (Tri Dao's implementation), vendored into PyTorch.

Before we read the trace any further, it is worth answering the question you should be asking by now: why is there a whole backend named "flash", and why does it matter so much?

It has been revealed that let's go back to the math backend for a moment. Its real problem was not the count of 20 kernels, it was what those kernels handed to each other.

Industry observers note that step 1 builds the full score matrix attn = q . k.T, which is [seq, seq] per head. For a sequence length of 4096 that is 4096 x 4096 ≈ 16 million numbers for a single head. That matrix is written out to the HBM (the GPU's main memory), if there is even enough space to do so. Then, it is read back to be scaled, written again for the mask, read again for the softmax, and so on. Attention's cost is dominated by this back and forth traffic to HBM, not by the matmuls themselves.

FlashAttention attacks exactly this. Instead of computing the whole s matrix and only then reducing it, it walks over k and v in tiles, keeps a running softmax as it goes (the "online softmax" trick), and accumulates the output one tile at a time. The full [seq, seq] score matrix is never written to HBM, it only ever lives on-chip. This is the single idea that lets the entire attention pipeline collapse into one fused kernel that stays in bf16 on the Tensor cores.

In a recent development, here is where flash surprises people who read profiler footprints. It is the fastest backend, yet the profiler reports it with very low occupancy (shown in Figure 16). To see why that is fine, we need three quick definitions.

Recent findings suggest that A GPU kernel is essentially a series of instructions executed by many small execution units. These individual execution units (threads) take care of loading variables, adding them together, storing them back, etc. For each kernel, we launch many, many threads, and to keep track of them, we group them by blocks.

In a recent development, blocks are scheduled onto Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), the main compute units of a GPU. A block lives entirely on one SM, and an SM can host multiple blocks at once if it has enough resources. Those resources include registers, shared memory, maximum resident threads, and maximum resident warps. So when we say a kernel has low occupancy, we mean each SM has fewer resident warps than it could theoretically support.

If you want to know more about threads, blocks, grids, etc. here is a great resource.

If you click the flash kernel in the trace, its footprint tells the story (Figure 17).

Flash uses a lot of per-thread registers and a large amount of shared memory per block. For example, if a block has 128 threads and each thread uses 255 registers, that block needs 128 × 255 = 32,640 registers. On an Ampere SM with 65,536 registers, only two such blocks fit at once. Each 128-thread block has 128 / 32 = 4 warps, so two blocks give only 8 resident warps. Against a maximum of 64 resident warps, that is roughly 13% occupancy. Flash has low occupancy not because it is poorly optimized, but because each block is deliberately very "heavy" in on-chip resource usage.

And that is the whole point. High occupancy helps hide latency by keeping many warps ready to run, but it does not make the work itself efficient. Flash spends those registers and that shared memory on purpose, to keep attention tiles on-chip, reuse data aggressively, and avoid ever materializing the full attention matrix in global memory.

In a recent development, by now the pattern is familiar. Like flash and efficient, cuDNN gives us one fused, flash-style kernel per forward (Figure 18). So the natural question is: if flash already fuses attention, why does PyTorch ship yet another flash backend? The answer is who writes the kernel and how it is built, and that difference is what makes the trace look different.

Industry observers note that flash and efficient are fixed, pre-compiled kernels vendored into PyTorch. You get the same binary every time. cuDNN is NVIDIA's own deep learning library, and its attention kernel is generated and tuned for the specific problem at hand. It is closer in spirit to torch.compile's codegen than to a fixed cuBLAS binary. You can read that straight off the (very long) kernel name:.

That one fact, generated per problem, explains everything else that looks unusual in the trace.

No transposes: The CPU lane goes from _cudnn_attention_forward straight to a couple of aten::empty allocations and then the kernel, with zero aten::transpose (Figures 19, 20 and 21). Flash and efficient each insert four (metadata) transposes to reshape the tensors while cuDNN consumes the native [B, H, S, D] layout directly because its generator emits a kernel for that layout.

According to recent reports, it launches through cuLaunchKernelEx, not cudaLaunchKernel: Every other kernel in this whole series went through the runtime API cudaLaunchKernel. cuDNN uses the driver-level extended launch, which carries launch attributes (Figure 22).

The profiler reports 0% achieved occupancy: Do not take that at face value, it is a measurement gap, not a stalled GPU. CUPTI (the profiling backend) cannot attribute occupancy to a driver-API (cuLaunchKernelEx) launch the way it does for cudaLaunchKernel, so the field reads 0. The footprint fills in the truth (Figure 23): 240 registers × 256 threads = 61,440 registers per block against the SM's 65,536, so only one block fits per SM (8 warps ≈ 12.5%), right in line with flash.

Sources indicate that the "no transposes" story tempts us to expect cuDNN to be the leanest backend on the CPU. It is the opposite.

Even with zero transpose ops, cuDNN spends about 214 µs per forward on the CPU, more than flash (138) or efficient (117). Almost all of it sits in aten::scaled_dot_product_attention self time (26% of the whole run) and _cudnn_attention_forward. That is cuDNN's runtime engine selecting and preparing the plan (the "knob" search) on every call.

Industry observers note that fewer visible ATen ops did not mean less CPU work, it moved the work into the library, where the profiler can only show it as one fat, opaque bar. When a trace suddenly gets cleaner, the work has not always disappeared, sometimes it has just moved somewhere the profiler cannot break down.

Sources indicate that on the GPU, cuDNN (186.3 µs) lands between efficient and flash. On this very flash-friendly shape, hand-written FlashAttention-2 edges it out. cuDNN often wins on other shapes (larger head dimensions, different sequence lengths) precisely because its generator retunes per problem, but that retuning is also what you just paid for on the CPU.

Before we wrap up, here is a single table to review every attention variant we profiled and the one lesson each trace taught us.

If you take away only one thing from the whole series, let it be the habit we repeated before every single trace which is to guess first, then look.

Recent findings suggest that state out loud what you expect the trace to contain, open it, and treat any mismatch as the most interesting thing on the screen. Every real insight in these three posts, the hidden Memcpy, the addmm epilogue, the 20 kernel math backend, flash's "wrong-looking" occupancy, cuDNN's fat CPU bar, came from a guess that did not match the trace.

Profiling is not a separate, intimidating skill reserved for GPU experts. It is just the discipline of looking closely and asking "wait, why is that happening?" until the answer clicks. You now have the vocabulary and the reflexes to do that on your own models. Open a trace, form a guess, and go find the mismatch.

Thanks for reading the Profiling in PyTorch series. Now go profile something. 🤗.

Smartphones have defined personal computing for nearly two decades. They changed how people communicate, work, navigate and find information. They also still depend on screens, app switching and a lot of manual effort.

Artificial intelligence is starting to change that relationship. Emerging personal devices can respond to natural language, use context and offer help when it is needed instead of waiting for constant input. For developers, that raises practical questions: where should a model run, what should an interface look like without a large screen, and how much data should leave the device? This article walks through those questions and includes a small, tested helper for one of them. Product details change quickly, so check each platform's current documentation.

According to recent reports, the smartphone interaction model is screen-centered: open an app, navigate menus, enter a command. AI-powered devices combine machine learning, sensors and conversational interfaces to interpret a request with fewer manual steps.

Navigation is a simple example. On a phone, you check the map or listen to directions. A wearable could give timely audio instructions or a visual cue based on location and movement. That does not mean the phone goes away. Personal computing may instead spread across interconnected devices, with the phone continuing to supply connectivity and processing.

In a recent development, contextual computing means a system uses relevant information about the environment, user activity or earlier interactions. A traditional app responds to explicit commands. An AI-assisted one can also interpret natural-language requests and combine several inputs. A personal assistant might use calendar and location data, with permission, to suggest when someone should leave for an appointment.

Multimodal AI, which McKinsey describes as AI that can handle several kinds of data at once, including text, images, audio and video, makes interactions feel more natural than touch controls alone.

Recent findings suggest that context only helps when the underlying information is reliable. Developers need to manage permissions, data accuracy and user expectations, or the feature will feel intrusive or wrong.

According to recent reports, smartwatches and fitness trackers already indicated the value of getting information without pulling out a phone. AI extends this to other products, including smart eyewear, earbuds and connected accessories.

In a recent development, smart glasses are one example of familiar accessories gaining intelligent features without a conventional screen. Depending on the model, they can support voice assistance, hands-free photography, audio playback and interaction with AI assistants. Several makers sell them, and guide pages such as ai glasses describes how the category is presented to buyers. Capabilities differ widely, so compare sensors, battery life, privacy controls and the software platform before building for or buying any one device.

According to recent reports, for interaction design, the point is to deliver help while the user keeps doing something else. That changes what an app should show, say and ask.

In a recent development, many AI features rely on cloud infrastructure. The cloud offers large models and plenty of compute, but adds network delay and requires sending data off the device. On-device AI runs supported models on personal hardware. It can reduce latency, support some offline features and limit how much sensitive information is transmitted.

Sources indicate that local processing has costs. Small devices have limited memory, battery and thermal headroom, so teams balance model size, compute demand and response quality. Hybrid architectures split the work between local hardware and cloud services, and are a practical answer for many applications.

According to recent reports, A hybrid app needs a rule for where each request runs. The Python module below is a deliberately simple example. It takes the task (model size, whether the data is sensitive, the latency the user will tolerate) and the device state (free memory, battery, connectivity, measured round-trip time) and returns device, cloud, ask_user or unavailable.

The tests cover the main cases: a live caption on glasses stays on the device when the network is too slow, a large model that does not fit goes to the cloud, sensitive data stays local or triggers a question to the user when the model will not fit, an offline device runs only what fits, and low battery pushes a heavy job to the cloud.

Run it with python3 test_route-py.

Ambient computing describes technology that blends into everyday environments instead of demanding continuous attention. Consumers may reach connected services through speakers, watches, glasses and other devices. Someone could start a task with a voice assistant, get a reminder on a watch and continue on a laptop without recreating the context.

That requires reliable synchronization, interoperable services and consistent identity across devices. AI can help interpret requests and coordinate interactions, but a seamless experience still depends on well-designed software architecture. Developers should decide how information moves between devices, what happens when connectivity fails and how people stay in control of automated actions.

According to recent reports, apps built around large screens and touch navigation may not translate well to devices that rely on speech, audio feedback or compact visual displays. Google's Android XR developer documentation describes building for several device types, including XR headsets, audio glasses and display glasses, and lists tools such as the Jetpack XR SDK, Unity, OpenXR and WebXR.

Whatever the platform, a few priorities recur:.

Not every interaction benefits from AI. Predictable tasks may be better served by a conventional interface, so use intelligent features where they measurably improve usability.

Probably not soon. Phones are likely to remain a hub for connectivity and processing, while wearables and ambient devices handle some everyday interactions.

Running a machine learning model directly on personal hardware, so a task can run without sending each request to a remote server.

When the model is too large for the device, the data is not sensitive and the network is fast enough. Many apps use a hybrid, as in the routing helper above.

Interaction relies more on voice and audio, displays are small or absent, and messages must be short and timely because the user is busy doing something else.

In a recent development, personal computing is moving toward a connected, context-aware ecosystem of wearables, on-device processing and ambient interfaces. That transition needs careful attention to privacy, security, accessibility and usability. The products that last will be defined less by the hardware people carry and more by how naturally and responsibly technology supports what they are trying to do.

Introducing Real World VoiceEQ: Measuring the human quality of voice AI

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (968 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Existing benchmarks suggest voice AI is nearing human-level performance but real-world conversations tell a different story.
  • Sources indicate that voice is rapidly becoming AI's primary interface.
  • Over the last few years, voice models have improved dramatically.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Existing benchmarks suggest voice AI is nearing human-level performance but real-world conversations tell a different story.

Sources indicate that voice is rapidly becoming AI's primary interface. From customer support and healthcare to education, entertainment, and personal assistants, speech is increasingly replacing text as the way people interact with AI.

Over the last few years, voice models have improved dramatically. Word error rates continue to fall, latency has reached conversational speeds, and many established benchmarks are approaching saturation. Yet anyone who regularly uses voice AI knows something still feels off.

Sources indicate that voice models can sound like different people over the course of a conversation, miss hesitation or uncertainty, and struggle with accents, noise, or emotional speech. Those shortcomings are easy to miss in benchmarks focused on latency and word error rate. People care whether a voice system can truly listen, respond appropriately, and remain natural and reliable in real conversations.

To measure those qualities, we built Real World VoiceEQ—a benchmark designed to evaluate the human quality of voice interaction. It assesses whether voice systems can recognize, produce, and respond to the acoustic information transcripts leave out, from tone and emotion to speaker identity and background context.

Real World VoiceEQ evaluates more than 40 leading proprietary and open-source voice models across 15+ key evaluation dimensions and more than 60 metrics spanning Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Text-to-Speech (TTS), Speech-to-Speech (S2S), and Speech Understanding.

Recent findings suggest that real World VoiceEQ was developed from more than 1 million individual human ratings collected across different demographics, speaking styles, and acoustic environments. The current benchmark includes 785,000 TTS ratings and 48,000 STS ratings, making it one of the largest human evaluations of voice AI conducted to date.

Sources indicate that every evaluation was conducted using Kairos, our flexible, voice-native evaluation platform. The same infrastructure enables frontier AI labs and enterprises to run custom evaluations tailored to specific use cases, identify granular failure modes in production voice systems, generate human preference data, and continuously improve models through reinforcement learning and human feedback.

The race for a single "best" voice model is giving way to a collection of specialized capabilities.

It has been revealed that today's leading systems optimize for different strengths—including technical accuracy, emotional understanding, conversational intelligence, expressiveness, and robustness. One model that excels at repeating booking reference numbers, bank account details, or complex pharmaceutical names may struggle to produce emotionally expressive speech. Another may sound remarkably natural but be less reliable on precision-oriented tasks.

As voice AI matures, measuring progress increasingly requires evaluating these capabilities independently rather than collapsing them into a single overall score. In our TTS evaluations, no system configuration ranked among the top five across all eight capability groups—underscoring why there is no single "best" voice model.

Speech-to-Speech models showed the widest variation of any category we evaluated. Some systems recognized emotion exceptionally well but struggled to respond naturally. We found that access to audio did not guarantee that agents used the paralinguistic information it contained. Some systems remained largely transcript-driven, relying on the words being spoken while overlooking cues such as tone, pacing, hesitation, emphasis, and volume.

Sources indicate that humans naturally use these cues to infer confidence, uncertainty, frustration, sarcasm, and empathy. Today's models often miss them.

In a recent development, imagine a banking agent asking whether you recognize a potentially fraudulent transaction. A confident "Yes" and a hesitant "…yes…" may have completely different meanings, even though the transcript is identical. Humans recognize that difference immediately. Many of today's voice models do not.

Many established benchmarks are nearing their limits and don't reflect real-world conditions. Models still struggle with accented speech, overlapping speakers, emotion, background noise, and longer conversations. In our evaluation, performance varies far more across leading open-source and proprietary models than traditional benchmarks suggest. In one example, transcription word error rates on noise-backed speech were roughly four times higher than on music-backed speech, showing how a single background-audio score can hide the real failure mode.

Sources indicate that in preliminary research, we found signs that some models may be optimized for established public benchmarks. Several reproduced known errors in reference transcripts, followed arbitrary spelling conventions, and even reconstructed masked words that were not present in the audio.

Sources indicate that LLMs are now widely used to evaluate text-based models, but our findings suggest that speech-language models (SLMs) should be used more carefully for voice evaluation. When we compared leading SLMs with trained human raters on text-to-speech assessments, agreement was highest on tasks with clear, verifiable answers, such as pronunciation accuracy.

It has been revealed that agreement declined on more subjective evaluations. SLMs sometimes appeared to infer emotion from text-based contextual cues, and agreement was weakest for open-ended judgments such as whether a voice fit an acting role or maintained a consistent identity. Automated evaluators can be valuable for well-defined tasks, but they are not yet a substitute for human listeners when judgments depend on acoustic-context, perception, and social interpretation.

Recent findings suggest that as voice becomes one of AI's defining interfaces, speed and technical accuracy alone will no longer determine which systems succeed. The models people ultimately choose will be those that can understand, express, and respond like humans—not just under ideal benchmark conditions, but across the complexity of real-world conversation.

For decades, speech AI has advanced by optimizing against quantitative metrics on standardized benchmarks; from WER for transcription accuracy to objective perceptual metrics like PESQ and DNSMOS for speech quality. We hope Real World VoiceEQ can extend this paradigm by providing a human-grounded metric for evaluating the components of synthetic voice interactions.

Read the full technical report and explore the public leaderboards—or get in touch to learn how Hume can evaluate your voice model or agent using Real World VoiceEQ, or design custom evaluations tailored to your specific use case.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, newly introduced York State Senator Jeremy Cooney has filed a bill that would bring prediction markets into the state's tax base instead of banning them. The proposal puts a state lawmaker at odds with New York's own lawsuit against Kalshi.

Revenue raised under Jeremy Cooney’s FUTURES Act would flow into a Futures Fund for Early Education to pay for universal pre-K.

The timing gives the bill extra weight. Attorney General Letitia James had sought to stop Kalshi at a virtual hearing held the day the bill was filed. Governor Hochul and James declared on July 31, 2026, that Newly introduced York had sued KalshiEX LLC for running an illegal gambling operation through its prediction market.

Industry observers note that cooney’s bill states that CFTC-registered markets “may operate within the state of Latest York lawfully.” That language sets it against the state’s executive branch. It also marks a shift from his earlier bill, S8889, introduced in January. That version would have required operators to get a license from the Department of Financial Services. “I’m placing a bet on the future of UPK in New York,” Cooney mentioned in his release.

Industry observers note that licensed mobile sportsbooks face a far heavier tax than the bill proposes. The gap could widen in practice. Operators would be allowed to deduct some operating expenses from taxable revenue, which sportsbooks cannot do.

Recent findings suggest that the scope is narrow. The bill covers sports contracts only, so election, economic and culture markets fall outside it. Its official summary also covers the use of prediction markets in election violations. Elected officials and some state employees would be barred from trading.

Sources indicate that the consumer rules borrow from regulated betting. Operators would have to verify identity and age, run self-exclusion programs, and offer deposit limits and cooling-off periods. They would also file a yearly consumer-protection audit with the attorney general. The minimum trading age, however, would be left to federal authorities instead of Fresh York’s sports-betting minimum of 21.

Sources indicate that age also came up in court. The state argued that Kalshi lets younger customers bet. Justice Crane asked the organization to consider safeguards for users aged 18 to 20. Kalshi’s lawyers stated the company could look at limiting access to its contracts for those users in Newly introduced York.

Latest York is not alone in treating prediction markets as a taxable business. North Carolina’s new law recognizes the CFTC’s exclusive federal authority over prediction markets. It taxes platforms at 6% of net trading-fee revenue from state residents.

Industry observers note that A judge denied New York's TRO against Kalshi. Hours later, New York introduced a bill to regulate and tax prediction markets.

Sources indicate that the judge denied the State's request for a temporary restraining order against Kalshi. According to Kalshi, the judge… https://t.co/1T7RAZh7j6.

Industry observers note that oregon may go higher. Senate Majority Leader Anthony Broadman told OPB he will probably seek a rate above North Carolina’s, perhaps 8%, in the 2027 session. That money would go toward wildfire costs. If more states follow, platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket, along with their licensed sportsbook rivals, would face higher costs.

In Upcoming York, S10748 was sent to the Senate Rules Committee on the day it was introduced, and it remains pending there.

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The CSS scroll-state() query, surprisingly, has nothing to do with whether you’re doom-scrolling in a state of existential dread.
  • According to recent reports, while scroll-state(), with those slimming parentheses, looks like a function, it’s not technically one.
  • In the following demo (which we’ll dissect in a bit), a “Back to Top” link slides in from the bottom as you scroll down the page.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The CSS scroll-state() query, surprisingly, has nothing to do with whether you’re doom-scrolling in a state of existential dread. It does, however, allow you to change the CSS used based on scrolling behavior. Far from doom, that’s pretty neat-o speedo. (Okay, you’re right, there’s nothing neat-o about a speedo). You can do lots of things that used to require JavaScript, like revealing the navigation when a user scrolls up or animating in a back to top link once the user scrolls down.

According to recent reports, while scroll-state(), with those slimming parentheses, looks like a function, it’s not technically one. It’s a container query (@container) like style(). Since scroll-state() is a query, the website is basically asking the browser whether a particular feature of a container has a specific value. If it does, the styles within the brackets will apply. If it doesn’t have that feature at all or has the feature, but the value is different, the @container query is false and the styles in the brackets will not apply.

In the following demo (which we’ll dissect in a bit), a “Back to Top” link slides in from the bottom as you scroll down the page.

scroll-state() has four possible features and each of those has a variety of possible values.

Asks if a container has been scrolled in a given direction:.

Asks if a container can be scrolled in a given direction:.

Asks if a sticky-positioned element is stuck:.

Asks if a snap target has been snapped on a particular axis:.

Recent findings suggest that first let’s look at the scrolled feature. This is the demo we saw at the beginning where we animate a back-to-top link when we scroll down:.

When the scroll container is scrolled toward the block-end (downward in this case) the translate applies and the .toplink element animates up into the visible area. Because we’re using a transition, when we scroll a different direction (up and down/block-start and block-end are the only options here), it nicely animates out.

Industry observers note that while the scrolling direction in the demo above is pretty clear, what if this page was translated into a different language? Or we had a hero image that covered the entire viewport? One way we could indicate the scroll direction would be to have an arrow or other signifier animating and pointing in the correct direction. (I’m more a believer in constructing your page such that scroll direction is pretty obvious; however, I can foresee situations where an indicator was the best user experience or where translations/writing-mode changes could obscure what scrolling direction was appropriate.).

Industry observers note that one nice thing about the scrollable feature is that when you scroll to the end of the scrollable area, it shuts off. So when we scroll to the block-end of the page (bottom of the page in this instance) scrollable: block-end is no longer true and our scroll indicator will revert to its default (in this case, display: none).

According to recent reports, you could also combine the scrollable and scrolled features to remove the scroll indicator once the container has been scrolled either in the block-start or block-end direction. (We need both, because if we’re down in the middle of the page and we scroll up, scrolled: block-end will no longer be true and the scroll indicator will appear again.).

It has been revealed that another way we could enhance our demo is to have our navigation stick at the top while we’re scrolling down and change the look of the navigation once it’s stuck. The stuck feature must be on the element that gets stuck (as opposed to the scroll container, as was the case above). Also, because the container is set on the element that gets stuck, you cannot select the element itself from within the container query. You’ll need to position: sticky a wrapper element and “demote” all styles you want to change to the child.

In a recent development, the work of setting up the stuck feature happens in that .header-wrapper, but since we can’t apply styles to the container from within the container (not even with :has()). We need most of the styling to be in the element.

Changing the size of an element in the header that affects the size of the header can lead to conflicting results. i.e. you scroll to a position where the header is stuck, which initiates the size change, but that reduces the size, which pulls it away from the stuck point, which cancels the size change which makes it stuck again, which initiates the size change and round and round we go. Even a small change can make it impossible to even scroll past the stuck point. Adding a transition can help with this and make scrolling work again, but you can still scroll to a place where the resizing happens in a loop. In the following demo, if you scroll down to a pixel or so past where the header touches the top of the viewport, you should see the stutter step.

Industry observers note that there is one weird trick to fix this, though. No, really, there is! (shakes fist at the internet for making “one weird trick” an unbelievable phrase.) The one weird trick is to set a height on the element that’s getting stuck (.header-wrapper in the case above). Ideally, set it smaller than the final size of the header if you’re making the header smaller. This prevents the element from resizing because of a change in its content’s size. This does require the header content to overflow. If that’s a no-go for you, you’ll have to change its size with transformations. The transformed element has a sort of placeholder that stays in the DOM where the transformed element originally lived. This placeholder is what’s used to determine the sticky position and does not change based on what happened in the animation.

We can also add some styles when scroll snapping has been applied and that scroll has snappity-snapped (technical term). Similar to the stuck feature, snapped should be defined on the element that is snapped, not on the scroll container. If scroll snapping has not been applied to the element, then the snapped feature returns false and the container query does not apply.

First, we set up our scroll snapping in the scrolled container.

Note: As with most scrolling CSS (scrolling animations, etc.), if you’re using the document’s default scroll, the element is what’s being scrolled, not the .

The slide s are what we’re going to snap to the size of the viewport:.

Sources indicate that as remarked above, the container type and name go on the snapped item. And then we modify descendants of the slide once it snaps:.

Again, as with stuck, you cannot apply styles directly to the snapped element/the container, but only to the children of that element/container.

Welcome Inkling by Thinking Machines

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 🤗 Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Small, the next generation of the Inkling family.
  • Inkling is Thinking Machines' family of open multimodal models, and it now spans two generations on the Hub:.
  • According to recent reports, in this post, we start with the first-generation architecture, then walk through what changed in Inkling 2 Small and how to run it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Update: Inkling 2 Small is here! 🤗 Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Small, the next generation of the Inkling family. We have updated this post with a new section on Inkling 2 Small, covering what changed in the architecture and how to run it with transformers.

Inkling is Thinking Machines' family of open multimodal models, and it now spans two generations on the Hub:.

According to recent reports, in this post, we start with the first-generation architecture, then walk through what changed in Inkling 2 Small and how to run it. The rest of the post covers inference, use cases, post-training, and deployment, with examples built on the first-generation checkpoints.

Recent findings suggest that inkling is the first large open model with ~1T parameters and 1M context window to natively receive image, text, and audio inputs, trained on 45 trillion tokens of text, images, audio and video. It’s focused on reasoning across modalities such as audio, images, and text. It is intended for domain adaptation via fine-tuning. We’ve tinkered (pun intended) with this model to build some demos and explore the architecture, and we think it’s great for building a new wave of multimodal reasoning apps.

It has been revealed that inkling is a decoder-only multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) model with 975B total and 41B active parameters. There are a lot of things going on, so let’s break each part down:.

Here’s a quick glance of the architecture.

Relative attention: Instead of RoPE, which is the usual method to inject positional information in transformers models, Inkling uses relative attention to encode position information. Each attention layer learns position directly in the attention logits. Aside from key-query-values, there's a fourth projection producing a per-token, per-head relative feature R. This projection tensor is then tweaked with distance information (distance between the key and the query vector) and propagated into the attention module.

Industry observers note that hybrid attention: The decoder layers alternate between global attention (attending to the full context length at once) and sliding window attention (attending to a fixed context window in a sliding fashion). The architecture has a pattern of 5:1 sliding window to global attention layers. This hybrid attention scheme provides efficiency in computation. The final layer uses global attention to help build feature-rich representations.

According to recent reports, short convolution: The model uses a distinctive short 1D convolution, or SConv over the hidden states. SConv reads the current token and the previous W-1 hidden states, with W being the sliding window size. The intuition here is that SConv helps with local attention while freeing the attention and MoE modules from local representations.

MoE with shared experts sink: In Inkling, the router scores both routed experts and shared experts. Top-k selection is performed over 6 experts, plus 2 shared experts always active.

Recent findings suggest that vision understanding: The model includes a simple hierarchical MLP patchifier consisting of several linear layers. Each layer merges pixels progressively, until the final layer produces one embedding per patch.

Audio understanding: The architecture employs a discretized mel spectrogram, where each of the audio chunks (of 100 ms) are converted to the mel scale and then classified into the exact mel spectrogram bin.

The multimodal towers are relatively simple modules, unlike other models that employ separate encoders for each modality. Each image patch passes through the image embedding tower and the audio chunk is passed through the audio embedding tower to get both media embeddings. Image inputs also include an additional temporal dimension for video processing. We expect this capability to be useful for downstream fine-tuning, but we haven’t evaluated out-of-the-box video performance. The tower folds the patch grid, a small local block of neighboring tokens is stacked into the channel dimension and goes through hMLP. The audio waveform is converted to mel scale, which is then classified into a discrete mel bin. These mel bin values are embedded in the audio embedding tower and the embeddings are then summed to construct the final audio input.

In a recent development, inkling 2 is the next generation of the family. It takes text and image inputs (but no audio), and generates text. It keeps the core ideas of Inkling's decoder:.

Recent findings suggest that almost everything around that core was redesigned, though. The layers read from the residual stream differently, attention is bounded and gated, the MoE is simpler and wider, and the vision tower is now a real vision transformer.

Here's how the two generations compare:.

Let's go over the most notable changes together:.

Industry observers note that block attention residuals: In a standard transformer, every layer adds its output to the residual stream, and the next layer reads it. Inkling 2 has no single residual stream. Instead, it groups its 48 layers into 8 blocks of 6 and keeps one sum per block:.

A sublayer (attention or MLP) doesn't read one of these sums directly. It attends over depth, which means at each token position, it treats the finished block summaries plus the current partial block as a short sequence, and takes a softmax-weighted mix of them.

It has been revealed that the query is a single learned vector per sublayer. The keys and values are the RMS-normalized block summaries at that position. So the weights differ from token to token, depending on what each block wrote there.

Industry observers note that in other words, each sublayer learns how much to draw from each earlier stage of the network, rather than always reading the sum of everything. By the last layer, there are up to 9 sources to choose from (the embeddings, 7 finished blocks and the current partial block), and the final norm reads its input the same way. Global attention layers learn three queries, so their query, key and value projections can each draw on a different mix of blocks.

Sources indicate that dynamic short convolutions: The short convolutions on keys and values in the global attention layers are now dynamic. The 4 taps of each convolution are a fixed learned weight plus a per-token weight predicted from the input, shared within each key/value head. So the model can change, token by token, how much local context goes into each key and value. All short convolutions also rescale their residual sum to keep its variance stable through depth.

A leaner, wider MoE: Each layer has 384 routed experts with 8 active per token, and the shared experts are gone.

A latest vision encoder: Inkling encoded images with a lightweight hierarchical MLP. Inkling 2 uses a 23-layer vision transformer based on the Perception Encoder. It has the following properties:.

Several images are packed into one sequence, and each image only attends to itself.

Recent findings suggest that inkling 2 uses the same Auto classes as Inkling. Make sure to have updated transformers to run the model.

Inkling comes with day-0 transformers support and is supported in major inference engines like SGLang and vLLM.

In a recent development, this model is huge. The bf16 checkpoint requires 2 TB of VRAM, while the nvfp4 version requires 600 GB of VRAM. You can try the model through serverless inference routers like Inference Providers, or use ggml quants for local deployment with llama.cpp.

The easiest way to infer with transformers directly is to use the any-to-any pipeline. You can use either the 16 bit "thinkingmachines/Inkling" on Hopper or later GPUs, or the quantized NVFP4 checkpoint "thinkingmachines/Inkling-NVFP4" on Blackwell Nvidia GPUs. Make sure to have the latest version of transformers (5.14.0 was released today) (pip install -U transformers).

After initializing the pipeline, you can pass in the prompt as follows.

Going one level lower, you can use Auto classes. For inference, you can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class for models and AutoProcessor class for processors. For different reasoning tasks, the tokenizer takes in a reasoning_effort argument. Existing options for reasoning effort are "none", "minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", and "max".

Industry observers note that for multimodal inference, you can use the same classes. We provide example snippets for each different modality in the model card.

Inkling also takes in audio input. Below is an example inference snippet, which still uses the same AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

For more realistic parallel deployment in a cluster of several nodes, please refer to the Slurm section below.

SGLang is one of the fastest deployment frameworks for Inkling at the time of release, as it includes a custom model implementation. The launch command below shards the model across 8 GPUs and serves an OpenAI-compatible API on port 30000.

Recent findings suggest that match --tp-size to your GPU count. Add --mem-fraction-static (e.g. 0.85) if you need to leave more headroom for the KV cache.

According to recent reports, vLLM is strong for production serving. A single vllm serve command downloads the weights from the Hub, shards the model across your GPUs with tensor parallelism, and starts an OpenAI-compatible server on port 8000. You can view the vLLM Recipe for the model here to customize to your hardware.

In practice, you might need multiple nodes and a distribution tool like SLURM (see below). Key parameters are --tensor-parallel-size to the number of GPUs on your node, and use --max-model-len to cap the context window if you hit KV-cache memory limits.

According to recent reports, you can infer with this model using several inference providers through Hugging Face. You can see all the code snippets to consume here. Below you can see how to use with the OpenAI client.

Using the “:auto” suffix routes to your preferred provider in your settings; you can also use “cheapest” or “:fastest” as well. For this release, we cover the inference costs for 2 hours within the release for everyone.

Note: audio support in Inference Providers is work in progress and will be added shortly.

Sources indicate that you can use llama.cpp to run quantized versions of the model on limited hardware. Unsloth have quantized the model down to 1-bit precision, reducing VRAM consumption by 95% over the original model.

This starts an OpenAI-compatible server running at http://localhost:8080/v1 that you connect to in your preferred tool or clients. Heading there, you can start chatting with the model, and set it up with your favorite MCPs, pass in images or files conveniently and more!

Llama cpp also ships with a built-in UI that supports tools, mcp, and agentic workloads. Checkout Inkling running at 1-bit precision in the llama app:.

Inkling GGUFs are also runnable in Unsloth Studio with dynamic 1-bit GGUFs which retain ~74.2% of top-1% accuracy whilst being 86% smaller.

It has been revealed that pi is a minimal coding agent harness you can use with different language models. You can use Pi with either an inference engine server endpoint, such as llama.cpp, or with Inference Providers on Hugging Face by adding this to your ~/.pi/agent/models.json after installation.

Industry observers note that then you can start Pi in your project directory by calling pi and you’re good to go! In this demo, we give the model a hard math reasoning problem and it uses tools in pi to solve it.

Inkling is focused on broad multimodality reasoning and low token consumption, so try it out with document processing or audio tasks.

MTP adds extra layers to the model that predict several tokens at once, not just the next one. During inference, the extra layers act as “drafters” for speculative decoding, speeding up generation without compromising performance. With MTP, you get the exact same generated outputs, multipliers in generation speed-up at small memory cost in VRAM (due to serving the drafter). Thinking Machines also provides an MTP drafter with this release.

Sources indicate that we have prepared a small suite of reasoning questions from expert-level sources and university entrance exams. We have taken photos of the screen with watermarks in the screenshot to challenge the model. The model has solved all of them on high one, failed one in highest and medium reasoning efforts, so we provide a link to the model answers for you to check out how the model sounds and provide the number of tokens the model has taken to solve each of them. Note that we provide no system prompts in these vibe evals, and these reasoning questions should often be run with a good system prompt. The vibe eval images and results live here.

We have vibe-evaluated the model on some audio reasoning examples from BigBenchAudio and a few multilingual audio examples of GlobeAudio (Russian and Chinese multi-choice questions asking the last word in transcription). The BigBenchAudio examples we tested consist of logical statements and questions that either ask for formal fallacies (whether an argument can be logically deduced from the context given in audio) or object counting (stating multiple distinctive objects in the audio, asking for the total count of a certain one). Although this benchmark is initially made for speech-to-speech reasoning, we just want to see audio reasoning capabilities of this model. For GlobeAudio, the questions are relatively straightforward, so we ran with reasoning efforts of 0.1. We ran the first example of each language within GlobeAudio. All tests pass on all questions and efforts, except for second formal fallacy example on lowest effort, so we only provide the number of tokens spent in each question against reasoning effort. Vibe eval results and audio files live here.

If you would like to use Inkling for post-training, Thinking Machines have built tinker, a managed tool for post-training open weight models. Their cookbook includes examples for fine-tuning, distillation, and reinforcement learning.

According to recent reports, we post trained Inkling with tinker and OpenEnv, an agentic RL environment tool. We used the ECHO algorithm that trains a model to predict the environment without a verifier, applying next-token cross-entropy loss to tokens produced by the environment, alongside the usual policy learning on agent actions. This teaches the policy an implicit world model without requiring a separate model, teacher, or additional rollouts. Check out the example.

According to recent reports, if you’re working with Transformers Reinforcement Learning we suggest using Inkling as a teacher model in a knowledge distillation setup. For example, take advantage of Inkling’s document understanding abilities to improve the performance of a smaller (on-device) model. In this example, we use the transformer reinforcement learning library and the GOLD algorithm to distill knowledge. GOLD is handy here because it matches token logits between different tokenizers, so you can distill to any model on the hub.

Below you can find each Inkling checkpoint as well as their VRAM requirements.

Sources indicate that to deploy Inkling on a cluster, we provide SLURM scripts serving with transformers API, as well as how to query the endpoint with different modalities. You can adapt these scripts to vLLM or SGlang by updating the commands. These scripts live here.

You can deploy an Inkling-Small NVFP4 checkpoint using Inference Endpoints. We provide a pre-tested configuration to deploy it on 8 RTX PRO 6000s with an aggregated VRAM of·768 GB, giving large space for KV cache, costs $ 22 per hourly uptime (scales to zero when unused). To deploy, run hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4 using the Hugging Face CLI or alternatively, head to https://endpoints.huggingface.co/new/thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4. With this setup, you can get 140 TPS (single user inference, prepared for multi-user support with continuous batching).

Once the endpoint is up, you can query as follows.

Releasing a natively multimodal model (text, vision, and audio) open-weights is a huge step forward for the open-source AI ecosystem! Having variable and controllable thinking effort built into a MoE architecture makes Inkling a really attractive foundation for fine-tuning. Excited to test out the smaller 12B active parameter variant for local agent workflows at https://geometrydashsubzero.io.

Judge orders Kalshi to geofence four New Mexico tribes, clashing with CFTC access rule

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readwrite

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A federal judge in Newly introduced Mexico has blocked Kalshi's sports-event contracts on the lands of four tribes and ruled that the Commodity Exchange Act does not override tribal gaming law.
  • Kalshi has lost a key round against four Newly introduced Mexico tribes.
  • In a recent development, the tribes filed suit in May.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A federal judge in Newly introduced Mexico has blocked Kalshi's sports-event contracts on the lands of four tribes and ruled that the Commodity Exchange Act does not override tribal gaming law. The order requires geographic restrictions just as the CFTC is telling exchanges to drop them.

Kalshi has lost a key round against four Newly introduced Mexico tribes. On November 23, U.S. District Judge Margaret Strickland granted the Mescalero Apache Tribe and the Pueblos of Isleta, Pojoaque and Sandia a preliminary injunction that gives Kalshi 14 days to stop offering sports-event contracts on their lands. Strickland also denied its motion to dismiss, so the lawsuit now goes forward.

In a recent development, the tribes filed suit in May. They argue that Kalshi’s sports contracts violate the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (IGRA) and the tribes’ gaming compacts with Fresh Mexico. In their view, the contracts allow unauthorized wagering on tribal lands. Under IGRA, only tribes can authorize gaming on Indian lands.

Kalshi argued that the Commodity Exchange Act overrides both IGRA and the tribal-state compacts. Strickland disagreed. In her reading, that statute leaves the federal regulator without sole authority over the contracts, Tribal Business News reported. She also rejected Kalshi’s claim that IGRA’s injunction provision only allows suits against parties to a tribal-state compact.

Location was central to the ruling. To Strickland, a Kalshi user taking a sports position from a reservation is like a casino patron placing a bet. In her reasoning, the wager takes place wherever the bettor is physically located. The order cites a declaration from a Mescalero Apache Tribal Gaming Commission agent. She opened Kalshi’s app at several places on the reservation and found sports contracts on offer.

Kalshi cited the CFTC’s impartial-access requirements in opposing the injunction. Strickland ruled that the harm to tribal sovereignty outweighed the compliance burden. She also noted that Kalshi already uses geofencing elsewhere.

Recent findings suggest that that reasoning runs straight into the CFTC’s newly introduced directive on Regulation 38.151(b). The interpretation was published in the Federal Register on November 10, 2026, as document 2026-22863. The exchange therefore faces a court order to geofence alongside a regulatory push to remove such limits.

The legal theory also matters beyond New Mexico. The tribes rely on IGRA and their compacts, not state gambling law. As a result, CFTC preemption arguments may not protect Kalshi on tribal lands. If other tribes copy the approach, prediction-market operators could face geofencing obligations on reservations nationwide.

LATEST: Kalshi asserts that Native American Tribes have no regulatory authority over the activities of non-members, seeks the dismissal of the New Mexico Tribes' federal lawsuit asserting that Kalshi's offering of online sports-event contracts on Indian lands violates IGRA pic.twitter.com/gkLkM1x2KD.

— Daniel Wallach (@WALLACHLEGAL) June 25, 2026.

Tribal results have been mixed so far. Earlier in 2026, a federal judge in Wisconsin refused a similar injunction sought by the Ho-Chunk Nation. He did so even though he found the tribe likely to succeed on the merits. In California, District Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley granted two tribes a preliminary injunction after a Ninth Circuit ruling in September. It was the first injunction any tribe had won against Kalshi.

The timing leaves little room. The CFTC’s deadline for exchanges to drop domestic geographic restrictions lands only days before Kalshi must comply in New Mexico, SBC Americas reported.

#230195. Andy Clarke answers six questions about Standout Designs for the Web
