  • We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself.
  • But it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Docker is officially launching its new brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change.

Let’s start with the big picture. We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself. AI is creating possibilities that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago.

But it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control? Or, put more simply: how do we get to a point where we can actually trust agents?

That one seemingly simple yet infinitely complex question is why we’re here today, introducing you to a fresh Docker.

A new Docker, but a familiar story.

Ok, not exactly here, but once upon a time, a decade or so ago, the tech industry was at a similar inflection point. Digital transformation was the term du jour, promising a fresh way of engaging customers and powering the global economy. There was one big constraint, though: teams needed a better way to build, ship, and run software consistently across any environment.

Enter a company you might have heard of: Docker.

In a recent development, together with all of you, Docker built the standard trusted by millions of developers. For over a decade, developers have relied on us to make software portable, open, reproducible, and secure. Docker turned the frustration of “Well, it works on my machine!” into the assurance that “Yes, it works everywhere.”.

According to recent reports, today, of course, the challenge confronting us is new and evolving, and we all need to evolve with it. We cannot simply continue to do what we’ve always done and expect to succeed in this new era. That applies to business leaders, developers, tech companies, everyone. It certainly applies to Docker. That’s what this rebrand is about: evolving to meet the moment for our customers.

In a recent development, let me be unequivocal: this is not about leaving Docker’s legacy or heritage behind. We’ve spent more than a decade earning your trust. This is about building on that foundation, not replacing it.

The qualities you value us for aren’t changing. We’re still committed to openness and industry collaboration. We’re still, and always will be, developer-first. We’re still fanatical about simplicity, and about showing up everywhere you need us.

Recent findings suggest that on the product front, the containers you know and love aren’t going anywhere. Containers still play a huge role in the software development lifecycle. As long as that’s the case, Docker will continue leading the way.

Agents have introduced a upcoming problem. Containers isolate workloads. But agents aren’t workloads. Agents are actors.

Recent findings suggest that agents make their own decisions about what to run, what to access, and what to change. Developers and enterprises need solutions built specifically to isolate and govern them, so they can give those agents real autonomy without giving up control.

Docker’s next chapter is about delivering exactly that: security, isolation, and governance, so we can all trust agents to do meaningful work without feeling like we’re always one step from catastrophe.

In case I haven’t made it blindingly obvious yet, the newly introduced Docker is all about trust.

Trust Docker because our track record speaks for itself. Trust Docker because we’re proven, neutral, and secure. Trust Docker because it’s pretty darn clear you can’t trust the agents to manage themselves.

Trust us because we have a software supply chain that is already the standard for building securely. Trust us because nobody isolates agents where they run better than we do. Trust us because we’re taking a comprehensive approach to improving governance and minimizing risk across the entire enterprise.

Trust Docker because we’re not egotistical enough to think we can solve a challenge this big alone. Trust us because everything about our history, our heritage, and our actions over the past year tells you we’ll partner with the smartest and build alongside the best, and not create vendor lock-in.

Industry observers note that most of all, trust Docker because we’re not just talking the talk. We’ve got the goods to back it up: trusted supply chain for your agents to build from, trusted runtime to isolate your agents, and a trusted ecosystem to ensure all the layers of trust are covered, whether made by Docker or not.

As our product team innovated to meet the moment and our messaging in the market began to shift, one thing became clear: the speed and scale of evolution happening inside Docker called for an equally momentous evolution on the outside. Something that makes it unmistakably clear that it’s a latest day for Docker. Something that claims and demonstrates, loud and clear, for all the world to see, that Docker is not just about containers anymore.

Something, dare I say, whale sized.

I’m talking, of course, about our beloved Moby.

If you know Docker, then you know Moby, and if Docker is evolving, Moby should too. The only question was to how and to what extent? We looked at a lot of whales, folks. (I may or may not have been seeing whales in my sleep.) Ultimately, with the help of our friends at the strategic brand transformation tech giant, Motto, we landed on a newly introduced Moby for the new Docker.

Watch Moby’s transformation here:.

In many ways, Moby is a microcosm for Docker and the changes we’re making: the Moby you love and trust, evolved for a upcoming era. Just as the new Docker is no longer singularly defined by containers, neither is the new Moby.

We’ve got lots to show you. Poke around our new website. Find and engage with the new Docker brand on social media. And if you want to see what trust in the agentic era looks like in practice, try Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance. We’d love to hear what you think.

It has been revealed that wherever this newly introduced era takes us, Docker will always honor and cherish the trust you continue to place in us. Now, let’s go build what’s next.

Chief Marketing Officer, Docker.

Terri Avnaim is the CMO of Docker, where she leads global marketing and shapes the manufacturer’s positioning and go-to-market strategy for the agentic era.

  • In a recent development, give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge.
  • Two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that ALTK-Evolve and ACE both let an agent learn from its own trajectories. The difference is what they do with what they learn — and that decides the token bill.

In a recent development, give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge. It mis-paginates an API, resolves the wrong person, or returns a value when none was asked for. The model knows the APIs; what it hasn't internalized is how to use them reliably. That's learnable from the agent's own history.

Two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here). Both are a form of agentic memory — turning an agent's past trajectories into reusable lessons and feeding them back at inference time, no weight updates, no human labels. They even agree on the hard part. Where they part ways is delivery.

A note on words, because the two systems name things differently: we'll call the raw thing an agent learns a lesson. ACE organizes its lessons into one comprehensive, evolving playbook; we consolidate ours into individually retrievable guidelines. Same lessons, two containers.

Both systems refuse to compress.

It has been revealed that ACE names the failure modes precisely: brevity bias — optimization collapsing toward short, generic instructions — and context collapse — a model asked to rewrite its whole context each step summarizing the detail away. Its answer is to keep a rich, itemized playbook, with a helpful/harmful counter on every bullet, and let the model distill relevance at read time.

Sources indicate that we reach the same conclusion from the other direction. Every distinct guideline keeps a support count — how many independent episodes produced it — and we never summarize the store down to a handful of rules. A lesson five different tasks discovered is a different object from one that appeared once, and both are worth keeping.

So on the core question — should you compress an agent's hard-won lessons into a tidy summary? — ACE and ALTK-Evolve give the same answer: no. Count them, don't collapse them. ACE's per-bullet counters and our support counts are two spellings of the same idea.

Two places: how the memory is built, and how it's delivered — and it's the delivery difference that reveals up in the token bill.

Consolidation (how the store is built). ACE grows one playbook through a Generator → Reflector → Curator loop, applying incremental delta updates and de-duplicating by embedding. We cluster near-duplicate lessons and merge within a cluster, support-conserving — when several lessons merge, the survivor inherits their combined count, so the store shrinks without losing the record of how much experience backs each guideline. We also extract typed guidelines — strategy, recovery, and optimization — with causal attribution and provenance back to the source trajectory, and at subtask granularity, so a lesson learned on one app can transfer to another.

Sources indicate that delivery (what reaches the model at inference). This is the one that drives the numbers. ACE injects the comprehensive playbook on every step, the same way regardless of model or task. We treat delivery as a dial, not a constant: a small fixed core of high-support guidelines, extended per task with a handful selected for the task at hand (cosine or LLM-guided, priority-weighted) — or, when a model has the headroom to use it, the full consolidated set. The same lessons are available to both agents; the difference is that ACE always sends all of them, and we send however many a given model can actually use.

On AppWorld, with the same base ReAct agent, running both systems in-house:.

Sources indicate that on the strong model we're better on both metrics at ~40% of ACE's inference cost. On the weak model we edge ACE 56.0 to 54.8 — close enough that we call it a tie on accuracy (a repeat run of ours landed at 54.8, matching ACE almost exactly, which is within this benchmark's run-to-run noise) — at about one-seventh the cost.

A fair word on cost: ACE's own efficiency story is about building its context cheaply. Ours is on a different axis — serving it. Retrieving a few guidelines per task instead of injecting the whole playbook on every step is where the tokens go, and it's the direct consequence of the delivery difference above.

Sources indicate that where does the accuracy come from? The by-difficulty breakdown tells two different stories:.

Recent findings suggest that figure 1. Post-memory Task Goal Completion by difficulty, ours vs. ACE. On DeepSeek-V3.2 (right) we win Easy, Hard, and Overall; ACE only edges Medium. On gpt-oss-120b (left) ACE leads easy and medium, but per-task selection wins the hard tasks — and the aggregate. Each system improves from its own no-memory baseline (see the by-difficulty reference tables under Method notes below).

Industry observers note that the two models tell different stories. On gpt-oss-120b, ACE's full playbook has the edge on Easy and Medium — there's enough of the task solved by generic instruction-following that a comprehensive prompt helps more than it distracts. But on Hard tasks, where the model has to pick the right lesson rather than wade through all of them, curated retrieval pulls ahead — and that's the tier that decides the aggregate. On DeepSeek-V3.2 the story flips: the stronger model absorbs ACE's full playbook well enough to edge us on Medium, but we lead Easy, Hard, and Overall — with more capacity to spare, more lessons (delivered our way) keep helping instead of crowding each other out.

We give each model its best configuration — the full consolidated set for the strong model, selective retrieval for the weaker one, because a large context overwhelms a weaker model rather than helping it. (Exactly how much to inject, and how it scales across the capability spectrum, is the focus of our follow-up post.).

According to recent reports, both systems refuse to compress an agent's hard-won experience into a tidy summary — that part, we agree on. The difference is whether delivery is fixed or calibrated: ACE sends the whole playbook every step no matter what; we send however much of the guideline set a given model can actually use. That calibration is what bought the numbers above — same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of ACE's inference cost — and on the weaker model, it was the difference between guidance that helped and guidance that got in the way.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

In a recent development, appWorld test_normal, 168 tasks. A ReAct code agent (each step writes Python; the environment returns the output). TGC = Task Goal Completion; SGC = Scenario Goal Completion, which requires every variant of a scenario to pass. Memory is mined from train/dev only; results are single runs (pass@1), as is standard on this benchmark.

In a recent development, the ACE numbers are our own runs of the ACE agent, evaluated in-house on the same AppWorld splits and the same base models as ALTK-Evolve (DeepSeek-V3.2 and gpt-oss-120b). The ACE paper reports on a different base model (DeepSeek-V3.1), so running it ourselves keeps the comparison controlled for model and harness. Both systems are the same ReAct agent and differ only in the prompt template — which is why the two no-memory baselines differ (72.0 vs 79.8 TGC); we don't rest the comparison on that baseline gap, only on the claims a prompt tweak can't touch: same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of the tokens.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenJDK and Oracle disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) on November 17, and NGINX released fixes for two HTTP/2 flaws the next day. Docker began publishing fixed images for both in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog starting that same day.

What we know about Java4Shell is that it’s a memory-corruption bug in the Java runtime that can let an attacker with no credentials run code inside a Java application. Many container images contain a Java runtime, including application images that bundle their own, so it affects teams well beyond the ones that write Java.

Sources indicate that docker Hardened Images are the trusted foundation your applications should run on, because a flaw in the runtime inside an image is fixed only when that image is rebuilt, and Docker rebuilds its hardened images as soon as upstream fixes become available. Fixed images for the Amazon Corretto, SapMachine and Azul Zulu runtimes and for NGINX are in the catalog today, with Eclipse Temurin following as soon as Adoptium completes its fixed builds.

Sources indicate that to decode Base64 swiftly, the HotSpot JVM uses a hand-written routine built on AVX-512 instructions. That routine miscalculates a length when the input ends in unexpected padding and writes up to 62 bytes past the end of a buffer on the Java heap. Calif, the researchers who found it, turned that into heap disclosure and remote code execution.

Recent findings suggest that they demonstrated code execution before authentication against default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and after authentication against Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. They note there is no universal exploit: each application needs its own, and they have not published those. As of November 18 there are no public reports of exploitation in the wild.

It has been revealed that oracle rates the issue 8.1 (High) under CVSS 3.1. The researchers rate it 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0. CISA has issued an alert urging immediate patching.

All three of these must be true.

To check a host’s CPU, run this on the host or Kubernetes node. Hardened runtime images have no shell, so it will not run inside the container.

grep -m1 ‘^flags’ /proc/cpuinfo | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep -E ‘^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$’.

The host is affected if all four flags are printed.

Two other ways to check, for when a shell on the node is hard to get.

Ask the JVM. This works in hardened images:.

docker run –rm –entrypoint java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -w UseAVX.

Sources indicate that useAVX = 3 means the JVM is using AVX-512 on that host. Treat the host as affected until the full check notes otherwise. A value of 0 to 2 means AVX-512 is not in use. On ARM64 nothing is printed. The answer applies only to the host the command ran on.

Ask Kubernetes. kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type highlights the architecture and instance type of every node. If you run Node Feature Discovery, nodes with the instruction set carry the label feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-cpuid.AVX512VBMI=true.

Sources indicate that check build runners and CI workers as well. They run Java, and they talk to the network.

If you run it, treat it as affected and keep the flag set. We recommend moving to Java 25 or updating to Java 27. Application images that bundle Java, such as Keycloak, Jenkins, Kafka, Elasticsearch and Solr.

It has been revealed that they follow the bundled runtime, which for many of them is Temurin, and they are rebuilt once the runtime they use is fixed. Until then, set the flag yourself.

Set the mitigation flag yourself on every JVM that is still waiting for a fixed runtime, and check what each image already sets before you do. Treat the flag as a stopgap, because a JVM is protected only if the flag reaches it when it starts, and a deployment setting or a start script can override it or drop it. A fixed runtime is the only thing that closes the glitch, so move to the fixed image as soon as it is published.

Industry observers note that the CPU check and the mitigation flag in the steps below apply to any image that runs a HotSpot-based OpenJDK build. The version strings in this post come from Docker Hardened Images, so for an image from another source, confirm the fixed build in that source’s advisory.

The fixed build can only come from whoever builds your image, because the Java runtime and the system packages your application runs on come from the image underneath it. That dependency is why a hardened image is a necessary step toward a trusted software supply chain. With Docker Hardened Images, tracking each vendor’s fix and rebuilding on it is work Docker does for you. The images are minimal and secure by default, and they are built to serve as a trusted and verifiable upstream for your builds. You can move a service onto one by following the migration guide.

In a recent development, A container often runs more than one JVM, for example when a build tool forks a JVM for tests, an application server starts helper processes or a CI agent starts a JVM for every build step. The flag protects only the JVMs that receive it, and the variable most people reach for first is JAVA_OPTS, which Java does not read at all.

The JVM itself, however it is started. Includes javac, keytool and other JDK tools.

Yes, through the inherited environment.

In a recent development, A Java 8 JVM that sees it refuses to start. Some DHI FIPS images already set this variable.

Only the java launcher, Java 9 and later.

Yes, when the child is started with java.

Sources indicate that not read by javac, keytool or other JDK tools. DHI FIPS images set it. Java 8 ignores it.

Nothing downstream inherits it.

JAVA_OPTS, JENKINS_JAVA_OPTS, MAVEN_OPTS, ES_JAVA_OPTS and similar.

A start script, which copies the value onto one java command line.

According to recent reports, each script has its own rules. If nothing in the image reads the variable, it does nothing.

Recent findings suggest that five rules follow from that table. We tested each on DHI images.

JAVA_OPTS only works where a script reads it. With JAVA_OPTS=”-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics” set and a plain java command, the intrinsic stays on. No warning is printed.

In a recent development, A flag on the command line stops at that process. We started a JVM with the flag on its command line and had it start a second JVM. The child ran with the intrinsic on. With JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS in the environment, the child ran with it off. A child started with a cleared environment gets nothing, whichever variable you use.

According to recent reports, check what the image already sets before you set anything. In Docker and Kubernetes, your value replaces the image’s value. It is not appended.

docker inspect –format ‘{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}’ \  | grep -E ‘^(JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS|JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS)=’.

Sources indicate that our FIPS images use these variables to configure the FIPS provider. dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:21-fips sets both. When we replaced its JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS with only the flag, the JVM started normally, but the org.bouncycastle.fips.approved_only property was gone. Nothing warned us. If the command prints a value, copy it and add the flag at the end:.

env:  – name: JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS    value: “ -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics”.

Not every FIPS image uses the same variables, so run the check for each image.

Keep JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS away from Java 8. Java 8 is not affected and does not know the flag:.

Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -XX:-UseBASE64IntrinsicsUnrecognized VM option ‘UseBASE64Intrinsics’Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.

It has been revealed that adding -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions to the variable does not help on Java 8. Where Java 8 shares an environment with a newer Java, either scope the variable to the containers that need it or use JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS, which Java 8 ignores. Java 11 accepts the flag, so it is harmless there.

Sources indicate that verify the process, not the environment. Running java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version inside a container starts a new JVM. It tells you what the environment gives a new JVM, not what the JVM already serving traffic was started with. For the running process, use the startup log line. JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS prints one too, starting with NOTE: Picked up. In an image that includes the JDK you can also ask the process directly:.

jcmd VM.flags | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics.

The answer must be -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. If the flag reached the JVM through an environment variable, it will not show in the process’s command line, so ps is not a reliable check.

Some applications discard these variables on purpose. Elasticsearch’s start script, for example, ignores JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and expects ES_JAVA_OPTS. Check your application’s documentation.

According to recent reports, pull the new image and redeploy. Four things catch people out:.

Recent findings suggest that then confirm with java -version that what is running reports a fixed build. After that, remove the flag from every place you set it.

The day after Java4Shell, NGINX released fixes for two memory errors in the way it handles HTTP/2 connections, tracked as CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. A crafted request can crash a worker process, and where an attacker gets past the operating system’s memory protections it can run code inside that worker. Both flaws need HTTP/2 to be enabled on the server, and the same releases fix other NGINX issues that do not depend on HTTP/2, so enhancement either way.

The Docker Hardened Images for NGINX were rebuilt on NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 and published on November 18, the same day as the upstream release. To patch, pull the image again and redeploy, and move any tag pinned to an older exact version to a fixed one. nginx -v prints the version, and the fixed ones are 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. The notes on pull policy, mirrors and your own images in the section above apply to NGINX images in the same way.

The vulnerable code is in the Java runtime inside the image, and if you are using DHI, shipping the fix becomes our job. Whether that code can be reached in your deployment depends on things an image cannot see: the CPU it is scheduled onto, the options you start it with, the processes it starts, and the traffic you send it.

With Docker Hardened Images, Docker will.

Tell you what we know, and update this post.

Three jobs stay with you whichever image you run.

It was only four weeks ago that the news was PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Calif, the security research team that found Java4Shell and helped find PHP2Shell, says it used AI to find this flaw in about an hour and that the whole effort cost less than $200 in tokens. When a flaw like this can be found and weaponized at that price, it is reasonable to expect more of them.

If you lead a team or answer for how your organization builds and ships software, the questions after a week like this one are whether you were exposed and how rapidly you can prove you were not. It is imperative to have a trusted foundation in place before the next flaw appears, and Docker Hardened Images is that foundation to adopt. This week Docker began publishing fixed Java and NGINX images to the catalog within a day of each disclosure, with the images still waiting listed in the status table above. Each image ships with a signed SBOM and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, so you have a record of what it contains and how it was built.

The Docker Hardened Images catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, and moving one of your services onto a hardened image typically means changing one line in its Dockerfile. If you are not building on Docker Hardened Images yet, start today.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Update resolves work-blocking popup, but affected customers may need an administrator command prompt to install it.

Industry observers note that microsoft has released a fix for a baffling bug that threw a blank window over Office applications and brought work to a standstill. The problem appeared when users launched an affected Office app, which could display an empty dialog box with no text and no buttons.

Because the dialog offered no way to close it, some users were locked out of their work entirely, unable to continue until the glitch was resolved.

The good news is that there's an enhancement to fix the problem – version 2611, build 16.0.20625.20142. The bad news is that you might not be able to launch the applications to perform the update because of that blank dialog window.

Microsoft instructs affected customers to save their work, close all Office applications, and open Command Prompt as administrator. They can then force the update with: "%programfiles%\Common Files\Microsoft Shared\ClickToRun\officec2rclient.exe" /update user updatetoversion=16.0.20625.20142.

The glitch affects a swathe of Microsoft 365 products – Excel, Word, Outlook, PowerPoint, Access, and OneNote.

People reported the problem on Microsoft's forums, where volunteer moderator Stefan Blom noted that "this seems to be a common error at the moment" and suggested users try an Office repair or the more thorough Online Repair.

Sources indicate that online Repair reinstalls Office, however, some users reported activation and sign-in problems alongside the blank windows, which may hint at the cause. Microsoft has yet to elucidate.

Other users found that rolling back Office resolved the concern, while several reported that signing in with another application, such as Edge, fixed things.

For administrators preparing fleets of devices, a dialog that blocks first use creates another deployment headache. One user with E3 licensing reported: "We can't just hand off a staged machine without getting call[s] that our fresh users can't get Office to work because of the blank licensing window.".

Microsoft has shared a fix for the problem, but has not stated which versions of its productivity applications were affected, nor has it explained what went wrong.

It has been revealed that the fix is welcome. An explanation of how Office ended up blocking people with a window containing nothing at all would be welcome too. ®.

Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway: A fully-managed ingress solution for ECS services

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck.
  • Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.
  • ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck. For every new service, teams must provision and connect Application Load Balancers (ALBs), AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates, AWS WAF web ACLs, and security groups, then keep those resources in sync as services scale, patch, or operate. This per-service overhead slows down deployment velocity and increases the risk of configuration drift across an organization.

Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.

ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.

According to recent reports, ECS Gateway offers host-based routing using ALBs and enables up to 25 services to share a single ALB, optimizing infrastructure costs. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs as capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. Each service receives a unique DNS hostname, giving your teams a ready-to-use endpoint the moment provisioning completes.

A first look at ECS Gateway In the ECS console, platform team can create a gateway and sets its configuration. The infrastructure role is an IAM role that ECS assumes to provision and manage networking resources such as ALBs, security groups, and certificates in your account. To create a gateway, provide a gateway name and select an infrastructure role. You can optionally associate the gateway with ECS clusters during creation or later.

According to recent reports, choose a load balancing scheme, either public or VPC-internal traffic routing. Under Additional Settings, you can also set up a listener, port, maximum count of load balancers the gateway can scale to, and a web ACL lets you protect your web applications. Some settings, including the name, scheme, VPC, subnets, IP address type, listener protocol and port cannot be changed after gateway creation.

Using AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), call CreateGateway with a name (unique per account), an infrastructure role, and a configuration object. No infrastructure is provisioned until a service connects with a gateway connector.

Once the gateway is created, you can take a look at the detailed configuration, gateway routes, load balancers, and associated clusters.

Now associate the gateway with one or more clusters (many-to-many), to make it available to ECS services on those clusters.

Use AssociateGatewayWithCluster to make the gateway available to services on a cluster:.

Recent findings suggest that to create and manage the ECS Gateway programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Gateway documentation.

ECS Gateway:Behind the scenesA gateway can be associated with up to 10,000 clusters, and a single cluster supports up to five gateway associations. This many-to-many relationship gives platform teams the flexibility to share a gateway across environments or assign multiple gateways (for example, public and private) to a single cluster.

Platform teams can control access by choosing which gateways to associate with which clusters. For additional control, use IAM policies to restrict who can deploy services to specific clusters.

Industry observers note that application teams add the gateway connector to each service definition in CreateService or UpdateService. If you have an existing ECS service with its own load balancer, you can adopt ECS Gateway incrementally by calling UpdateService to add a gateway connector. Both ingress paths remain available, allowing you to validate the gateway connection before removing the existing load balancer configuration.

Sources indicate that at deployment time, Amazon ECS evaluates the gateways associated with the cluster and connects the service to every compatible gateway. A gateway is compatible when its access type matches the service’s connector filter, it is in the same VPC as the service, and it covers all Availability Zones used by the service’s configured subnets.

For each connection, Amazon ECS assigns the service to an ALB with available capacity and provisions the per-service resources: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, a listener rule routing traffic for that hostname to the service target group, and a service security group allowing inbound traffic only from the ALB security group. If no existing ALB has capacity, ECS creates a upcoming one (up to maxAlbCount referring to quota limit). Once provisioning completes, the gateway route becomes ACTIVE, and the service URL is ready to receive traffic.

ECS Gateway handles common operational scenarios automatically:.

Things to Know Here are a few vital details to keep in mind:.

Industry observers note that now available Amazon ECS Gateway is available now in all commercial AWS Regions where ECS is available at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when services connect to a gateway, including applicable ALB charges, CloudWatch logs and metrics, ACM certificates, and data transfer charges. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Pricing page.

To get started, create your first gateway today in the ECS console, and send feedback to AWS re:Post for ECS or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Introducing OlmoEarth embeddings: Custom embedding exports from OlmoEarth Studio for downstream analysis

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth | 📊 Documentation: https://docs.olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings | 💻 Learn more about OlmoEarth: https://allenai.org/olmoearth.
  • Sources indicate that olmoEarth Studio, our platform for building Earth observation models, now lets you compute and export embedding vectors—compact numerical representations of Earth-observation data produced by our open source OlmoEarth foundation models.
  • Embeddings are a fast, cost-effective entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they support a wide range of downstream tasks, from similarity search to segmentation to unsupervised exploration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth | 📊 Documentation: https://docs.olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings | 💻 Learn more about OlmoEarth: https://allenai.org/olmoearth.

Sources indicate that olmoEarth Studio, our platform for building Earth observation models, now lets you compute and export embedding vectors—compact numerical representations of Earth-observation data produced by our open source OlmoEarth foundation models. The source code and model weights are publicly available alongside the research paper, so the community can inspect exactly how these embeddings are generated.

Embeddings are a fast, cost-effective entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they support a wide range of downstream tasks, from similarity search to segmentation to unsupervised exploration. Locations with similar surface characteristics end up with similar vectors; locations that differ land far apart. OlmoEarth embeddings have shown strong performance in our own benchmarking and in independent evaluations. The exported Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) are lightweight and easy to share. Choose your area of interest, time range, encoder variant, resolution, and imagery sources via the Studio UI or API, and get back a COG you can use however you like. If your application requires higher performance, Studio also supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

It has been revealed that custom-computed embeddings are now available for users of OlmoEarth Studio. Reach out if you're interested in gaining access. Instructions for using the publicly available OlmoEarth models to compute your own embeddings are available here.

In a recent development, global structure in OlmoEarth embeddings from seasonal Sentinel-2 imagery across 1.1M samples. Colors indicate 15 k-means clusters in a PCA-reduced embedding space.

In a recent development, computing embeddings follows the same workflow as any other prediction in Studio. First configure a model and run it, and then download the results. Several parameters tailor the output:.

Different visualization options applied to the same embedding raster.

It has been revealed that studio delivers a COG with one band per embedding dimension. Vectors are stored as signed 8-bit integers (int8). Values range from -127 to +127, with -128 reserved for nodata. To recover floating-point vectors, see dequantize_embeddings in olmoearth_pretrain.

Because everything is computed on demand rather than pulled from a pre-computed global archive, your embeddings reflect exactly the conditions you care about. You can generate monthly embeddings to capture seasonal dynamics, not just annual snapshots.

Sources indicate that the examples below all use OlmoEarth-v1-Tiny (192-dim) embeddings at 40-meter resolution with Sentinel-2 L2A composites (annual for most examples; monthly for change detection). Tiny is a lightweight encoder but still highly performant; for your own applications, you can swap it for a larger variant at the cost of higher compute and storage.

Sources indicate that pick a query pixel, extract its embedding, and compute cosine similarity against every other pixel. The result is a heatmap showing where the landscape looks most and least like your query pixel.

Industry observers note that this query sits near the Merced urban center in California. Urban fabric and road corridors light up coherently while agricultural parcels stay dark. The model distinguishes built-up surfaces from cropland without any labels.

Switching the query to a small agricultural window, we define the query vector as the mean of the embedding vectors over that window, then pull Sentinel-2 imagery at the highest- and lowest-similarity locations to see what the model treats as similar and dissimilar.

In a recent development, the most similar patches (0.89 and above) are all agricultural parcels with irrigated fields. The least similar (around zero) are an airport with surrounding bare ground, a reservoir with dry terrain, and arid rangeland. No training data, no labels, just a dot product in embedding space.

Similarity search tells you "where is it like this?" but sometimes you need discrete labels across a region. Because the representations are already rich, a simple linear classifier can produce a wall-to-wall land-cover map from very few labeled pixels.

Industry observers note that to test this, we labeled just 60 pixels (20 per class) over Ca Mau, Vietnam, a coastal mangrove region. Using ESA WorldCover 2021 as the label source for three classes (mangrove, water, other), we randomly sampled 20 pixels per class, trained a logistic regression with per-feature standardization, and predicted every pixel in the region.

It has been revealed that from 60 labeled pixels, the classifier produces a coherent map with weighted F1 = 0.84. Mangrove stands, tidal channels, and open water are delineated across the entire region. The classifier saturates quickly: increasing from 30 to 300 labels barely changes accuracy, because the embeddings are doing most of the heavy lifting.

The core of the analysis is a few lines of Python:.

Sources indicate that this is a linear probe, a standard evaluation for foundation models. The fact that a logistic regression over 192 dimensions recovers land-cover boundaries from so few labels means the Tiny encoder has organized these ecological distinctions during pretraining. Larger variants (Base, 768-dim) encode even richer representations.

If you have ground-truth polygons, field survey points, or a coarse existing map, you can train a similar classifier and produce a wall-to-wall map for your own region of interest.

Because Studio can generate embeddings at any temporal resolution (monthly through annual), you can compare two time periods directly to identify where surface conditions have changed. Below, we computed monthly Sentinel-2 embeddings for the same region in September 2023 and September 2024 and measured per-pixel cosine distance. The Park Fire (July-September 2024) burn scar in Butte County, California lights up immediately.

No labels or training required—just two embedding COGs and a few lines of Python.

Sometimes you have no query location or reference labels. You just want to understand what structure exists in the embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a clean way to do this: reduce to three dimensions, map to R/G/B, and display as a false-color image. Similar embeddings get similar colors automatically.

In a recent development, flevoland, in the Netherlands, is a reclaimed polder landscape with a regular grid of agricultural parcels. The PCA false-color image reproduces those boundaries with high fidelity. Different crop types, water bodies, and urban areas each get distinct hues. The embedding has internalized landscape structure without ever being told what a parcel or crop is.

This kind of unsupervised view is a quick way to see what structure the model has picked up across your area of interest.

Sources indicate that similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA exploration are simple operations on standard raster data that run in seconds. The power comes from the embeddings: learned representations that compress earth observation data into vectors capturing rich information about each location from many sensors and millions of training examples.

Industry observers note that custom embedding exports are available now. Create a project, configure an embeddings model, and compute your embeddings. The exported GeoTIFF works with any geospatial tool: QGIS, GDAL, rasterio, or your own scripts. For end-to-end code reproducing the examples in this post, see the embeddings tutorial, which includes working code for similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA visualization. To get hands-on without any local setup, try the Colab notebook.

The examples in this post all use frozen embeddings with no task-specific training. Embeddings are a great entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they enable fast, cost-effective generation of results, work well in resource-constrained environments, and are easy to share. For applications that require higher performance, OlmoEarth Studio also supports SFT, training a task-specific model head on your own labels, which typically outperforms linear probes on frozen features.

It has been revealed that while we are always working to improve our pretraining approaches, it's vital to check the quality of the embeddings for your use case using some of the techniques described above. Performance also depends on the quality of the input imagery—persistent cloud cover, atmospheric artifacts, or missing observations in the composite period can affect the resulting vectors.

According to recent reports, sentinel-2 L2A imagery from the European Space Agency, accessed via Microsoft Planetary Computer. ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 for mangrove reference. The global clustering visualization uses OlmoEarth-v1-Base (768-dim) with seasonal Sentinel-2 composites at patch size 8, instance-level embeddings over 1.1M pretraining samples.

#230143. Prove your AI agent guardrails work

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3132 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Docker ↗ Open Full Page

Prove your AI agent guardrails work

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3132 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You ask a coding agent to clean up one repository.
  • Industry observers note that in Sandboxing Claude and MCP, Hrittik walked through running Claude Code and an MCP server inside Docker Sandboxes using its command-line interface, sbx.
  • Models and providers will change, but the access rules still need to hold.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You ask a coding agent to clean up one repository. If it has broad permissions, it may also reach your home directory, use your development credentials, and send requests to services you never approved. That gap between the task and the access you grant can turn a routine coding session into a data leak or lost work.

Industry observers note that in Sandboxing Claude and MCP, Hrittik walked through running Claude Code and an MCP server inside Docker Sandboxes using its command-line interface, sbx. That walkthrough started with outbound access blocked, allowed the endpoints needed for the task, and inspected requests to other destinations, including telemetry. The useful part was seeing an actual request fail at the network boundary.

Now extend that workflow to a team. Models and providers will change, but the access rules still need to hold. A sandbox limits what an agent can reach on one machine. Organization governance adds shared rules, a managed way to run agents, and records of policy decisions. In this post, we’ll look at how one laptop can affect the whole organization, review two reported incidents, and connect them to four Docker controls: network policy, filesystem policy, managed credentials, and MCP access. Then we’ll test the network and filesystem controls with a simple bank administrator demo.

According to recent reports, if an agent exposes a developer’s SSH key or cloud token, every system that accepts that credential may need investigation. The security team must work out what left the machine, replace or revoke exposed credentials, and check whether anyone used them. Deleted work can also halt development. Keep backups of work that has not yet reached the repository.

The compliance consequences depend on the data and the organization. A personal data breach can trigger GDPR notification duties, subject to the applicable risk thresholds. HIPAA has separate requirements for covered entities and business associates following breaches of unsecured protected health information. India’s DPDP framework also includes breach duties, but those provisions are scheduled to take effect in May 2027. For a SOC 2 examination, the question is whether the relevant controls operate as described. SOC 2 is not a breach-notification law.

Data sovereignty adds another question: where does the data go, and who controls it? Before approving a model API endpoint, establish where prompts and outputs are processed and stored, who can access them, and which contracts and laws apply. A provider’s nationality alone does not answer those questions. Network policy can restrict the destination, but it cannot prove how the provider handles data after receiving it.

Sources indicate that this gets harder when developers choose and configure agents independently. A rule on one laptop may be missing on the next. An ignore file may stop one component from reading a file while another component includes it in an upload. Written policy needs matching controls in the software that runs the agent.

It has been revealed that in July 2026, developers reported two incidents where a coding agent went far beyond its task. In one, data left the machine. In the other, files were deleted from it.

In an X post that has since been deleted, a user remarked Grok had uploaded their entire user directory, including SSH keys, a password manager database, and personal files. A Hacker News discussion brought wider attention to the claim. The home-directory claim remains the user’s account. The separate investigation below tested repository uploads.

In a recent development, researcher Cereblab intercepted Grok Build CLI traffic and found a background upload running alongside the coding task. In a test with a 12 GB repository, about 5.1 GiB had left the machine before the capture stopped, and the upload was still running. The data went to Google Cloud Storage. Fake secrets planted in the repository also appeared in the traffic without being hidden. At the time, turning off “Improve the model” did not stop the repository uploads.

In a recent development, in a reproducible follow-up, the researcher rebuilt the repository from a captured Git bundle, an archive of tracked files and Git history. The bundle included files the agent had been told not to read. Telling the model not to read a file didn’t stop the CLI from packaging and uploading it in the background.

There was a subsequent change. The researcher’s updated timeline indicates whole-repository uploading was disabled server-side on July 13 and remained off when retested on July 22.

The fix does not change the lesson. A coding agent is more than the model. It includes the CLI and any background processes, and those can act without the model asking. Give the whole application only the access its task needs. This is the principle of least privilege.

On July 10, Matt Shumer wrote: “GPT-5.6-Sol just accidentally deleted almost ALL of my Mac’s files.” He shared the agent’s acknowledgment and confirmed that Full Access was enabled. His follow-up described the loss of his home directory.

A separate experiment shows why blocking one command is a fragile response. Developer LinearUncle reported that, after a plugin blocked rm, the agent tried unlink, find -delete, and apply_patch. A later attempt to move files to Trash through the GUI failed on permissions; a call to Node’s fs.unlink succeeded. The plugin’s own documentation describes it as an additional guardrail and recommends sandboxing and backups.

The common matter is excessive access. A model can choose a different tool, and a background process can run outside the model’s visible workflow. Filesystem and network boundaries need to constrain both.

Docker Sandboxes runs each agent in a microVM, a lightweight virtual machine with its own Linux kernel and Docker Engine. A workspace mount shares a host directory with the sandbox. A proxy on the host checks outgoing connections against network policy. The isolation documentation explains these boundaries.

It has been revealed that that gives a developer a useful starting point. Share the project needed for the task, restrict outbound access, and inspect failures before adding permissions. Unnecessary telemetry endpoints can remain blocked while the required model and package services are allowed.

Choose mounts carefully. A writable mount shares real host files, so changes and deletions inside it affect your machine. Check additional mounts too, including shared agent skills where enabled. Docker’s clone mode gives the agent a private copy of a Git repository so you can review its commits before bringing them back. Isolation limits access, but files in a writable host mount still need backups. Clone mode still exposes the host repository for reading, including ignored files. Keep secrets outside it.

According to recent reports, local settings leave a rollout problem. A teammate can choose different rules or run an agent directly on the host. The organization needs a managed way to run agents, a way to require its use, and visibility into which sessions it covers.

The diagram below shows how organization and team policies reach managed sandbox sessions, where access checks occur, and how policy decisions feed audit records.

According to recent reports, figure 1. Organization and team policies govern access for enrolled, licensed sandbox sessions.

Docker AI Governance lets administrators manage sandbox rules and MCP access centrally. MCP, short for Model Context Protocol, connects agents to tools and data sources. Administrators define policies in Docker Home. On developer machines, sandbox mount checks, the host proxy, and Docker’s MCP gateway enforce the relevant rules. This gives teams shared access rules and records they can review when something goes wrong.

In a recent development, network policies allow or deny destinations such as domain names, IP addresses, and IP ranges written in CIDR notation. For a restricted workflow, start with access denied and allow only the destinations the task needs. Under organization governance, local allow rules cannot grant extra access. Deny rules win, and developers can add local network restrictions.

This can block a background upload to an unapproved destination. But an approved hostname may still handle several kinds of traffic. In the Grok investigation, model requests and storage uploads used different URL paths on the same hostname, so a hostname-only allow rule would not distinguish them. Docker AI Governance now supports more granular network policies: on an allowed host, rules can match the HTTP method, URL path, and query parameters. For example, a policy can permit an agent to open a GitHub pull request while blocking requests to merge it. These finer-grained rules complement filesystem restrictions, which limit the data an application can collect and send.

It has been revealed that filesystem policies control which host paths may be mounted. A writable mount needs both read and write permission; a read-only mount needs read. If a filesystem deny rule and an allow rule match the same request, the deny wins. The decision happens when the sandbox is created. Once a writable mount exists, the agent can modify or delete files within it, regardless of whether it uses rm, a patch tool, or a programming language API.

For proxy-managed credentials, the host proxy adds authentication to outbound requests. The agent can authenticate to an approved service without receiving the raw secret inside the microVM. Credentials can also be scoped to a named sandbox.

Recent findings suggest that this reduces the need to paste API tokens into prompts or store them in the workspace. The protection applies to proxy-managed credentials. A real token placed in an environment variable, a mounted file, or a passthrough login response may still be visible inside the sandbox. Limit what each credential can access and how long it stays valid. Storing a token through the proxy does not change its permissions or expiry.

According to recent reports, MCP access policies govern server registration and subsequent requests through Docker’s MCP gateway. With MCP enforcement active, access requires an explicit permit, and a forbid rule overrides it. Administrators can control tool calls, resource reads, and prompt retrieval, rather than treating an approved server as permission to do everything it offers.

Registration and use are separate decisions. Blocking new registrations does not stop access to a server that is already registered. Rules checked on each request handle that case. Direct connections to remote MCP servers also need network controls because they bypass Docker’s gateway. Check where each server runs too: local stdio servers run on the host, outside the sandbox VM. Their host access needs separate review.

The next diagram summarizes the four controls to review together: network access, host mounts, managed credentials, and MCP tools.

Figure 2. Network, filesystem, credentials, and MCP controls apply to the whole agent application.

Recent findings suggest that administrators manage organization and team policies in Docker Home. Group mapping can keep Docker teams in sync with the organization’s identity provider. Policy updates take up to five minutes to reach developer machines. Network changes then apply to newly introduced requests. Filesystem changes require removing and recreating affected sandboxes because existing mounts keep their original access.

Sign-in enforcement is also part of deployment. IT distributes it through endpoint management so developers must authenticate as members of an approved organization. This prevents personal-account bypass within sbx. Your endpoint controls also need to cover agents introduced outside that managed workflow.

Suppose you are a bank administrator. Developers want to use coding agents, and you need to enforce the bank’s access rules. Let’s keep the demo to two simple requirements:.

In a recent development, we’ll use fictional logs and a shell sandbox to check both boundaries without needing a model API. The results below describe what to expect when you run the demo.

Industry observers note that install sbx on macOS or Linux and sign in with an AI Governance licensed test user. You’ll also need permission to manage policies and audit delivery in a test organization:.

Run these commands in your host terminal to create a workspace and a separate directory containing a fictional bank log:.

Sources indicate that next, enable AI Governance for your organization. In Docker Home, open AI Platform → Manage and turn on AI Governance:.

According to recent reports, figure 3. Enable AI Governance in Docker Home before configuring organization policies.

Next, create the bank’s network and filesystem access rules.

First, let’s look at network access. In a bank, you don’t want employees’ coding agents connecting to just any website. For this demo, we’ll allow the sandbox to reach only hrittikhere.com (standing in for the bank’s website) over HTTPS.

Once AI Governance is enabled, open AI Platform → Network access → Create policy and enter the following values:.

With this as the only applicable network allow rule, all other destinations remain blocked by default.

In a recent development, the curl checks below request headers without following redirects, so they need only hrittikhere.com:443. If you later add -L to follow a redirect to www.hrittikhere.com, allow that exact hostname on port 443 as well.

Recent findings suggest that next, let’s protect the bank’s logs. Employees may need a coding agent to work on a project, but that agent should not be able to read or modify sensitive logs in the home directory. We’ll allow access to the demo workspace and block access to bank-logs.

Open AI Platform → Filesystem access → Create policy.

Note: Use ~ in policy paths, not $HOME; environment variables are not expanded by the policy engine.

Sources indicate that first, allow the project workspace with the values below. A writable workspace needs both Read and Write permissions for sandbox creation to succeed:.

In the same bank-demo-filesystem policy, add a second rule named bank-demo-logs to deny access to the protected logs:.

~/sbx-bank-demo/bank-logs~/sbx-bank-demo/bank-logs/**.

The workspace allow rule covers workspace and its descendants; it does not include the sibling bank-logs directory. The logs are protected by the explicit deny rule.

Save the policies. You can also check their rules and scope in the Platform UI. Allow up to five minutes for policy sync, then inspect the active rules:.

Industry observers note that figure 6. Active organization rules allow hrittikhere.com:443 and the workspace, and deny bank-logs mounts.

Create a fresh sandbox with only the approved workspace:.

From the host terminal, run the following requests inside the sandbox. The –max-time 15 option caps each request at 15 seconds, so a stalled request times out instead of hanging:.

Figure 8. The request to example.com returns HTTP 403; the network log confirms the policy decision.

You can also check the network log to confirm that the failure came from policy enforcement:.

The network log distinguishes allowed traffic from requests blocked by policy:.

Figure 9. The network log records hrittikhere.com:443 as allowed and example.com:443 as blocked.

Run both commands below from your host terminal so $HOME expands to the same host path. First read the fictional log on the host, then request that path inside the sandbox:.

Recent findings suggest that figure 10. The host can read the fictional bank log.

Industry observers note that the sandbox command should fail with “No such file or directory” because bank-logs is not mounted. This checks filesystem isolation; the next command tests mount-policy enforcement:.

Figure 11. The unmounted bank-logs path returns “No such file or directory” inside the sandbox.

Now check whether a developer could add the logs as a read-only mount:.

Creation should fail with a mount policy denied error:.

Recent findings suggest that figure 12. The bank-demo-logs rule rejects the read-only mount with a Read policy denial.

According to recent reports, A read-only mount still requires Read permission. The bank-demo-logs rule denies Read, so :ro does not bypass the policy.

You can also review the policy decisions in the Docker Home UI under AI Platform → Audit logs → Audit events. Filter by the test user and time, then inspect the denied mount request for bank-logs. Look for filesystem_mount, the deny decision, the resource path, and the user. If Cloud delivery was disabled during the test, enable it and repeat the mount request.

Industry observers note that figure 13. Audit events record the denied bank-logs mount and allowed workspace mounts.

These audit records capture governance decisions, not every file operation or the agent’s prompts and output. sbx policy log highlights network traffic; use the audit view for the mount decision. Docker also supports local JSONL audit files and Cloud delivery for hosted search, CSV export, and SIEM forwarding.

The bank now has a simple access-control check: the approved site is reachable, an unapproved site is blocked, and protected logs cannot be read or mounted. This supports the bank’s compliance work; it does not establish compliance on its own.

After reviewing the results, remove the sandbox:.

You can then remove the fictional demo files and the test policies.

Putting AI governance policies in place is only the first step. The real challenge is making sure those policies are practical, consistently enforced, and easy to verify as more developers start using coding agents. A few good practices can help teams reduce unnecessary access, apply the right restrictions to different workloads, and maintain visibility into what agents are doing. Here are five recommendations to keep in mind when rolling out Docker AI Governance across your organization:.

The same questions apply when agents run in continuous integration (CI) jobs or other environments: which host files can they access, which services can they reach, and which credentials can they use? Check which controls each environment supports and repeat the tests there. A policy on a developer’s laptop does not automatically protect an unrelated container or production cluster.

For security teams, useful evidence connects a licensed, signed-in user to an active policy, a blocked action, and a record they can find. Check sign-in enforcement and license coverage alongside policy. An empty audit dashboard may mean some sessions were never covered.

Sandboxing limits an agent’s access on one machine. Governance applies shared rules to managed sessions across the organization. Providers will fix individual failures, but the next failure may look different. Limit which files, services, and credentials it can affect, then test those limits and check the records.

Recent findings suggest that start with the local sandboxing walkthrough, inspect your rules with sbx policy ls, and run the bank demo with your platform or security team. Use the Docker AI Governance documentation and announcement to plan a small rollout. Expand it after you have checked both the blocked actions and the audit records.

Docker rolls out a fresh brand built on trust. Learn why Docker is evolving for AI agents, what stays the same, and how to run agents securely with Docker.

Recent findings suggest that coding agents can reach more than their task needs. See how Docker AI Governance controls network, filesystem, credential, and MCP access, then test it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities.
  • It has been revealed that using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process.
  • According to recent reports, continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting concerns by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define.

It has been revealed that using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes.

According to recent reports, continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting issue by how close its attack path runs to those systems.

According to recent reports, continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path.

Recent findings suggest that for each confirmed glitch, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate.

AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in actionTo show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities. Before I can review concerns, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum User Guide.

The Overview page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my Code integrations, the Environments built on them, and the status of any AWS collector that supplies AWS resource context.

It has been revealed that I open one of my environments. The Issues tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues.

The Overview rates it High severity, with the status Completed and the remediation already Delivered to GitHub. The Risk assessment explains why. Continuum rates its Exploitability as Exploitable, with an evidence level of Static proven and a validation run status of Completed. Likelihood is High, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. Impact is Moderate, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other consumers in the same tenant. A Proof section includes the source analysis behind the verdict.

According to recent reports, the Remediation section shows a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled Continuum fix, and I choose View pull request to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the issue is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A Contributing findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from.

The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow.

The Findings tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that concerns are built from.

Industry observers note that the Scans tab indicates the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use Configure scan frequency to change the cadence or Queue scan to run one on demand. The Configuration tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context.

In a single workflow, I work through the validated complications in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships.

According to recent reports, now available AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is available today in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions. For pricing, visit the pricing page.

To learn more, visit the AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page and the User Guide. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • SR-1 Freedom gets a shorter boom and larger antennas, with roughly two years to finish design, construction, and testing.
  • NASA has settled key design choices for its planned nuclear-fission-powered spacecraft, Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, following a mission review in October.
  • Industry observers note that targeting launch in late 2028, SR-1 would be the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SR-1 Freedom gets a shorter boom and larger antennas, with roughly two years to finish design, construction, and testing.

NASA has settled key design choices for its planned nuclear-fission-powered spacecraft, Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, following a mission review in October.

Industry observers note that targeting launch in late 2028, SR-1 would be the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit. It is designed to demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion and deliver a capsule carrying three helicopters to Mars.

There have been some changes since NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman showed off the concept [PDF] at the agency's Ignition event in March. Improved shielding and spacecraft design will allow a shorter boom between the reactor and the spacecraft's main body, protecting its electronics and the SkyFall payload. The shorter boom will, according to NASA, "reduce weight, simplify assembly, and help streamline the spacecraft’s design.".

The revised design also includes larger X-band antenna dishes to transmit data to Earth.

Decisions are still pending on how many radiator panels the vehicle needs, the output power levels of the nuclear power module, and how long the reactor will operate.

In a recent development, currently, the mission calls for the spacecraft to start its reactor once it has left Earth orbit and gradually ramp up power. After a period during which performance data will be sent back to Earth, the reactor will be shut down until after the SkyFall capsule, containing a trio of Mars Ingenuity-class helicopters, is delivered to Martian orbit.

Solar arrays will power the spacecraft during its cruise to Mars. The fission reactor will then be reactivated to let engineers collect more data on its performance in deep space.

NASA also awarded a $39.3 million contract to Johns Hopkins University's Applied Physics Laboratory to develop the heat rejection system for the nuclear power module.

"Further maturation of the spacecraft plans will focus on reducing risk, simplifying the design, and staying on schedule," the agency noted.

It has been revealed that the latter part regarding the schedule is certainly a challenge. Meeting the late-2028 launch target leaves roughly two years to finish designing, building, and testing the spacecraft.

Industry observers note that ESA is also targeting late 2028 for its long-delayed Rosalind Franklin rover. Missing the intended Mars departure opportunity could push SR-1 into a later launch window, although NASA has not specified a fallback schedule. ®.
