NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1560 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders.
  • According to recent reports, we fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach.
  • In a recent development, neoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

According to recent reports, we fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

In a recent development, neoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

According to recent reports, modernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

According to recent reports, neoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:.

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

It has been revealed that pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

Sources indicate that to get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:.

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

Industry observers note that we report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

Sources indicate that † Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:.

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Industry observers note that before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding newly introduced documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

It has been revealed that neoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

According to recent reports, we provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Industry observers note that visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:.

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

It has been revealed that neoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

Industry observers note that neoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

Breaking: An Overview of Go's Tooling: Version 2

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 40 min read (8041 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Alexedwards

⏱️ ~40 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • My fresh book guides you through the start-to-finish build of a real world web application in Go — covering topics like how to structure your code, manage dependencies, create dynamic database-driven pages, and how to authenticate and authorize users securely.
  • Recent findings suggest that way back in 2019, I wrote the blog post An Overview of Go's Tooling.
  • Sources indicate that but a lot has changed in the past 7 years, and some of the information in that original post is now painfully out-of-date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My fresh book guides you through the start-to-finish build of a real world web application in Go — covering topics like how to structure your code, manage dependencies, create dynamic database-driven pages, and how to authenticate and authorize users securely.

Black Friday sale: 30% off until the 1st December!

Recent findings suggest that way back in 2019, I wrote the blog post An Overview of Go's Tooling. It was a popular article and IIRC, ended up being one of the most-read items in the Go Weekly newsletter that year. It's also one that I personally still come back to fairly often, when I want to remind myself of a specific command that I can't remember.

Sources indicate that but a lot has changed in the past 7 years, and some of the information in that original post is now painfully out-of-date. So this is a version 2 of that post... fully updated for the module-enabled, gopls-integrated, token-fuelled world that we now live in 😊.

One of the biggest improvements to Go's tooling has been the introduction of latest ways to run third-party tools. We now have three options — go install, go run, and go tool — each suited to slightly different use cases.

In a recent development, the first option is to install the tool on your local machine using the go install command. You can run this command from anywhere on your machine, and it will download the necessary source code for the tool and create an executable binary in your GOBIN directory. So long as your GOBIN directory is on your system path, you can then run the tool whenever you need it.

For example, to install the latest version of govulncheck, check its install location, and run it, you can do this:.

Using go install tends to be a good option for general-purpose tools that happen to be written in Go, where you don't need to pin a specific version for use within a project or necessarily keep up with the latest release. Personally, I tend to use it for installing tools like hey, which I often use for things outside of Go development.

Sources indicate that the second option is to use go run to execute a specific version of a tool without installing it. For example, to run the latest version of govulncheck you can use the following command:.

I've written in detail about using go run to execute tools previously in this post, but this option is really useful when there is a tool you want to quickly run on an ad hoc basis.

Personally, I often use go run in this way during code reviews, when I want to do a one-time run of a specific static analysis tool using the latest version.

I also find this approach useful in small solo projects where I don't have to worry about tool version differences with other developers. I'll often create a Makefile which uses go run to execute the latest version of code-quality tools — similar to this.

Lastly, there is now the option to add a tool as a module tool dependency to your go.mod file. At a very high level, you can use the go get -tool command to add the tool as a module dependency, and the necessary version information and checksums will be added to the go.mod and go.sum files. For example:.

And then you can run the specific version of the tool listed in the go.mod file with the go tool command, like so:.

This is a great option when you are working with a team of people, where for consistency and reproducibility you want to make sure that everyone is using exactly the same version of a tool.

I've previously written a much more detailed tutorial about how to use the go tool functionality, and I recommend checking that out for more information.

In a recent development, another major development in recent years has been gopls. This is the official language server for Go, which you can use with any text editor or IDE that supports the Language Server Protocol (LSP).

If you're not already familiar with LSP, it's essentially a protocol that allows text editors to communicate with external programs called language servers, which act as the "brain" behind smart editor features.

The Go language server supports a wide range of smart editor features, including:.

To use gopls, the first thing you need to do is install it on your computer using the go install command, like so:.

Once gopls is installed, you then need to configure your editor to use it.

If you're using Zed or Helix, they should automatically detect gopls on your machine and start using it without any additional setup.

In a recent development, if you're using VS Code, you'll need to install the official Go extension. To do this, open the Extensions Panel, search for golang.go, and install this extension. After you restart and open a .go file, you should see a lightning bolt next to the Go version in the status bar at the bottom of your editor. This indicates that the language server is running.

For other editors, the steps are a little more complicated. Please see the official setup steps for Vim and Neovim, Emacs and Sublime Text.

Sources indicate that once your editor is configured, you should see smart editor features become available. For example, here's a screenshot of documentation when hovering over the http.Error() function in VS Code.

It has been revealed that the go doc tool remains the de facto way to view the documentation for standard library packages in your terminal. You can use it to view the documentation for an entire package, or for a specific type, function or method. For example:.

You can also use the -src flag to view the relevant source code:.

In a recent development, since Go 1.25, you can also use the -http flag to start a documentation server and browse the documentation locally in your web browser. For example, to view documentation for the bytes package in your browser you can run the following command:.

Sources indicate that to display information about your current Go operating environment, you can use the go env command. This can be particularly useful if you're working on an unfamiliar machine.

If there are specific values that you're interested in, you can pass them as arguments to go env. For example:.

To show documentation for all go env variables and values you can run:.

If you have your text editor setup to use gopls, there is a good chance that your .go files will automatically be formatted according to the Go conventions each time they are saved, as well as having their import lines automatically added, removed and sorted as necessary.

If you're not using gopls, or you want to format files outside of your text editor (for example, as part of a pre-commit hook or CI pipeline), you can use the gofmt tool to format them. For example:.

In these commands, the -w flag instructs the tool to rewrite files in place, the -s instructs the tool to apply certain simplifications to the code, and the -d flag instructs the tool to output diffs of the changes. If you want to only display the names of changed files, instead of diffs, you can swap this for the -l flag instead. Note that gofmt works recursively, so if you pass it a directory like . or ./cmd/foo it'll format all .go files within that directory tree.

Alternatively, you can run the go fmt command — which is essentially a wrapper around gofmt -l -w — like so:.

Often, as part of a quality audit check in a CI pipeline, I want to check that .go files are formatted correctly, without actually changing anything. To do this, I usually run gofmt -l . and check that the output from this command is empty. There's an example of this in the audit check in this Makefile.

According to recent reports, it's also worth mentioning the goimports tool, which formats your .go files in the same way as gofmt, but also updates your import lines — adding, removing and sorting the lines as necessary. You can run it like so:.

You can use the go mod tidy command to automatically add missing dependencies to, and prune unused dependencies from, your go.mod and go.sum modfiles based on the imports in your .go files.

Sources indicate that it's a good idea to run this periodically to keep your modfiles synchronized with your code. Personally, I try to run this before each commit to make it easier to see exactly which code changes were responsible for adding or removing a dependency when looking through the version control history.

If you want to check if the modfiles are synchronized without actually changing them, you can use the -diff flag like so:.

Recent findings suggest that this is a really useful command to use in audit checks and CI pipelines, because when you run it with -diff it will print out any changes and then exit with a non-zero code. If no changes are needed, it will exit with code 0.

It has been revealed that it's also worth mentioning that running go mod tidy ensures your modfiles include the dependencies needed across all possible build tag, OS and architecture combinations. Commands like go run, go test and go build are more selective, and only require dependencies for the current build configuration. This is why you might sometimes see additional lines appear in your modfiles unexpectedly when running go mod tidy.

For debugging Go applications, the standard tool to use is Delve. It allows you to set breakpoints, step through your code line by line, and do things like inspecting the values of variables and viewing the current call stack.

You can install Delve by running:.

Recent findings suggest that nowadays, the easiest way to use Delve is generally via the debugger integration in your text editor. For example, in VS Code you set breakpoints by clicking in the gutter next to a line of code, start a debugging session by opening the 'Run and Debug' panel, and use the debugging toolbar to step through your application and inspect what's happening as it runs.

In a recent development, it's also possible to use Delve outside of a text editor and start an interactive debugging session in your terminal. For example, assuming you installed Delve using the go install command above, you could start debugging an application in the ./cmd/web directory by running:.

You can then use Delve's commands to set breakpoints, continue execution, step through your code, and inspect variables, in much the same way as in a text editor.

There is a nice introduction on how to use the terminal-based debugger in this post, and more information about debugging with Delve can be found in the official Delve documentation.

Industry observers note that go 1.26 made major changes to the go fix command, updating it so that it now automatically 'modernizes' your code to use the latest Go idioms and standard library APIs. When you run it, it will do things like replacing interface{} with any, and rewrite code to use functions like slices.Contains() rather than manual loops.

You can see a complete list of the analyzers that go fix supports, and what they do, by running go tool fix help:.

At its most basic, you can use go fix like this:.

Sources indicate that however, it's crucial to be aware that go fix will silently rewrite your .go files in place. If you want to know in advance what changes it will make without actually applying them you can use the -diff flag like so:.

Sometimes, when looking at the diff, you might decide that you want to make some, but not all, of the changes. For example, there have been times when I've decided that my original code was clearer without the modernizations applied by the embedlit and mapsloop analyzers. You can disable specific analyzers individually like so:.

Since the release of gopls, the simplest, safest and most flexible way to refactor your code is by using its code transformation features in your text editor. For example, you can inline function calls, extract code into a function, rename identifiers, and move or remove parameters across your codebase, all in a few clicks.

For example, in VS Code you can use the 'Rename' and 'Refactor' options in the right-click menu to refactor code like so:.

More information, including a description of all supported refactoring features, can be found in the official gopls documentation.

However, if you don't want to use gopls, or are using a text editor that doesn't support it, you can still use gofmt with the -r flag to implement a rewrite rule that can assist with certain refactoring tasks. I've written more about this in my 2019 blog post on Go tooling here.

Industry observers note that there are a few live reloading tools available for Go, which you can use to automatically rebuild and restart an application whenever certain files change. These are especially useful when developing web services, because they let you make changes to your code or template markup and then check the results in a browser without having to manually restart the application each time.

Industry observers note that the most mature and popular live reloading tool for Go is air-verse/air. You can run it using settings in a TOML configuration file , like so:.

Recent findings suggest that or you can configure it using command-line flags. For example, to watch all directories and rebuild the ./cmd/web application whenever a file with an extension in the set .go, .tmpl, .css, .js or .sql changes, you could use the following command:.

Here's a video illustrating the air live reloading functionality when developing a web application:.

Go's language server, gopls, includes an experimental MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that exposes some of its functionality to AI coding assistants (such as Claude Code or OpenAI Codex). This effectively allows the assistants to leverage the same "smart features" that your text editor has access to, rather than just relying on reading your files.

Assuming that you have gopls installed, you can configure your AI coding assistant to use the gopls MCP server by following the instructions in the official Go MCP documentation.

It has been revealed that you can also run the gopls mcp -instructions command to get guidance for using the MCP server, which you can then provide to your coding assistant. For example:.

It has been revealed that another MCP server worth mentioning is mrjoshuak/godoc-mcp. This allows AI coding assistants to look up Go package documentation directly, which can be more token-efficient than reading through source files. You may wish to try this if you're using AI assistants heavily and want to reduce token usage.

In late 2022 the Go team released govulncheck, which checks your codebase against the Go vulnerability database to find known vulnerabilities in any standard library packages or third-party dependencies that you're using.

Unlike many other vulnerability scanners, it only flags vulnerabilities that actually affect you... meaning that a vulnerability in a part of a package that your code doesn't use won't be flagged.

It's an excellent tool, and I recommend running it routinely before you deploy a newly introduced version of your application to production.

Long term, the plan is for govulncheck to become part of the main go command, but for now you can run it like so:.

Recent findings suggest that another really helpful tool is gosec, a static analyzer that looks for potential security problems in your code. You can run it like so:.

Sources indicate that in my experience it's not uncommon for gosec to flag issues which on further inspection are false positives in the context of your specific codebase, or where you are deliberately using something insecure. When this happens, you can annotate the specific code with a #nosec comment to instruct gosec to omit it from future reports. For example:.

Recent findings suggest that the venerable go vet command should still be your first port of call when it comes to static code analysis. It runs a relatively small set of checks, but the checks have a high signal-to-noise ratio and if go vet reports an issue, then it's very likely to be a problem you should address.

It's normally best to run go vet with its default settings, like so:.

You can see a complete list of the checks that go vet runs in the 'Registered analyzers' section of the help documentation:.

And you can also disable specific analyzers if you don't want their checks to run. For example, to disable the composites analyzer, which checks for unkeyed composite literals, you can run go vet like so:.

The staticcheck tool is kind of like go vet on steroids. It carries out around 160 different checks on your code — the vast majority of which are related to code correctness and performance, although it also includes a handful of checks for for 'stylistic' complications like comment formatting too.

The complete list of checks, along with their respective ID codes and descriptions, can be found here.

According to recent reports, it's crucial to note that staticcheck does not run all checks by default — only a subset of them. But you can configure exactly which checks are run using either the -checks command-line flag or a config file. For example:.

The nilaway tool is really useful for finding potential nil-pointer panics in your code. It's similar to the older nilness tool in what it aims to do, but is more comprehensive in its checks.

If you're not worried about nil-pointer panics in your test code, and only want to check your production code, you can also run it with the -exclude-test-files flag enabled. Like so:.

The errcheck tool has been around for a long time (14 years!), and it remains a great way to check for unhandled errors in your code.

You can run it with its default settings like so:.

It's worth mentioning that, by default, errcheck only reports errors which are completely unhandled. It doesn't report errors that are handled by ignoring them and assigning them to the blank identifier _.

To include these errors in the report, you can run it with the -blank flag enabled, like so:.

Recent findings suggest that it's worth noting that not every error always needs to be handled. For example, it's conventional to ignore errors returned by http.ResponseWriter.Write(), or errors from fmt.Fprint() when writing to standard streams. Or you might deliberately choose to ignore errors from nice-to-have non-critical cleanup operations, where you decide that handling errors would add more complexity to your codebase than it's worth.

So it's possible to exclude specific functions from the errcheck report by creating an exclude file and passing it via the -exclude flag like so:.

It's also worth mentioning the shadow tool, which identifies instances of variable shadowing in your code.

This tool was also built by the Go team and has been around for a very long time, but has never been included in the default go vet analyzers or the go command because it is notoriously noisy and reports a lot of instances of variable shadowing that aren't actually problematic.

Nonetheless, it's still worth knowing that it exists. Personally, I do use shadow occasionally when I'm doing a code review of a large codebase, and skim through the results to see if anything jumps out as looking unexpected or out of place.

The revive tool is a code linter, and is kind of the spiritual successor to the now frozen and deprecated golang/lint package.

There is some overlap between revive and the staticcheck tool that we talked about earlier, but revive focuses more on checking code style and conventions, whereas staticcheck focuses more on finding bugs and performance issues.

Generally, revive is good to use on projects where you have multiple contributors and you want to maintain common standards in terms of code and comment style.

You can run it with its default settings like so:.

Normally though, I prefer to run it using the -formatter=stylish flag, which groups failures by file and includes links to the specific documentation for each failure.

You can also disable and customize specific checks by creating a TOML configuration file and passing it via the -config flag, like so:.

Deadcode is an excellent tool for finding functions in your code that aren't being used, which you can potentially delete or comment out. Similar to govulncheck, the deadcode tool is officially maintained by the Go team, but isn't currently part of the go command.

You can run deadcode with the default settings like this:.

Sources indicate that but it's important to note that by default, deadcode does not consider code in _test.go files when checking if something is used or not. This means that functions which are only used by your tests can incorrectly be reported as dead code. So to make sure test files are included in the check, I almost always run deadcode with the -test flag enabled, like so:.

Another neat way to use deadcode is when you are looking at a function and can't figure out why it exists, or you're struggling to fully trace where it is being called from.

Recent findings suggest that if you run deadcode with the -whylive flag, you'll get a report showing the shortest path from a main() function in your program to the code in question. For example, let's say you have the module example.com, and you wanted to trace where the internal/response.HTMLRenderer.Render() method is being called from, you can run a command like this:.

If you've made the decision in your codebase to wrap errors before returning them to the caller (which is generally a good idea to help with debugging), the wrapcheck tool helps you find any instances where you've forgotten to do this.

According to recent reports, if you are running a lot of tools as part of your code quality checks, you might want to consider Golangci-lint to help with this. It acts as a wrapper around many of the tools we've talked about above, running them in parallel and outputting the results in a single consistent format.

Alternatively, and slightly more simply, I often use a Makefile with a single audit task that runs the tools I want, similar to this.

In a recent development, personally, when I want to upgrade to a newly introduced version of Go on my primary development machine, I have a simple Bash script that I run to download and install the new version. The script and instructions are available here if you'd like to take a similar approach. I then run it like:.

Sometimes it's useful to have multiple versions of Go installed on your machine. For example, you might want to test your code against different Go releases, or try out a new version without replacing your existing one.

You can do this using the go install golang.org/dl/... command. For example, to install Go 1.26.0 alongside your existing Go installation, you can run:.

You can then use this alternative version by running the versioned executable instead of go. For example:.

It's crucial to note, though, that Go 1.21 and newer support automatic toolchain switching. So running a versioned Go command inside a module that requires a newer toolchain may cause Go to automatically download and use that newer version instead. If you want to disable this, you can set the GOTOOLCHAIN environment variable to local, like so:.

To check for dependency updates, the best tool around is probably oligot/go-mod-upgrade. You can run it like so:.

This launches an interactive tool which lists all dependencies that have upgrades available. You can then select the ones you want, and they'll be upgraded to the latest available version.

In the past, if you want to use a modified version of a dependency (for example, you temporarily want to use a local fork until a patch is merged upstream), you would use the go mod edit command to add a replace rule to your go.mod file pointing to the modified version, as described here.

Although this approach does still work, an alternative option is to create a Go workspace and a go.work file in your module root.

For example, assuming that you are in the root of your module, and the modified dependency you want to use is located in the directory /local/code/mydep, you can create a workspace and a go.work file that references the current module and modified dependency like so:.

The go.work file that is created should then look like this:.

And when you run the code in your module, the modified dependency should be picked up and used, rather than resolving the dependency from the module cache in the normal way. Note that the dependency still needs its own go.mod file, and that the dependency's module path must match the import path your code uses.

Go workspaces are also really useful in the scenario where you are developing two modules at the same time which rely on each other. When you want to do this, you can create a go.work file in the parent directory of the two modules, which points to the two module directories. For example, if you have two modules located at /local/code/a and /local/code/b, you could create a go.work file in /local/code that references them both like so:.

For more information about Go workspaces and go.work files, please see the official tutorial.

In a recent development, if you ever look at your go.mod or go.sum files and wonder "why is that listed as a dependency?", you can find out by running the go mod why command. This will show you the shortest path from a package in your main module to a given dependency. For example, to see why golang.org/x/sys is listed as a dependency you can run:.

It's also worth knowing about the go mod graph command, which prints a plain-text module requirement graph.

Industry observers note that the output from this tool is just a plain text listing, not a visual graph, but I've had some success with dumping the output from go mod graph into AI tools and asking them to generate a visualization. Alternatively, if you want something more reliable and reproducible, you might want to consider trying the samber/go-mod-graph and bayraktugrul/modview tools, which will generate visualizations for you.

Downloaded dependencies are stored in the module cache on your computer. If you're not sure where your module cache is located, you can check by running the go env GOMODCACHE command.

If you ever want to clear the module cache — which can be useful if your cache has become corrupted or want to rule it out as the source of a bug — you can use the go clean tool like so:.

But be aware that this is a blunt instrument — it will remove the downloaded dependencies for all projects on your machine.

You can use the go test tool to run the tests in your project like so:.

If the code you’re testing leverages concurrency, or you’re running tests in parallel, then you may want to use the -race flag to enable Go's race detector during the tests. This will increase the running time of the tests, but it's an easy tweak that can help find data races that occur while the tests are running.

If any of your tests need access to VCS information in debug.BuildInfo, you should also make sure to use the -buildvcs flag when running tests, like so:.

If you want to only run some specific tests, rather than all the tests in a package, there are a few ways to do this.

If you're using VS Code or GoLand as your text editor, the simplest way is via the testing functionality built into your editor. For example:.

If you're not using an editor that supports this kind of functionality, you can also use go test with the -run flag to run specific tests. This accepts a regular expression, and only tests which have names that match the regular expression will be run. When using this, I normally also use the -v flag to enable verbose output, so I can make sure that the tests I expect are actually being run 🙂.

It's also worth mentioning that Go caches test results at the package-level. If a package hasn't changed between test runs, then the cached test result will be displayed with a "(cached)" annotation next to it. If you want to force your tests to run in full, you can use the -count=1 flag, or mark cached test results as expired by using the go clean tool.

A final flag that I sometimes use is -failfast, which will stop further tests in a package from running after the first failure.

Industry observers note that note that if you're running tests in multiple packages (for example by using go test ./... ), then the tests in the other packages which didn't have the failure will continue to run.

As an alternative to go test, you may also want to consider using the gotestyourself/gotestsum tool. This is effectively a wrapper around go test which prints the test output in a nice way, similar to this:.

It's also possible to enable test coverage analysis when running tests by using the -cover flag. This will display the percentage of code covered by the tests in the output for each package, similar to this:.

Alternatively, you can use the -coverprofile flag to generate a coverage profile and view it in your browser by using the go tool cover -html command like so:.

This will give you a navigable listing of all the test files, with code covered by the tests displayed in green, and uncovered code in red.

If you want you can go a step further and set the -covermode=atomic flag to make the coverage profile record the exact number of times that each statement is executed during the tests.

When viewed in the browser, statements which are executed more frequently are shown in a more saturated shade of green, similar to this:.

If you don't have a web browser available to view a coverage profile, you can see a breakdown of test coverage by function/method in your terminal with the command:.

In a recent development, for quick and simple load testing of a web application or API, one of the best tools around is rakyll/hey. For example, if you want to load test the http://localhost:5051 endpoint by sending 10,000 requests with up to 100 concurrently, you can do so like this:.

The output includes useful information such as the number of requests per second, response-time distributions, and summary counts of HTTP response status codes.

hey supports a bunch of configuration options, which you can find by running:.

Alternatively, if you want a more sophisticated general-purpose load testing tool, you may want to consider tsenart/vegeta or grafana/k6, both of which are written in Go (although k6 test scenarios are typically written in JavaScript).

In a recent development, occasionally you might want to stress test something in your application by running a test multiple times in succession. This can be useful for checking for sporadic or intermittent failures, or when you're trying to reproduce an intermittent bug that you've been seeing.

It has been revealed that there are a couple of ways to do this, but the simplest is by using the go test flag -count. For example, to run the TestFooBar test 500 times, you could run:.

In a recent development, it's vital to note that -count repeats test executions in serial. Tests containing a t.Parallel() instruction can still run concurrently with other parallel tests within each execution, but the repeated executions themselves won't overlap.

If you want to repeat the same test multiple times in parallel, you can use the stress tool.

To use the stress tool, you'll first need to compile a test binary for the specific package you want to test. You can do this using the go test -c command. For example, to create a test binary for the package in your current directory:.

Recent findings suggest that in this example, the test binary will be output to /tmp/foo.test. You can then use the stress tool to execute a specific test in the test binary like so:.

Note: In the example above I've used the -p flag to restrict the number of parallel processes used by stress to 4. Without this flag, the tool defaults to using a number of processes equal to runtime.NumCPU().

Go 1.18 introduced support for fuzz testing, which makes it possible to run tests with randomly generated inputs in an attempt to find bugs and unhandled edge cases.

For example, let's say that you have a Slugify() function which takes input text like "An example string" and turns it into a slug like "an-example-string".

You could create a FuzzSlugify fuzz test for it like so:.

In this example, the calls to f.Add() provide some seed corpus values for the fuzz test, which give Go a starting point for generating additional inputs. You don't need to provide seed values, but it's generally a good idea to include a few representative examples.

When you run go test ./... in the normal way, the FuzzSlugify test will be run, but only using the seed corpus values.

To actually trigger fuzzing, you need to run it with the -fuzz flag. This takes a regular expression matching the name of the specific fuzz test you want to run. It's only possible to run one fuzz test at a time, and if multiple fuzz tests match the regular expression you'll get an error saying -fuzz matches more than one fuzz test.

You also need to pass in the path to the package that contains the fuzz test — you cannot use ./....

So, for example, to execute the FuzzSlugify fuzz test in the ./cmd/web package, you would run the following command:.

In this example, the fuzz test found a problem with the Slugify() function — specifically, when the input text is "0\t0", the whitespace \t character is not removed. It's also notable to note that, in this example, a file has been created at testdata/fuzz/FuzzSlugify/dde7a120ccdf11af containing the failing input. This input will be included in the seed corpus every time you run go test in the future (even when not using the -fuzz flag), so that the bug doesn't accidentally get reintroduced.

Industry observers note that fuzzing will continue indefinitely until either a failure is found or you terminate the run manually (e.g. with Ctrl+C). If there are no problems found, you'll see output which looks similar to this:.

The "upcoming interesting" count is the number of inputs discovered that increase the code coverage observed by the fuzzer. When the number of "new interesting" inputs starts to plateau, it can be a sign that you're not getting much additional coverage from continuing the test and you may want to terminate it.

Recent findings suggest that alternatively, you can set a fixed runtime for the fuzz test using the -fuzztime flag. For example, to run it for 30 seconds:.

For more information, I'd recommend checking out the official Go fuzzing documentation and the getting started tutorial.

Before compiling your application, it's sensible to run go mod verify to check that the dependencies in your module cache haven't been modified since they were downloaded.

I normally run go mod verify immediately before running go build, as part of an automated build process in a CI workflow or Makefile task. This helps to make sure that builds are reproducible, and you're not using an accidentally modified dependency during compilation.

To compile a main package and create an executable binary you can use the go build tool. Typically I use it in conjunction with the -o flag, which lets you explicitly set the output directory and name of the binary like so:.

In these examples, go build will compile the specified package (and any dependent packages), then invoke the linker to generate an executable binary, then output this to /tmp/foo.

It's notable to note that the go build tool caches build output in the build cache. This cached output will be reused again in future builds where appropriate, which can significantly speed up the overall build time.

It has been revealed that using the build cache comes with one key caveat — it does not detect changes to C libraries imported with cgo. So if your code imports a C library via cgo and you've made changes to it since the last build, you'll need to use the -a flag which forces all packages to be rebuilt. Alternatively, you could use go clean to purge the cache:.

According to recent reports, if you ever want detailed output explaining precisely what go build is doing behind the scenes, you can use the -v flag to print package names as they are being compiled, or the -x flag to print the detailed commands that are being run. You'll probably want to use these in conjunction with the -a flag, because otherwise you might not see much output as Go reuses packages from the build cache rather than recompiling them.

In a recent development, finally, if you run go build on a non-main package, it will be compiled in a temporary location and again, the result will be stored in the build cache. No executable binary will be produced.

Industry observers note that by default, go build will output a binary suitable for use on your current operating system and architecture. But it also supports cross-compilation, so you can generate a binary suitable for use on a different machine. This is particularly useful if you're developing on one operating system and deploying on another.

You can specify the operating system and architecture that you want to create the binary for by setting the GOOS and GOARCH environment variables respectively. For example:.

To see a list of all supported OS/architecture combinations you can run go tool dist list:.

For more information about cross compilation, I recommend reading this post.

When building your executable, you can use the -gcflags and -ldflags flags to change the behavior of the compiler and linker and see more information about what it's doing. You can see a complete list of available compiler and linker flags by running:.

Probably the most well-known and commonly-used of these is the linker -X flag, which allows you to "burn in" a (string) value to a specific variable in your application. For example, to burn in the value "bar" into the main package's global foo variable you can use it like so:.

For more information about the -X flag and some sample code see this Stack Overflow question.

According to recent reports, it's possible to reduce the binary size — typically by around 25% — by instructing the linker to strip symbol tables and DWARF debugging information from the binary. We can do this by using the -s linker flag, like so:.

It's not a Go-specific tool, but you can also use a tool like upx to compress the binary size further if you want. Please see this post for more information.

Once you have generated a binary, you can use the go tool buildid command to inspect its build ID. This is an identifier embedded in the binary by Go, representing the inputs to the build (code, compiler version, flags, etc.) and the resulting output. It acts as a "fingerprint" for the build, and is also used internally by Go's build cache.

For example, to check the build ID for the binary at /tmp/foo, you can run:.

In a recent development, looking at the build ID can be useful when checking for reproducible builds, as identical builds should produce the same ID. If two builds produce different IDs, it suggests that something about them is different.

For more information about Go build IDs and reproducibility, please see this post.

Recent findings suggest that another useful tool is the go version -m command, which lets you inspect a binary's build information — including the Go version, the module it was built from, its dependencies and VCS information. To inspect the binary at /tmp/foo, you can use it like so:.

A nice feature of Go is that it makes it easy to benchmark your code. If you're not familiar with the general process for writing benchmarks there's a good guide here.

To run benchmarks you need to use the go test tool, with the -bench flag set to a regular expression that matches the benchmarks you want to execute. If you don't want to run regular non-benchmark tests, you should omit them by using the -run=^$ flag. For example:.

I almost always run benchmarks using the -benchmem flag, which includes memory allocation statistics in the output.

In a recent development, by default, each benchmark test will be run for a minimum of 1 second, once only. You can control this with the -benchtime and -count flags:.

If the code that you're benchmarking uses concurrency, you can use the -cpu flag to see the performance impact of changing your GOMAXPROCS value (essentially, the number of OS threads that can execute your Go code simultaneously). For example, to run benchmarks with GOMAXPROCS set to 1, 4 and 8:.

To help analyze the results of the benchmarks, you can use the benchstat tool. This replaces the older benchcmp tool, which is now deprecated.

When you are using the -count flag to run benchmarks multiple times, you can use benchstat to easily see the median value and confidence interval across all the runs. For example:.

It has been revealed that you can also use it to compare benchmarks before and after a specific change. For example:.

Go makes it possible to create diagnostic profiles for CPU use, memory use, goroutine blocking and mutex contention. You can use these to dig a bit deeper and see exactly how your application is using (or waiting on) resources.

There are three ways to generate profiles:.

Using the -***profile flags when running benchmarks or tests will result in a test binary being outputted to your current directory. If you want to output this to an alternative location you should use the -o flag like so:.

My favourite way to inspect a profile is to use the go tool pprof -http command to open it in a web browser. For example:.

This will default to displaying a flame graph visually showing where your application is spending its resources, with wide boxes being the 'hot spots'.

You can also navigate to other views of the profile including top usage by function and source code:.

And also a graph showing the execution tree for your application, like this:.

If the amount of information is overwhelming, for CPU profiles you might want to use the -nodefraction flag to ignore nodes that account for less than a certain percentage of samples. For example, to ignore nodes that appear in less than 10% of samples you can run pprof like so:.

Sources indicate that and finally, if you're analyzing profiles for a web application created via net/http/pprof, you can also fetch the profile from the application and open the visualization in one step. For example, if your web application is running on http://localhost:4000 you could generate a 30-second CPU profile and view it like so:.

For more information about profiling and pprof, please see the official README.

Go also supports profile-guided optimization (PGO), which allows the compiler to use information gathered from profiling your application to make better decisions when compiling your code.

Sources indicate that normally, when compiling your code, the compiler has to make educated guesses about which functions are likely to be called frequently, which code paths are more common, and where it should make optimizations. PGO allows you to provide a CPU profile from a representative run of your application so that the compiler can make better-informed decisions.

For example, it may use this information to more aggressively inline frequently called functions, or optimize common code paths.

The good news is that using PGO is relatively straightforward. First you need to generate a CPU profile using one of the techniques described in the previous section. Then you need to pass it to go build via the -pgo flag when building your application. For example, if your CPU profile is saved as /tmp/cpuprofile.out, you can use it like so:.

Industry observers note that alternatively, you can rename your profile to default.pgo and place it in the directory containing your main package. Go will automatically detect this file and use it when building your application, so you don't need to specify the -pgo flag explicitly.

In practice, the recommended workflow is to collect a representative profile from your production application, use that profile when building your next release, and periodically collect latest profiles as your application evolves.

For more information, see the official PGO documentation and the Go blog post introducing PGO.

Sometimes profiling isn't enough to understand what's happening in your application. For example, a CPU profile can show you which functions are consuming the most CPU time, but it won't necessarily help you understand why a goroutine is blocked, why your application isn't making progress, or why a request is taking so long.

According to recent reports, for these situations, Go has a built-in execution tracer, which has been improved significantly in recent Go versions. It records runtime events such as goroutine scheduling, system calls, garbage collection, and other activity over a period of time. You can then use the go tool trace command to visualize and explore what happened.

Sources indicate that you can generate a trace from your tests or benchmarks, use net/http/pprof to create and download a trace for your web application, or use the runtime/trace package to generate traces from a running application. You can then use go tool trace to view the output in your web browser. For example:.

This will open an interactive visualization that lets you explore what was happening during the trace.

For more information, please see the Go blog post on tracing, the runtime/trace documentation, as well as this dotGo conference talk by Rhys Hiltner.

According to recent reports, I talked earlier about enabling Go's race detector during tests by using go test -race. But you can also enable it for running programs when building an executable, like so:.

It's critical to note that race-detector-enabled binaries will use more CPU and memory than normal, so you shouldn't use the -race flag when building binaries for production under normal circumstances.

It has been revealed that but you may want to deploy a race-detector-enabled binary on one server within a pool of many. Or use it to help track down a suspected race condition by using a load-test tool to throw traffic concurrently at a race-detector-enabled binary.

Recent findings suggest that by default, if any races are detected while the binary is running, a report will be written to os.Stderr. You can change this by using the GORACE environment variable if necessary. For example, to run the binary located at /tmp/foo and output any race reports to /tmp/race. you can use:.

Another complementary tool for helping to track down race conditions is amit-davidson/Chronos. This uses static analysis of your code to try to identify race conditions, rather than using real-time detection like Go's race detector. This means it can be a good option to try if there is a suspected race condition that you are struggling to replicate.

If you're confident that you've found an unreported concern with Go's standard library, tooling or documentation, you can use the go bug command to create a new GitHub issue.

This will open a browser window containing a GitHub issue pre-filled with your system information and reporting template.

You might like to check out my other Go tutorials on this site, or if you're after something more structured, my books Let's Go and Let's Go Further cover how to build complete, production-ready, web apps and APIS with Go.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Independent review will examine leadership, accountability, and how staff concerns were handled before former commissioner John Edwards resigned.
  • Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation.
  • Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Independent review will examine leadership, accountability, and how staff concerns were handled before former commissioner John Edwards resigned.

Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation.

Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise.

Edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a public official. He disagreed with some of its findings, but ultimately conceded that he had shown "poor judgment.".

That investigation, however, focused on Edwards alone. According to the terms of reference published on Thursday, it "did not consider the wider conditions in which that conduct occurred, and it was not designed to.".

The new review will cast a wider net. Monaghan wants to know whether staff could call out bad behavior further up the food chain, and what awaited those who tried.

It will also poke around the regulator's leadership and governance arrangements and its relationship with its sponsoring government department, including whether there were adequate ways for concerns to be escalated and those at the top to be challenged.

Current and former staff can give evidence confidentially and voluntarily, while Monaghan will be given access to relevant documents and existing material, including staff surveys and data on bullying, harassment and discrimination.

The ICO has confirmed it won't use confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements to prevent people from contributing to the review.

Recent findings suggest that monaghan decides which witnesses and documents are relevant, rather than the ICO or DCMS. Access remains subject to legal restrictions, and she must be told when material is withheld and why. She can speak to whoever she thinks is relevant and ask for the complaints, correspondence, and other paperwork she needs.

And if that leads her somewhere unexpected, she can ask to widen the investigation. DCMS can refuse, but it won't be able to quietly brush the request aside, and any decision not to expand the scope has to make it into the final report.

The review won't reopen the investigation into Edwards, make findings about the conduct of named individuals, or delve into the merits of the regulator's enforcement decisions.

Its arrival comes amid a broader shake-up at Britain's data watchdog. The old Information Commissioner's Office was formally replaced by the Information Commission on September 30, bringing with it a new board-led governance model.

The government first promised the wider review in July, shortly after Edwards' departure, but it didn't appoint its reviewer or nail down the terms until late November.

"We need to understand what is working, where things are falling short and, crucially, what needs to change," stated DCMS Secretary Lisa Nandy.

The watchdog won't have to wait long for its report card. Monaghan is expected to deliver her findings in the first quarter of 2027, after which they will be published and handed to Parliament. ®.

Typed indexes in Zig

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lvignoli

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The named integer or Newtype Index pattern prevents mixing up indexes on different arrays.
  • The above examples were not particularly illuminating to me.
  • In practice, to make good use of the pattern, a getter helper is required as the conventional way of accessing elements of the array.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The named integer or Newtype Index pattern prevents mixing up indexes on different arrays.

The above examples were not particularly illuminating to me. Andrew’s example don’t show much of how to enforce the safety at call site: any caller could call @backingInt (it used to be @intFromEnum) to recover a numerical index and pass it to the wrong array, or access array elements with a plain integer. And matklad’s one focus on building a tree data structure in a neat way, but that’s a totally different challenge that the introductory problem of mixing array indexes, so it was not a super convincing illustration for me.

In practice, to make good use of the pattern, a getter helper is required as the conventional way of accessing elements of the array. It can be a method on the array type—or the index type.

In a struct of array data structure, it is particularly valuable to have one typed index per slice rather than relying on careful naming.

Consider this spreadsheet example where it’s easy to mix up indexes:.

We can prevent such bug by enforcing compile time checking of field access with typed indexes.

Its clumsy to keep one index type and one accessor per field. We can use a bit of comptime to streamline the pattern, and make the recipe more generic to fit arbitrary structs. Here is a complete example.

Our spreadsheet has now several fields: a title, and row and column properties. When iterating over them, we have two kinds of indexes: row indexes and column indexes. Adding typed indexes is attractive to prevent callers from mixing them up.

It has been revealed that this enum gives us a way of referencing all the struct fields for which we will construct a typed indexed. If all fields were to be indexed, we would have used std.meta.FieldEnum(Sheet), but our spreadsheet has a title.

In a recent development, this checks at compile time that each Field enum variant name is indeed a field inside Sheet. As we’ll see later, we will have to access Sheet’s fields by name, so it’s good to check the names of Field variants match the names of Sheet fields.

This defines the kind of type indexes we’ll construct: one for row data slices and one for columns data slices. Each indexed field of Sheet has one correct typed index kind. We match them with an exhaustive switch over Field.

According to recent reports, we now have all we need to construct the two typed indexes of kinds .row and .col. A generic function returning a type at comptime is how to do it.

Sources indicate that the typed index type for row is Sheet.Index(.row), and for colum it is Sheet.Index(.col). Note the title case of the Index function, matching Zig’s convention for types.

Remains to give a way of making use of these types.

Industry observers note that this part may look complex if you are not familiar with comptime-enabled generics in Zig, so let’s be precise. This defines a method on Sheet that requires f to be a Field instance known at compile time. This allow to infer at compile time both the type of i and the return type.

Index(kindOf(f)) is just a chain of function calls on a known value. So it is comptime known. And most importantly, the type of i is bound to the one of f at compile time. Given the body of Sheet.kindOf, it’s easy to see that s.at(.row_width, i) will compile only if i has type Index(.row)!

The return type of Zig function must be comptime known, and it is the case here by using some reflection. @FieldType(Sheet, name) returns the type of the field of Sheet named name (given as a []const u8). @tagName(f) gives just that for the input enum variant. std.meta.Elem returns the element type for a collection type (here a slice). Finally, we return a pointer to allow the caller to mutate, but a value would work just fine for a read-only case.

This gives us a clear usage at call site.

The Sheet.Index(.row) syntax is particularly lovely: a method call feeling like a qualified concrete type.

Still, as I hinted earlier, this design it not completely hermetic to bugs. Nothing prevents you from forging a Sheet.Index(.row) from any integer with @fromBackingInt. And opaque types are really just for interaction with C.

Also, any caller can access Sheet fields directly (Zig has no notion of private fields.).

As for all Zig code, one must follow documented usage (“Direct access is discouraged. Use Sheet.at.”) and make good use of the public methods by proactively inspecting types.

#230069. Industry News: Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

Industry News: Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

📅 10 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui.
  • Sources indicate that workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes.
  • Industry observers note that you can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Sources indicate that workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

Industry observers note that you can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

Industry observers note that all the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

Recent findings suggest that this is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

It has been revealed that in Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

That same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

According to recent reports, there's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

According to recent reports, this is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

It has been revealed that the drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

Sources indicate that this is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

In a recent development, this is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

Recent findings suggest that background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

Industry observers note that canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

Industry observers note that there are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

Industry observers note that the image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

It has been revealed that so far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:.

ZeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

Industry observers note that this isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

In a recent development, every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

The same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node indicates up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:.

Now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

Sources indicate that AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:.

bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

Sources indicate that if you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

It has been revealed that whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

According to recent reports, really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes.

Analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?
