  • India’s free e-government platform has a critical SQL injection flaw that thousands of organizations must patch to protect up to two billion citizens.
  • Industry observers note that the platform is called the Digital Infrastructure for Governance (Impact and Transformation) – aka DIGIT – and is a modular suite that offers common services such as authentication and payment collection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

India’s Digital Infrastructure for Governance Impact and Transformation tool can leak data.

India’s free e-government platform has a critical SQL injection flaw that thousands of organizations must patch to protect up to two billion citizens.

Industry observers note that the platform is called the Digital Infrastructure for Governance (Impact and Transformation) – aka DIGIT – and is a modular suite that offers common services such as authentication and payment collection. Third party developers can also create DIGIT modules, and plenty have done so and now offer add-ons that handle tasks as diverse as managing birth and death certificates, revenue collection, and running water treatment plants.

DIGIT is ubiquitous in India, where all state and union territory governments use the platform, as do over 20,000 local government entities.

India also exports DIGIT under its policy of turning software created for its own needs into “digital public goods” (DPI) that it happily gives away to other nations. Nine nations have implemented DIGIT to some degree, among them Mozambique, Liberia, Senegal, Nigeria, Burundi, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Jamaica, and Sri Lanka.

Recent findings suggest that india’s population is 1.4 billion. Indonesia’s is 280 million and Nigeria is home to 240 million. DIGIT is therefore used by governments that serve over two billion people, some of whom are now at risk thanks to CVE-2026-136706, a 9.3-rated SQL injection flaw present in DIGIT which allows “improper neutralization of user supplied input while constructing SQL queries and execution in the affected User and Access Control Service components.”.

“An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted input through the affected API endpoint to the targeted system,” according to CERT-IN. “Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary SQL queries, potentially resulting in unauthorized disclosure, modification or deletion of database information on the targeted system.”.

eGov India, which oversees work on DIGIT, has released source code for an upgrade that fixes the problem.

While local government users of DIGIT typically access it as SaaS, through large implementations run by national or state governments, over 1,000 deployments are live across various cities and other entities.

Those orgs can therefore add patching DIGIT to their urgent to-do lists, along with fixing Java, PHP, vCenter and any other widely used technologies that suddenly need an urgent security update. ®.

InfoQ Homepage News Recap of Microsoft Ignite 2026: Copilot as the Work OS and Agent Governance.

Nov 26, 2026 10 min read.

Microsoft Ignite 2026, held in San Francisco and online from November 17 to 20, centered on running AI agents in production, with Microsoft positioning Copilot as the operating system for work and extending agent identity, governance, and cost controls across Azure, Foundry, Entra, and Defender.

It has been revealed that CEO Satya Nadella opened the keynote by acknowledging the November 12 Microsoft 365 outage, then positioned Copilot as the operating system for work, combining chat, coding, and autonomous agents in one experience. In his edited keynote remarks, Nadella argued that customers must be able to examine and independently verify what AI does, confirmed an AI Transparency Initiative aligned with NIST's Agent Standards Initiative, and rejected setups where models audit other models:.

These nested black boxes are simply unacceptable.

The Book of News groups the announcements by product area, and many of them ship as previews rather than in general availability.

Azure Cobalt 200 virtual machines are now generally available, a year after InfoQ reported on Microsoft introducing the chip at Ignite 2025 and two and a half years after the preview of Cobalt 100 VMs. According to the Azure announcement, the processor combines 132 Arm Neoverse V3 cores on TSMC's 3nm process, and the VMs run in 14 regions today, with 23 planned by the end of 2026. Microsoft claims up to 50% better CPU performance than Cobalt 100, plus up to 15% higher network bandwidth and 20% higher remote storage IOPS through Azure Boost. Customers can run cores at a fixed 3.2 GHz in Deterministic Mode or let them boost up to 3.6 GHz in Opportunistic Mode, and the lineup adds Mpsv4 VMs for high-memory workloads and storage-optimized Lpsv5 VMs. Amadeus reported more than 30% higher flight-search throughput than on Cobalt 100, and OpenAI's Vadim Filanovsky described a similar result:.

We saw higher throughput and lower latency on Cobalt 200.

Confidential computing gains three previews: multi-GPU confidential computing on VR72 for models larger than a single GPU, Azure Confidential Enclaves with AKS Kata CoCo containers, and Azure Confidential Clean Room for multiparty analytics without exposing raw data.

Customers can now deploy Foundry open-weight models and agents to their own AKS clusters. At the same time, an Agent Sandbox extension provides VM-level isolation for agent-written code, and Agent Grid applies central policy to agent, model, tool, and service interactions. Flex nodes extend AKS clusters to servers outside Azure. According to the AKS team's Ignite post, managed GPU node pools, which handle GPU drivers, device plugins, and Azure Monitor metrics, are generally available, with NVIDIA GB200 and GB300 support and mixed multi-instance GPU in preview. Confidential VM node pools on Azure Container Linux are also generally available on both Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP VM sizes.

It has been revealed that on the operations side, Azure Monitor health models are generally available and build a real-time health graph from telemetry, ranking incidents by business impact. The Azure Copilot deployment agent, also generally available, turns natural-language requirements into deployed workloads, and Azure SRE Agent picks up previews for customer-managed keys, Entra Agent ID integration, cross-agent communication, and multicloud investigations. For migration projects, Azure Catalyst is now generally available, with its agent (formerly the Azure Copilot migration agent) handling discovery, assessment, and planning. Separately, GitHub Copilot modernization adds a preview of BizTalk-to-Logic Apps migration.

It has been revealed that microsoft now pitches Sovereign Private Cloud as a full stack on Azure Local, with VMs and AKS at the base, followed by data services, Foundry Local, GitHub Enterprise Local, and Microsoft 365 Local. Darryl van der Peijl, a Microsoft MVP for Azure Local, Hyper-V, and Azure Arc, listed what shipped in his Azure Local Insider newsletter: Foundry Local on Azure Local and GitHub Enterprise Local are generally available, while a Sovereign control panel, Blob Storage and DocumentDB on Azure Local, multi-tenancy, and rehoming are in preview. The control panel assesses data residency, encryption, network exposure, and business continuity for Azure resources without enforcing any controls, and during the preview it runs in European regions only, with the service hosted in Sweden.

Van der Peijl singled out rehoming, which moves an Azure Local instance from Azure management to local management while VMs, AKS clusters, and data stay in place:.

It has been revealed that until now, going from connected to disconnected meant a migration project. Microsoft highlighted a script that does the rehoming in one run.

Azure Local also runs on arm64 for the first time, in public preview on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor Development Kit, which hosts containers on bare metal without a hypervisor. Windows Server 2028 entered preview through the Windows Server Insider Program, bringing a hardened Server Core, post-quantum cryptography, native NVMe enabled by default, NVMe over Fabrics, and boot from ReFS. According to van der Peijl, Microsoft added inference as a new pillar for the release, calling on-premises inference servers token factories, and is moving network drivers from kernel mode to user mode as part of its Windows resiliency work. Windows Admin Center vMode is now generally available at no extra cost and manages up to 1,000 Hyper-V hosts and 25,000 VMs, which Microsoft described on stage as "kind of a replacement for SCVMM.".

Sources indicate that foundry's main theme was continuous improvement. Multi-turn evaluation and production insights that group recurring failures and rank fixes are now generally available, while the agent optimizer, human annotation, rubric evaluators, Managed Training, and Programmed Training for custom SFT and reinforcement learning loops on open-weight models are in preview. The optimizer adjusts an agent's instructions, skills, and model choice, with a human approving each change before it ships.

It has been revealed that in a separate engineering post, the Microsoft team behind the optimizer described how the loop works. They reported that the reflector, a separate model that reads failing traces and diagnoses why an agent scored poorly, influenced results more than switching the agent's own model, for example between gpt-4o and gpt-4.1-mini. Developers drive the loop from the Azure Developer CLI:.

Writing on DEV Community, Hector Flores advised readers to treat Microsoft's claim that the model router saves up to 65% compared with a frontier model as a ceiling rather than a forecast, and he welcomed the human approval step in the optimizer loop:.

Self-modifying agents with no review gate are an incident waiting to happen.

On the model front, Microsoft-Decision-1.1 is generally available in Foundry, OpenRouter, and Vercel. Built on Gemma 4 26B A4B with added image input, it scores 68 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 and runs more than twice as fast as its predecessor, and Copilot uses it to route requests. MAI-Code-2 and MAI-Code-2-Flash are generally available on GitHub, MAI-Image-2.7 is in preview, and the model router now covers the top 50 models in a catalog of more than 11,000. OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol became generally available in Foundry, with Global Standard deployments covering 28 regions. On Standard deployments with short context, Sol costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, while Astra costs $8 and $40. Foundry IQ added knowledge graphs and an iterative retrieval model, Microsoft-Retriever-1, both in preview.

Microsoft also made Azure AI Gateway generally available as a standalone product, split out of the API Management AI tier, to govern, route, and monitor access to AI models and MCP tools across providers. It includes 10,000 free requests per gateway per month, with paid billing starting January 1, 2027, across 17 regions.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft IQ, which Nadella described as an externalization of the context system behind Copilot, is now generally available without a new SKU. It exposes Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, and Web IQ context to Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Foundry, and MCP-compatible harnesses, and Web IQ is now available to all Azure customers at a lower price. Business plugins, which package reusable context, skills, and tools with hierarchical inheritance and governance, are available through the Frontier program.

PostgreSQL got most of the attention on the data side. Azure HorizonDB is now generally available as a managed, PostgreSQL-compatible database with built-in vector indexing, and teams can lock it down with Entra ID, private endpoints, and their own encryption keys. Calling models from SQL through AI Functions and AI Pipelines is still in preview. The same holds for Fabric HorizonDB, a serverless variant inside Fabric that provisions in seconds and pauses when nobody uses it, and for a DMS path that moves existing Azure Database for PostgreSQL servers onto HorizonDB.

In a recent development, teams moving off Oracle can test a newly introduced Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration in Azure DMS, also in preview. Cosmos DB developers now have a generally available Rust SDK and semantic reranker, and Cosmos DB Shell lets them query from VS Code or the portal with MCP support built in. On Azure Managed Redis, the Redis 8 preview folds JSON, search, time-series, and vector search into a single version. Anyone who wants to develop against Azure SQL Database on a laptop can pull a preview container that needs no Azure subscription.

The Microsoft Copilot SDK 2.0 is generally available, built on a native Rust runtime, supported in six languages, and using the same agent harness Microsoft and GitHub run internally. The GitHub Copilot app now takes Azure DevOps repositories from clone to merge and runs tests in a real, signed-in browser. Copilot code review adds local reviews in the CLI and app, secret detection, adaptive review effort, and cross-repository context. Copilot Code, a natural-language app builder with cloud and local sandboxes, is in the Frontier program, with general availability planned for December and a macOS local sandbox still to come.

Sources indicate that the Copilot app now brings Chat, Cowork, Code, and Autopilot into one experience, and Office in Copilot puts Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside it as a generally available feature. Autopilot, a long-running personal agent with its own identity, memory, and tool access, is rolling out to Frontier customers. Salesforce in Copilot entered preview with more than 38 prebuilt sales skills, and zero-copy data federation between Salesforce Data 360 and Fabric OneLake is generally available. For spend control, Agent 365 FinOps previews cost visibility, policies, alerts, and Fabric-based chargeback.

Recent findings suggest that cost tracking also featured in practitioner reactions. In his newsletter, Microsoft principal AI apps architect Anurag Karuparti wrote that tokenomics is among the top challenges his customers raise, and he proposed a different unit for agent ROI:.

The metric that matters isn't just tokens consumed. It's cost per successful business outcome. That's how I think enterprises should start measuring agent ROI.

Writing for business leaders, Aaron Reich, CTO of the Accenture and Microsoft joint venture Avanade, built his Ignite analysis around trust rather than speed:.

It has been revealed that speed isn't the bottleneck anymore, trust is. As AI drives the cost of knowledge toward zero with apps being easier to build, agents doing more work, and abundant intelligence, the scarce things are hard and need more attention: institutional knowledge, judgment, accountability and trust.

At the Microsoft Hub, where he spent the week answering customer questions, Microsoft MVP Muhammad Atif noticed a change in what customers wanted to know:.

How do we actually put this into production? How do we scale AI and agents across the organisation? How do we govern and secure them? How do we control the cost as adoption grows?

In a recent development, entra now assigns Agent IDs automatically to discovered local agents, starting with GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code, and previews an MCP Firewall that controls access to MCP servers, tools, prompts, and transports. The Microsoft MCP Server for Enterprise, which gives agents permission-controlled access to Entra data, is generally available. Defender's runtime protection for local AI agents on Windows is generally available to Defender for Endpoint P2 customers, while Intune previews local agent governance that marks devices with unapproved agents as noncompliant. Agent 365 now has a generally available tools registry that lists the plugins, skills, MCP servers, and connectors agents use; MCP governance is in preview through Azure AI Gateway and LiteLLM; and Dynamic Agent Risk combines runtime, posture, and blast-radius signals into risk levels for each agent. Microsoft Perception, formerly Project Perception, is now generally available, with its Triage Agent covering about 80% of alerts in a typical Defender queue.

(Source: Microsoft Tech Community, Agent 365 blog).

In her Ignite recap, cloud and identity consultant Shannon Kuehn warned against handling agents as ordinary applications:.

Treat agents like apps and you'll spend 2027 cleaning up after them.

The complete list of announcements is available in the Microsoft Ignite 2026 Book of News, and Microsoft has made keynote and breakout session recordings available on demand on the Ignite website.

  • AWS now offers two fresh types of cloudy computers: emulated Androids and simulated iPhones.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Emulating Android, too, but offers just two handsets and one tablet.

AWS now offers two fresh types of cloudy computers: emulated Androids and simulated iPhones.

In a recent development, the cloudy colossus announced both virtual offerings on Wednesday. They’re part of its Device Farm service, which previously saw AWS offer developers the chance to test their software on actual iOS and Android devices that reside in the Amazonian cloud. AWS will now also host virtual devices running Android and iOS.

AWS touts the virtual mobile devices as superior to physical devices.

“With virtual devices, you can shift testing left to stages that need high speed and volume, such as pull requests, code merges, and smoke tests, and keep real devices for later stages that need high fidelity, such as regression and release testing,” the cloudy business unit argues in its launch announcement.

AWS also notes developers can get to work faster on a virtual iPhone or Pixel. “Virtual devices running the latest device and OS typically start in seconds, and others start in around a minute,” the outfit argues.

That may sound appetizing, but Amazon’s menu of virtual devices is short and bland.

In a recent development, when The Register logged on as an AWS user, the only emulated Android phone listed was a Google Pixel 10, running Android 15, 16, or 17. An emulated Pixel tablet running Android 17 is also on the menu.

At the time of writing, we could find only a virtual iPhone 16, running iOS 18.6, 23.61, and 27.0.

Sources indicate that analyst firm Counterpoint’s list of the world’s top 10 best-selling smartphones in Q2 of 2026 does not include a single Pixel device. The iPhone 16 occupies 10th place.

iPhone 17 models occupy the first, second, third, and seventh place on the list.

AWS might excite more developers if it adds emulators for the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, Galaxy A07 4G, A17 5G, A17 4G, and Galaxy S26, as they occupy the fourth, fifth, sixth, eighth and ninth places on Counterpoint’s list.

Amazon’s choice of a Pixel tablet is also an oddity given analyst firm IDC doesn’t list Google among its top five tablet vendors.

Recent findings suggest that amazon does offer physical Galaxy A17 devices and three versions of the iPhone 17. But Device Farm doesn’t offer any foldable devices, meaning developers struggling to wrap their heads around the iPhone Duo will need either ask Apple for a loaner or shell out $2,000 to acquire one.

Industry observers note that at least developers don’t have to change behavior to access the few virtual devices AWS offers, as existing Device Farm APIs and test frameworks will work on real or notional machines. ®.

#230063. Async GRPO with LoRA across HF Jobs: a bucket, a proxy, and no NCCL

Async GRPO with LoRA across HF Jobs: a bucket, a proxy, and no NCCL

📅 10 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that loRA support recently landed in TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer with PR #7017, and ships with TRL v1.14.
  • In a recent development, loRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret.
  • There is also a systems consequence of LoRA training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that loRA support recently landed in TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer with PR #7017, and ships with TRL v1.14. The asynchronous trainer can now train an adapter instead of the full model, and it syncs only the LoRA adapter to vLLM. This post covers a real-world project built on top of it, where training and inference no longer share a machine.

In a recent development, loRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret. They show that LoRA can match full fine-tuning for policy-gradient RL, even with rank 1. This stems from the fact that the advantage function only gives ~O(1) bits of information per episode, so there is not that much to learn from each step, from a total-bits-of-information point of view. A rank-1 adapter has enough capacity to absorb it.

There is also a systems consequence of LoRA training. A rank-1 adapter for a 1.5B model is a few megabytes, while the full model is around 3 GB. Instead of sending the full policy to the inference workers after every update, we can just send the adapter. vLLM can also keep several adapters loaded at once. Old rollouts finish with the policy they started with, while new rollouts use the latest one.

It has been revealed that TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer already separates training and generation. The trainer and vLLM can run on different machines and at their own speed. This is easy in a single-node or cluster setting where both processes share a filesystem or can form an NCCL group.

Industry observers note that what we want is to run the same setup with Hugging Face Jobs. Essentially, an HF Job is one container running on one VM. This means that one Job cannot spawn multiple nodes (at least for now) to hold a trainer and a fleet of vLLM servers (we are limited to 8xH200 at most per node). The AsyncGRPOTrainer is built for exactly that kind of scale, so the question became: how far can we get if we drop the requirement that the trainer and the inference servers share a node?

Recent findings suggest that well, with a full-weight sync, the answer would be "not far". Every revision would have to move gigabytes between machines, which is what NCCL is for in a dense cluster, but Jobs can't communicate across nodes. There is no shared local disk and obviously no shared localhost. With LoRA, a sync is only a few megabytes. For the filesystem part, HF Jobs provide volumes backed by Storage Buckets! These buckets can then be mounted as a FUSE filesystem in every Job and are enough to work as a shared FS between nodes. No network path between the Jobs is needed at all.

The setup ended up being quite small:.

It has been revealed that the new adapter-only sync path in AsyncGRPOTrainer works like this. The trainer does not send tensors to vLLM. Every few optimizer steps, it saves the adapter under /.vllm_lora/trl-policy-v{N}, publishes the directory with an atomic rename, then sends its path to vLLM's /v1/load_lora_adapter endpoint. vLLM loads the files from disk, so the rollout worker can then request model="trl-policy-v{N}".

According to recent reports, this is how runtime adapter loading already works in vLLM. The endpoint takes a path, not tensors, so the trainer and the server are expected to share a filesystem. On a Slurm cluster, that is the network filesystem. On Jobs, we get the same thing by mounting a Storage Bucket as a volume at the same path in every Job, as we mentioned earlier. Under the hood, it uses hf-mount, which exposes the bucket as a POSIX filesystem inside the container:.

Nothing in TRL or vLLM had to change for this. The trainer writes to /lora//.vllm_lora/ and the servers read from the same path. The path sent in the POST request is already valid inside every container.

According to recent reports, note that we also store the checkpoints and the final adapter in the bucket. The HF Jobs are ephemeral, but a preempted trainer can resume training, as the final adapter is always persisted to the bucket and is never lost when the Job stops.

Each replica uses one GPU and the stock vllm/vllm-openai image. We only need to enable runtime LoRA loading and reserve enough adapter slots.

Recent findings suggest that the number of adapter slots follows from max_staleness. In AsyncGRPOTrainer, every weight sync bumps the policy version by one, and max_staleness is how many versions a rollout sample may lag behind the current policy before the trainer discards it. With max_staleness=4, a sample generated under trl-policy-v3 is still used for training while the trainer is at v7. A rollout that started under v3 must also be able to finish under v3. So at any moment, vLLM has to serve the current policy plus the four before it. That is why the trainer keeps max_staleness + 1 adapter versions registered and unloads anything older. Each sync loads the new version before it unloads the oldest one, which needs one more slot during the swap. That gives --max-loras 6. With only five, vLLM would silently evict a policy that still has rollouts in flight at every sync.

Industry observers note that we pin vLLM to v0.27.1. vLLM moves fast, and the flags above and the runtime LoRA endpoints are the ones that version exposes, so treat the version as part of the recipe.

According to recent reports, there is another possible design where the trainer keeps only the latest adapter and always publishes it under the same name. We did not go that way, because vLLM keys its prefix cache by adapter name. With a single name, KV blocks computed under the previous weights would still match after the swap, so the prefill would not be redone and a rollout could get its prefix from one policy version and its decode from the next. The trainer would have no way to tell, and it would show up as ratio drifting away from 1. Versioned names make this impossible: a name always means one set of weights, and a cached prefix can never match a newer version.

It has been revealed that we chose sail/Sanity-Test-R1D-1.5B, the dataset from Defeating the Training-Inference Mismatch via FP16 (Qi et al., 2025). The reproduction code is in sail-sg/Precision-RL.

Recent findings suggest that the authors generated 40 answers for each MATH problem with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B. They kept problems with a success rate between 20% and 80%, yielding 1,460 questions. This dataset is really good for RL validation because the questions are neither already solved nor completely hopeless for that model, meaning the model can get a good early signal to train on and improve.

Recent findings suggest that this is awesome as a robust end-to-end test: if one vLLM replica silently serves the base model under an adapter name, we want to see that in the curve within a few dozen steps. Also, this dataset is small enough to cycle through in less than two hours.

We also take the hyperparameters from the paper's LoRA scripts in oat/scripts/lora: Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, LoRA rank 1 with alpha 2, a learning rate of 4e-5, 8 samples per prompt, 128 completions per step, a maximum of 3,000 generated tokens and a 4,096-token context.

The trainer uses the same vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1 image with TRL installed on top. We ran the PR branch at the time; the same code now ships in TRL v1.14. The training script is a normal AsyncGRPOTrainer script. The only Job-specific values are the output directory and the server URL.

Recent findings suggest that during initialization, TRL calls /server_info. If it finds a lora_config, it uses adapter-only sync. Configurations vLLM cannot serve directly, such as DoRA, modules_to_save, or a rank above --max-lora-rank, fall back to merged-weight sync with a warning. The log should contain Adapter-only vLLM sync enabled.

Industry observers note that now onto the fun stuff. We need a proxy between the trainer and the vLLM Jobs for two reasons:.

Exposed Job ports require an Authorization: Bearer header on every request. The proxy is where that header gets added, so TRL does not need to know about it.

It has been revealed that we want more than one GPU generating. On a single vLLM server, the usual way to get that is --data-parallel-size > 1, but TRL refuses adapter-only sync in that mode, for a good reason: a call to /v1/load_lora_adapter only reaches the DP rank that answers it, so the other ranks would keep serving the base model under the newly introduced policy name. On Jobs the question does not even arise, since each replica is its own machine. So the data parallelism has to live one level up, in something that fans the adapter load out to every replica.

Sources indicate that we therefore run a small proxy at 127.0.0.1:8000 on the trainer Job and point TRL to it as if it were a single vLLM server. Besides adding the header, the proxy does two things functionally:.

A quick reminder of why this matters. Generating a completion has two phases with very different workload profiles:.

Recent findings suggest that those keys and values are the KV cache. Because attention is causal, the KV of a token depends only on the tokens before it, not on what comes after. Two requests that share a prefix therefore share the KV of that prefix, and a replica that already has it in cache can skip that part of the prefill entirely. The whole game now is to find that replica, so a request can benefit from landing on the replica that has already seen its prefix.

vLLM stores its prefix KV cache in blocks of 16 tokens. Because of GRPO, the rollout worker sends G requests with the same prompt (in our case G=8). If they all reach the same replica, the first request computes the prefill and the next seven reuse it. With round-robin routing, half would go to a replica that doesn't have the prefix cached, and those four requests would redo the prefill work and waste valuable GPU compute.

Sources indicate that the job of our router is to track which replica has seen which block hash. One important detail is that the hashes are chained, so the hash of block 3 represents blocks 1, 2 and 3, not just block 3. This mirrors causal attention: the KV of block 3 is only valid if blocks 1 and 2 are the same too. We also seed the chain with the adapter name because the KV cache also depends on the adapter that generated it: a prefix cached for policy v3 is useless for policy v4!

The video walks through the entire decision process for choosing a replica. The steps below go through a real 135-token completion request example (from the Sanity dataset problems):.

1. Split the prompt into blocks. The router receives token ids and cuts them into 16-token blocks, just like vLLM. It only hashes complete blocks, so the last 7 tokens are ignored here.

2. Hash the prefix. Each block is hashed with the previous hash, starting from the adapter seed. h3 therefore identifies blocks 1, 2 and 3 in order. Two prompts with the same first k blocks get the same hashes up to hk. Once one block changes, every hash after it changes too. This is why we seed the hashes with the adapter name: the same prompt under trl-policy-v4 starts from another seed and cannot match entries from v3. This is what we want because the old KV blocks were computed with different weights.

It has been revealed that 3. Compare two prompts. Problem 1 has 103 tokens. Both prompts start with the same 23-token chat template. Their first block is identical, but block 2 already contains the problem text. The hashes differ from there.

Industry observers note that 4. Store the owners. For every hash, the router remembers which replicas served it and which hashes came after it (we cap the successor set at two because we only need to know whether a block has one continuation or several). After a few prompts, the template block h1 is owned by both replicas and already has several successors, h2 to h8 are owned by A only and each has a single successor, and h2' to h6' are owned by B only.

In a recent development, in practice, every prompt in a run starts with the same tokens. Here, it is the chat template and the system prompt, which amount to the first 23 tokens of all 1,460 problems. In an agent setting, it would be the tool descriptions, and in a multi-turn environment it would be the shared conversation history. These blocks are in every replica's cache within seconds, so matching on them tells us nothing about where a particular prompt lives.

According to recent reports, A block is common if every replica has served it, or if it has more than one successor. Common blocks are ignored during routing because they do not identify a particular prompt. More on this below!

It has been revealed that 5. Pick a replica. The router counts how many leading blocks match on each replica and removes the common prefix. What is left is the number of blocks specific to this prompt. Then:.

Here is the rule applied to four requests. Start from a state where replicas A and B both have 3 requests in flight, and only the template block h1 is known on both replicas.

6. Reuse the prefill. Request 2 is the reason for doing all this. It reuses the prefill computed by Request 1: blocks 1 to 8 are already in A's KV cache, so A skips straight to decoding the completion. Had it gone to B, B would have prefilled all 135 tokens again while A's cache sat unused. Request 3 demonstrates why the common rule is needed. Without it, the shared chat template would make every new prompt look like a cache hit. Request 4 keeps the load bounded. Saving one prefill is not worth letting a replica fall far behind.

The common prefix is the annoying part. Every request starts with the same system prompt and chat template. A simple longest-prefix match would give the first replica a match for almost every newly introduced prompt. We detect the shared prefix through fan-out instead: a block with several different successors is common, while a block that always leads to the same successor belongs to a particular prompt. Only the blocks after that common prefix count as affinity.

According to recent reports, the proxy also needs to broadcast the adapter loads to every replica. We treat the operation as all-or-nothing. Each replica has its own bucket mount, so they do not necessarily see a new adapter at exactly the same time. A No adapter found for error usually means that one bucket mount has not caught up yet, and we retry only that replica. For any other error, we unload the adapter from the replicas that accepted it so that a policy name never exists on only part of the replicas.

We also broadcast /pause, /resume and /v1/unload_lora_adapter in the same way. /health returns 200 only if every replica is healthy. /server_info and /v1/models only need one answer. From TRL's point of view, the proxy is a single data_parallel_size=1 server, so it selects adapter-only sync.

We initially wondered whether a Python asyncio proxy would become a bottleneck. It does not (at least at this scale). There are at most 128 non-streaming JSON requests in flight, and routing only computes a few hashes. One thread handles this easily. A more refined router that needs to handle more traffic would probably need to be written in a faster language (We see you 🦀).

In a recent development, the numbers below come from the trainer's logged metrics on trackio. The run uses Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, LoRA r=1 on all-linear, 128 completions per step and 8 rollouts per prompt. It runs for 500 steps and saves a checkpoint every 50 steps. The trainer uses an h200x2 Job and each of the two vLLM replicas uses one h200 Job. Running all three costs ~$20 per hour.

All 252 adapter loads succeeded 🎉: 126 syncs times 2 replicas. Six succeeded on the second attempt and 246 on the third.

At the end of the run, after 64,728 rollouts, the proxy's counters read:.

It has been revealed that with 8 rollouts per prompt, at least one of the eight requests must be cold. The theoretical minimum is therefore 12.5 %. The router gets 14.2 % unmatched requests, 84.5 % affinity hits, and 1.3 % spills. There is not much left to gain here unless we start looking at each replica's load using deeper inference-side metrics based on real measured load.

According to recent reports, the first configuration has a pretty obvious problem: the trainer is the bottleneck, not generation. Over the 500 steps, we have:.

The rollout queue stays full, and the worker is mostly blocked by backpressure. The second replica is basically useless in this configuration. We'll see later in the post how we went through runs that moved the bottleneck between training and generation to make the run 3.9× faster.

Industry observers note that figure 1. trackio run r1-dp2. Panels: reward with its 20-step rolling mean and 50-step block means, and ratio on a 0.99 to 1.01 axis. Reward climbs from 0.15 to 0.44 over 500 steps; ratio stays between 0.9993 and 1.0004 throughout.

According to recent reports, 500 steps took 3 h 27 min. Mean reward goes from 0.145 over the first 20 steps to 0.438 over the last 20. More importantly for this test, ratio stays at 1.000 for every step! The policy served by vLLM always matches the one used by the trainer to score the rollout. This held across all 126 syncs. Mean staleness was 1.5 policy versions, against a maximum of 4. The trackio dashboard has the full curves.

It has been revealed that we have our undeniable proof that LoRA AsyncGRPO works! Let's now see how we can improve our training runs by looking at the recent detailed AsyncGRPO metrics.

Async RL is a pipeline between training and generation. Making one side faster does nothing if the other side cannot keep up. Fortunately, in AsyncGRPOTrainer we've added enough timings and metrics to see this directly.

Recent findings suggest that all the useful metrics are documented in the Logged metrics section. perf/rollout_wait_s tells us how long the trainer waits for samples. rollout/backpressure_s tells us how long generation waits for space in the rollout queue. They are diametrically opposed to each other and should not both be high. Together with the queue size, they tell us which side is slow.

Recent findings suggest that we ran five experiments. Each one starts from a problem visible in the previous run's dashboard. Unless mentioned otherwise, the model, recipe and three-Job layout stay the same. The names below are the trackio run names.

We keep these four groups of metrics visible:.

The diagnosis is simple: a full queue with zero rollout wait and high backpressure means the trainer is too slow. An empty queue with rising rollout wait and no backpressure means generation is too slow. Comparing perf/mfu_wall_clock with perf/mfu_fwd_bwd also demonstrates how much time the trainer GPUs spend waiting instead of training.

Sources indicate that figure 2. trackio run r1-dp2. Panels: perf/step_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, sample/rollout_queue_size, rollout/backpressure_s. Step time and forward+backward overlap almost completely; the queue sits pinned near 476 of 512 and backpressure never drops below 11 s per rollout group: trainer-bound.

According to recent reports, perf/step_s is 22.9 s and perf/fwd_bwd_s is 21.9 s. Forward and backward take 96 % of the step time. The queue stays full and the trainer waits only 0.02 s for rollouts, and the rollout worker spends 15 seconds per group blocked by backpressure. The two vLLM replicas generate faster than the trainer consumes. The reported 4.6k tokens/s is not their actual limit; they simply have nowhere to put more output.

Sources indicate that the batch metrics explain the terrible 3.9 % MFU. batch/microbatches_per_step is 64 and batch/samples_per_row is 1.0. Each rank processes one sequence of around 1.2k tokens, 64 times per step. This comes from the reference recipe's per_device_train_batch_size=1. For a 1.5B model on an H200, this is completely latency-bound.

Industry observers note that the fix is not to change the batch size. We keep 128 completions per optimizer step and only change how they are laid out on the GPU: instead of one sequence per microbatch, we pack many sequences densely into each row. The trainer supports this through token-budget batching. With token_budget > 0, it packs several samples into one padding-free row per rank. An optimizer step processes gradient_accumulation_steps rows. We set token_budget=16384 and gradient_accumulation_steps=6.

Figure 3. trackio runs r1-dp2 and r1-dp2-tb16k overlaid over their first 154 steps. Panels: batch/samples_per_row, batch/microbatches_per_step, perf/step_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, perf/mfu_fwd_bwd, rollout/generated_tok_s. Packing takes samples per row from 1 to 13, microbatches from 64 to 6, step time from 23 s to 5.9 s, and generation from 4.2k to 27.5k tok/s with no change on the vLLM side.

It has been revealed that batch/samples_per_row goes from 1.0 to ~12.7 and the number of microbatches drops from 64 to 6. The rows are 95 % full! Forward and backward fall from 21.9 s to 5.6 s, while MFU rises from 3.9 % to 19 %. We now train on around 150 samples per step because the rows pack better than the mean-length estimate predicted.

In a recent development, generation also jumps from 4.6k to 25k tokens/s, even though we changed nothing on the vLLM side. The queue is no longer constantly full, so the replicas can finally run. This is why we do not like optimizing pipeline stages in isolation. We need to be careful to evaluate the whole system, as a slow stage can hide the real performance of everything before it.

perf/fwd_s is 1.34 s while perf/fwd_bwd_s is 5.6 s. A normal backward costs roughly twice the forward, and with frozen base weights it should be closer to once. A ratio of 3.2 is suspicious.

The reason is that AsyncGRPOConfig defaults to gradient_checkpointing=True. Every microbatch recomputes its forward during the backward. This also explains why a 16k-token row only uses 25 GB on a 141 GB H200! It's a memory optimization for this trainer, but we don't need it in this specific case: the model is small enough to fit into VRAM with the activations kept for the backward.

Figure 4. trackio runs r1-dp2-tb16k and r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt overlaid over their first 134 steps. Panels: perf/fwd_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, perf/weight_sync_s, sample/rollout_queue_size, perf/rollout_wait_s, perf/mfu_fwd_bwd. Forward+backward drops by one forward; the queue falls from ~420 to ~60, and rollout wait rises from 0.02 s to 0.5 s: the bottleneck shifts to generation.

With gradient_checkpointing=False, forward and backward drop to 4.6 s, almost exactly one forward less, and MFU reaches 23 %. The queue now falls to 71 and rollout wait rises from 0.04 s to 0.6 s. The trainer consumes samples faster than two replicas generate them. We successfully moved the bottleneck to generation.

In a recent development, this exposes two more costs. A 7.6-second weight sync every four steps now takes 25 % of wall-clock time. It was only 8 % when each step took 23 seconds. Also, backward is still 2.5 times slower than forward. With frozen base weights, there are around 2 seconds per step that do not look like normal model math.

According to recent reports, since generation was now too slow, we added a third replica. We also reduced the adapter retry interval from 2 s to 0.5 s in the proxy and disabled fsdp_reshard_after_forward to check whether FSDP2 re-gathers caused the extra 2 seconds in backward.

It has been revealed that figure 5. trackio runs r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt and r1-dp3-tb16k-nockpt overlaid over their first 134 steps. Panels: perf/weight_sync_s, rollout/generated_tok_s, rollout/inflight, perf/fwd_bwd_s. Sync falls from 7.6 s to 5.8 s; generation and forward+backward do not move; rollout/inflight reads 128 in both runs, which is the cap the third replica ran into.

Weight sync falls from 7.6 s to 5.8 s, so the shorter retry helps. Forward and backward stay at 4.6 s, which rules out resharding. Generation moves from 25k to only 26k tokens/s. The third replica does basically nothing.

Recent findings suggest that the reason was sitting in rollout/inflight: 128 in every run. The proxy highlights those requests split as 44 + 43 + 41 across the three replicas. max_inflight_tasks limits concurrency for the whole rollout worker, not per replica. A 1.5B model on an H200 processes 43 and 130 concurrent sequences at almost the same cost per token. Splitting 128 requests over three GPUs gives nearly the same throughput as splitting them over two.

Industry observers note that so vLLM was not the limit. Our own client-side constant was. We had set it conservatively because we did not know how hundreds of long HTTPS requests would behave through the public Jobs proxy. At this point, 130,000 rollout completions had crossed it without a single transport error.

max_inflight_tasks=384 and queue_maxsize=768, nothing else.

Figure 6. All five trackio runs (r1-dp2, r1-dp2-tb16k, r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt, r1-dp3-tb16k-nockpt, r1-dp3-inflight384) overlaid, x-axis in steps. Panels: perf/step_s, reward, sample/rollout_queue_size, sample/staleness_mean. Step time falls from 22.9 s to 4.8 s across the series while the reward curves stay on top of each other; the last run's queue refills to ~690 of 768 and its staleness settles at 2. Runs 2 to 4 were stopped early once the dashboard had answered the question.

With 384 requests in flight, each replica gets 128. The queue promptly fills to around 690 out of 768 and stays there. Backpressure returns to 5 seconds and rollout wait falls to 0.03 seconds. Training is the bottleneck again! Forward and backward take 4.6 seconds, weight sync adds an amortized 1.5 seconds, and median step time is 4.8 seconds.

In a recent development, mean staleness rises from 1.5 to 2.0 versions because samples wait longer in the larger queue. This is still below max_staleness=4, and ratio remains very close to 1.000.

Figure 7. trackio runs r1-dp2 and r1-dp3-inflight384, reward against wall-clock minutes since the first optimizer step. Same recipe, same 500 steps, same final reward; run 5 gets there in 52 minutes instead of 3 h 26 min.

Recent findings suggest that the final run is 3.9× faster and trains on 31 % more samples, with basically the same reward curve. Packing, disabling checkpointing and raising the in-flight limit made the difference. In each case, the dashboard made this clear within the first ten minutes.

LoRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret. They show that LoRA can match full fine-tuning for policy-gradient RL, even with sportzfy rank 1. This stems from the fact that the advantage function only gives ~O(1) bits of information per episode, so there is not that much to learn from each step, from a total-bits-of-information point of view. A rank-1 adapter has enough capacity to absorb it.

Really interesting take on how LoRA changes the systems side of RL training, not just the training itself. The idea of separating training and inference across different machines while only moving a small adapter instead of the full model makes a lot of practical sense, especially when working with HF Jobs. The “bucket, proxy, and no NCCL” approach feels like a good example of simplifying distributed infrastructure by moving the communication boundary to something much smaller and easier to manage.

I also like the connection to the LoRA Without Regret work, particularly the point that policy-gradient updates may not require huge adapter capacity to capture the useful signal. Sending only a few MB instead of several GB after updates can make a massive difference in both bandwidth and iteration speed. Would be really interested to see more details on how the bucket/proxy setup behaves at scale and whether there are any noticeable trade-offs once the number of inference workers or concurrent rollouts increases.

Support team put in an emergency order for vodka – lots of vodka – to bring PCs back online

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the end of the working week is often enough to drive tech support people to drink, which is why The Register likes to get the party started early.
  • This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Bruce," who told us that in the mid-2000s he worked for a global radio station.
  • "We used to have about 30 PCs, all running slightly different radio highlights depending on the time zone where we broadcast," he explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some clean-up jobs need powerful stuff.

According to recent reports, the end of the working week is often enough to drive tech support people to drink, which is why The Register likes to get the party started early. Friday mornings bring a new installment of On Call – the column in which we share your stories of doing whatever it takes to keep tech running.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Bruce," who told us that in the mid-2000s he worked for a global radio station.

"We used to have about 30 PCs, all running slightly different radio highlights depending on the time zone where we broadcast," he explained.

Recent findings suggest that the PCs were old clunkers running Windows 95 long after Microsoft ended support for the OS. Management knew the machines needed replacing, but funding was probably another year away.

In a recent development, "We had to coax them on till then," Bruce wrote. "And by coax, I mean we were buying RAM on eBay because nobody sold the 4MB sticks we needed anymore.".

Thanks to the tender ministrations of Bruce and his colleagues, the PCs kept humming and the radio stations stayed on the air.

Until a lovely spring Tuesday, when Bruce and his crew enjoyed a bucolic cup of tea in the first real sunshine of the season and received a call informing them that one of the stations was down.

One of Bruce's mates figured a cranky old PC probably just needed a reboot and headed off to fix it while the rest of the team enjoyed their tea.

And then the phone rang again to report another outage, so Bruce and the entire crew went back to work, chatting about which switch or other shared device could have taken out two PCs.

When they arrived in the office, the chap who had gone to reboot the first PC ran in and announced that the computer room had flooded.

Bruce and his teammates ran into that room and found dirty brown water all over the floor, walls, ceiling, and the racks holding the ancient PCs.

"Water was even spraying out of the front fans of the last two PCs that were still working," Bruce told The Register.

"After a lot of shouting words unfit to print, we all got to work ripping them out, shutting down what we could that looked to be working, and started lining them up outside in the car park," Bruce wrote. "Some of us then got to work stripping them down into component parts, others washed them down with isopropanol.".

As the isopropanol supply dwindled, one of the team arranged an urgent delivery of vodka.

"Luckily, it was a gloriously sunny day, so we quickly rinsed the PCs and left them to dry, strewn all over the car park," Bruce wrote.

Recent findings suggest that by this stage, he and the team were all filthy and exhausted. With the stations still offline, they had to rebuild the PCs and get them running again.

"We only lost two sticks of RAM, one sound card, and a power supply," Bruce wrote.

The culprit turned out to be a new hire on the facilities team who, while touring the building, had turned a random tap to see what would happen.

Recent findings suggest that "It released water from a stagnant iron tank that sat there rusting away for years," Bruce wrote. For reasons nobody understood, the tank drained through a pipe into the room housing the broadcast PCs.

Have you had to clean up hardware in a hurry, perhaps with odd substances or implements? If so, click here to send On Call your story. We'll raise a glass to each one of you who sends a story and do it again if we share it on a future Friday. ®.

#230060. Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

📅 15 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1825 w)

Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

📅 15 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.
  • According to recent reports, that is embarrassing onstage.
  • Industry observers note that most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.

According to recent reports, that is embarrassing onstage. In production, it is a reliability problem: a workflow that succeeded once may fail the next time a user makes the same request. For mission-critical work, such as reconciling a financial transaction or checking a contract for an obligation, that can be a showstopper.

Industry observers note that most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average. On AppWorld, a ReAct agent using GPT-4.1 succeeded on 77.4% of runs across five repetitions. But it succeeded in all five runs for only 53.0% of tasks — a 24.4-point consistency gap.

Industry observers note that most benchmarks report the first number. We built a way to measure the second — and improve it.

Sources indicate that in an earlier post, we introduced ALTK-Evolve — a system that turns an agent's own past trajectories into reusable guidelines, distilled automatically and injected back at inference time. It measurably improves task success, but those results only asked the average-case question too. This post introduces consistency guidelines, a upcoming guideline type in altk-evolve built on top of a diagnostic tool we call the Consistency Analyzer, that targets this gap directly.

Industry observers note that standard agent evaluation reports Mean@k: run a benchmark k times, average the pass rate. Often k=3, sometimes just 1. It's the number on every leaderboard, and it's what "77% accurate" means in practice.

Mean@k answers "how good is this agent, on average?" It does not answer the question a real user cares about: will it still be good if I ask this exact question again? For that you need Pass^k: the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds on all k runs.

In a recent development, ⚠️ Pass^k is not Pass@k. The familiar Pass@k is optimistic — it asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeded, the right question when you can verify and retry. Pass^k is its pessimistic mirror image: every attempt must succeed. Same letters, opposite question. Pass^k ≤ Mean@k ≤ Pass@k, always.

A ReAct agent backed by GPT-4.1 posts a Mean@5 of 77.4% — genuinely strong. But Pass^5 is only 53.0%. Nearly a quarter of the benchmark consists of tasks the agent can sometimes solve and sometimes can't, with nothing about the task changing between runs. We call this gap — Mean@k minus Pass^k — the consistency gap.

According to recent reports, this isn't a capability problem you fix with a bigger model. It's an orthogonal axis: an agent can be capable and inconsistent at the same time.

Every time an LLM agent decides something — which API to call, what argument to pass, whether to retry — that decision comes out of a probability distribution over next tokens. What matters is the shape of that distribution. A sharp one puts most of its mass on a single token: the runners-up are far behind, and the same choice comes out run after run. A flat one spreads comparable mass across several near-tied tokens, and which one wins is close to a coin flip.

The shape decides how much noise it takes to change the outcome. Sharp distributions are resilient — GPU floating-point non-associativity, request batching, and other platform-side effects nudge the numbers slightly, but nowhere near enough to reorder a clear winner. Flat distributions are vulnerable to exactly that nudge: near-ties may reorder under small perturbations. And because a trajectory chains dozens of decisions, a small per-step chance of flipping compounds into a large chance that some run goes differently. That's where a 24-point gap comes from.

This is also why the problem survives your decoding settings. Greedy decoding and a fixed seed both govern how a distribution gets turned into a token — they say nothing about the distribution itself. On a hosted endpoint the probabilities shift slightly from run to run, so the same prompt to the same model at temperature zero can still resolve a near-tie one way today and the other way tomorrow.

Our setup: the ReAct agent runs at temperature 0.0, so none of the variance above is ordinary sampling.

Which turns the problem into a search: which steps in a given trajectory were the flat ones — and what do you do about them once you know?

Consistency guidelines come out of a two-stage pipeline that plugs into ALTK-Evolve's existing machinery — with a new source signal driving what gets written.

1. Detect — the Consistency Analyzer. Given one recorded trajectory, the analyzer replays each decision step through controlled resampling, measuring how much the model's output actually varies at that point. Concretely, that's one additional model call per decision step, done once offline — issued with the sampling parameter set to draw k completions at once (k=5 by default) — replayed against the already-recorded context, not upcoming tool calls, not new environment interactions, and not a second end-to-end rollout of the task. This yields a consistency score per decision step that is written into a scorecard to pinpoint exactly which decisions are at risk of flipping on the next run. Detection is fully black-box — no logits, no model internals, no instrumentation beyond the trace you already have.

2. Generate — targeted guidelines. Every flagged step becomes a candidate consistency guideline in the standard ALTK-Evolve format, so it slots into the existing storage and retrieval pipeline. Here's a real example, generated by GPT-4.1 from a trajectory of the AppWorld task "How many activities are done in my bucket list as per my SimpleNote note?":.

[Guideline 1] When counting checkbox-style markers in note content, use a line-anchored regex match rather than a plain substring count — note titles often repeat the marker symbol in a legend line.

[Guideline 2] Always verify search results for note queries by checking for multiple matches and confirming the correct note before proceeding.

Sources indicate that nothing here is task-specific trivia. String-counting bugs and unverified search results are decision points that show up with high uncertainty across many AppWorld tasks. That's the point: the analyzer targets instability, not failure — so it catches steps the agent happened to get right this time but could easily get wrong next time.

Watch the 2-minute demo — five parallel runs of the agent split 3-2 on this task because of agent uncertainty about the counting strategy, then run again after these guidelines in context: all five agree.

We evaluated on AppWorld test_normal (168 tasks) with a ReAct agent on GPT-4.1, generating consistency guidelines from a single baseline trajectory per task and testing them on 5 fresh runs.

Mean@5 (%), aggregate — same scale as Pass^5 above.

According to recent reports, the consistency gap is cut roughly in half. Aggregate Pass^5 rises 53.0% → 69.0% while Mean@5 rises 77.4% → 81.0%, narrowing the gap between "looks capable" and "can be counted on" from 24.4pp to 12.0pp. Nearly a third of previously-inconsistent tasks become tasks the agent passes on every single run.

It has been revealed that the middle and hard tiers gain most. Medium +22.9pp (+44% relative), Hard +14.3pp (+45% relative) — effectively tied in relative terms, with Medium ahead absolutely. Easy gains +12.2pp, having had the least room. This is consistency guidelines doing what they're designed to do: finding and stabilizing the specific decision points where an agent's own uncertainty was leaking into the outcome.

Sources indicate that mean@5 never drops. Preserving average accuracy was a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have: a system that boosts Pass^5 by trading away Mean@5 would just be shifting unreliability around, not fixing it. Mean accuracy holds or improves at every difficulty level.

Sources indicate that applied to a different but related task in the same AppWorld scenario — another variant of the scenario the guidelines were mined from — consistency guidelines still lift Pass^5 by +13.0pp, only 3 points below the same-task number. A guideline derived from one run isn't just patching that run; it's capturing something that transfers.

The sharper evidence comes from a weaker model, gpt-oss-120b. Same-task Pass^5 rose +6.0pp from a much lower baseline (10.1% → 16.1%) — and, interestingly, the similar-task generalization number (+8.7 pp) actually exceeded the same-task gain, suggesting the guidelines were capturing genuinely reusable failure patterns rather than memorizing one trajectory's specifics.

Try the ALTK-Evolve — the open-source repo now includes the Consistency Analyzer and consistency-guideline generation used in these experiments — or read the technical report on arXiv for the complete methodology.

If accuracy numbers you can't reproduce on your own tasks sound familiar, we'd like to hear about it — concrete examples of flip-prone behavior in your own agents are exactly the kind of feedback that shapes what we build next. Open an issue or a discussion.

Great perspective on agent reliability. Measuring consistency alongside accuracy seems especially important as AI agents move into workflows where reproducibility matters. The Consistency Analyzer approach is a fascinating way to identify unstable decisions without requiring full task replays.

The useful split is the one most dashboards still refuse to print: Mean@k answers “how good is this agent on average?” Pass^k answers “will the same request still succeed if I ask again?”.

Once you’ve watched a trajectory chain dozens of near-tied tool choices, a strong average with a wide consistency gap is exactly the demo that fails live. Capability and consistency are orthogonal — buying a bigger model can lift Mean without closing the gap.

Sources indicate that what I want teams to take from the Consistency Analyzer framing is operational, not the guideline machinery itself: treat flip-prone decision steps as first-class eval targets. One offline resample pass over a recorded trace is a cheaper reliability signal than another end-to-end leaderboard screenshot.

Practical ask for anyone shipping agents from this: do you report Pass^k (even k=3) next to Mean@k in the release gate, and do you refuse the “stable” label when the consistency gap is still large on your hard tier?

Recent findings suggest that reproducible reliability will not remove disagreement about which guidelines to inject. It will make the disagreement about the right metric.

Thanks, and you've landed on exactly the operational takeaway we hoped for: flip-prone decision steps should be eval targets in their own right. Beyond that, knowing where they are also turns the eval into a diagnostic: a consistency gap tells you that an agent is unreliable, while the flip-prone steps tell you where and why.

On your release-gate question: we'd strongly encourage it, and k=3 is a sensible default. A few things we'd suggest to anyone adopting Pass^k as a gate:.

I'd like to understand your closing point better. In our experiments, we didn't choose among individual guidelines: for each upcoming task, we injected the guidelines derived from the most similar task. I'm curious where you see the disagreement about which guidelines to inject arising.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Mock Service Worker Releases v3.0 with ESM-Only Build, Socket-Based Interception and GraphQL Subs.

Nov 26, 2026 2 min read.

Mock Service Worker, the API mocking library maintained by Artem Zakharchenko, has released version 3.0, nearly three years after the Fetch-based v2.0 rewrite. The release ships as ESM-only, completes the library's GraphQL story with subscription support, and introduces a socket-based interception algorithm in Node.js that Zakharchenko describes as going as deep into the runtime as JavaScript will allow without recompiling Node.

The headline breaking change is that MSW is now distributed natively as ECMAScript Modules only, with support for Node.js v18 and v20 dropped in favour of v22, v24, and v26. TypeScript 5.9 is now the minimum supported version. Several transitive dependencies have been removed, including graphql (now a proper optional peer), path-to-regexp, picocolors, and statuses. The result is a library tarball that drops from 416KB to 234KB, with type definitions shrinking by half, from 190KB to 90KB.

Alongside ESM, v3.0 introduces granular entrypoints that replace the single msw import with designated paths for each protocol:.

In a recent development, graphQL subscription support, a long-standing community request on the project's tracker, lands in this release. Building on the WebSocket interception shipped previously, subscription handlers can now be defined against a graphql.link() and publish events on demand, closing the gap between MSW's HTTP, WebSocket, and GraphQL coverage.

Sources indicate that an experimental defineNetwork API is introduced as the eventual replacement for setupServer and setupWorker. The new primitive splits interception into sources (where traffic comes from) and handlers (how it is answered), allowing teams to replay HAR files, combine custom interceptors, or hand control of request timing to a test runner. The first ecosystem package to expose it directly is @msw/cloudflare, which wraps the API for Workers environments.

The most technically significant change sits in the underlying Interceptors library. Zakharchenko writes that after seven attempts at the problem, the team has moved network interception in Node.js down to the TCP and TLS wraps, the JavaScript bindings for Node's C-level network code. Moving any lower, he notes, would require recompiling Node.js itself. The newly introduced architecture supports arbitrary socket-based protocols, with SMTP cited as an early example. Nock already relies on the Interceptors library for its Node.js support.

Recent findings suggest that A GitHub discussion reports failing tests after upgrading, traced to MSW now intercepting the browser-issued OPTIONS preflight requests that previous versions quietly ignored. Separately, a developer in discussion #2771 challenged the earlier decision to deprioritise Jest and JSDOM, arguing that a runner with 46 million weekly downloads warrants a formal breaking-change note rather than a quiet docs change.

In the Node-only space, MSW continues to compete with Nock, fetch-mock, and undici's built-in MockAgent, though as a recent comparison notes, none of those cover both browser and server with a single handler definition.

According to recent reports, teams on v2 should consult the official 2.x to 3.x migration guide before upgrading. Full release notes are available on GitHub.

Mock Service Worker is an open-source, MIT-licensed JavaScript library for mocking network traffic using Service Workers in the browser and runtime-level interception in Node.js. It is used widely for frontend and full-stack testing, and now covers HTTP, WebSocket, Server-Sent Events, and GraphQL including subscriptions.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Huntington Ingalls Industries lands deal despite MoD pledge to buy British wherever possible.
  • Britain's Royal Navy is investing £142 million ($185 million) in underwater drones to tackle sea mines, but the contract has gone to an American defense supplier.
  • The Ministry of Defence (MoD) notes that the UK's ability to protect vital sea routes will be strengthened through the procurement of these Uncrewed Underwater Vehicles (UUVs).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Huntington Ingalls Industries lands deal despite MoD pledge to buy British wherever possible.

Britain's Royal Navy is investing £142 million ($185 million) in underwater drones to tackle sea mines, but the contract has gone to an American defense supplier.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) notes that the UK's ability to protect vital sea routes will be strengthened through the procurement of these Uncrewed Underwater Vehicles (UUVs).

These will form part of the Royal Navy's move toward a "Hybrid Navy" comprising a mix of crewed, uncrewed, and autonomous platforms in order to meet future challenges.

The UUV selected for the job is the REMUS 620, built by Huntington Ingalls Industries (HII), the largest military shipbuilding tech giant in the United States. HII has a facility at Portchester, on the south coast of England, but is still a US-owned company.

We asked the MoD how the award fits its pledge to prioritize buying British wherever possible, and what share of the contract's value will support UK industry.

The contract includes HII's Sea Launcher automated launch and recovery systems and will bring support services previously delivered overseas to the UK. HII claims it will support 15 jobs, while the MoD identifies Portchester among the locations benefiting.

According to recent reports, HII says this is the largest international order in its 25-year history of supplying uncrewed systems. The MoD has previously acquired REMUS 100, REMUS 300, and REMUS 600 vehicles for mine countermeasure operations.

The latest vehicles will locate sea mines to support clearance operations and help keep shipping routes open.

By using drones to comb a body of water for explosive devices, the Royal Navy's crews can be kept a safe distance from any potential immediate threat. Traditionally, this work has been conducted by specialist crewed ships such as the Hunt class or Sandown class, but these are being retired from service in favor of uncrewed systems.

The Royal Navy also operates SWEEP, an uncrewed boat towing equipment that mimics a ship's magnetic, acoustic, and electric signatures to trigger mines from a safe distance.

The new REMUS underwater vehicles can be sent ahead of other vessels to search beneath the surface, making minehunting operations safer, faster and more flexible, according to the MoD.

"This investment strengthens our ability to protect freedom of navigation, which is critical to our security and our economy," remarked Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP.

In a recent development, like others in the portfolio, REMUS 620 resembles a naval torpedo. It is capable of operating at depths of 600 meters and has an endurance of up to 110 hours on a single mission. The drones will be integrated with SeeTrack and Neptune software developed by SeeByte in the UK, which is already used by the Royal Navy.

In trials revealed in October 2025, a REMUS 620 demonstrated launch and recovery using a submerged test fixture replicating a Virginia-class submarine's torpedo tube. The work could enable submarines to deploy and retrieve underwater drones on future missions. ®.

#230054. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured
