General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows.
  • In a recent development, as models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift.
  • This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

In a recent development, as models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

Sources indicate that this work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project highlighted they were worth trying.

According to recent reports, before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

According to recent reports, we showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

Sources indicate that A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:.

According to recent reports, BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

Sources indicate that A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

In a recent development, this depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. New words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Reproduce the shared-prefix result with:.

Sources indicate that caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

It has been revealed that the next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

In a recent development, each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

In a recent development, repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on latest input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

It has been revealed that across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

Industry observers note that the overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

Industry observers note that the next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the upcoming merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:.

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Recent findings suggest that every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

Sources indicate that the benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we initiative to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:.

According to recent reports, the department declared the precautionary shutdown on Friday morning. "We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems," it noted.

"We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3) to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimize any disruption.

Industry observers note that "Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal. If an online service you need is unavailable, please try again later. As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links.".

Recent findings suggest that the Register contacted both the DWP and NCSC for more information. The DWP declined to comment beyond the statement issued publicly.

According to recent reports, GC3 coordinates responses to incidents affecting government. The Government Cyber Unit leads the wider Government Cyber Action Plan, backed by more than £210 million. It is led by the government CISO, Bella Powell.

Officials have not commented on any of the usual details one would expect from a cyber incident disclosure, including the specific services that were downed, when they are expected to return, or whether any data is thought to be compromised, even at this early stage.

The UK government has also been criticized recently for investing heavily in AI cyber defenses, while the issue of legacy and aging IT continues to be neglected in the background.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

Industry observers note that MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are big MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

It has been revealed that stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

Concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make upcoming transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.

Breaking: How WinHelp files work

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1222 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Quin

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I wanted Paperback to be able to open some old WinHelp .hlp files I had laying around, so I wrote libhlp, a pure-Rust reader for them.
  • Microsoft never documented the format, but Manfred Winterhoff did, in helpfile.txt, which ships alongside his decompiler, helpdeco.
  • Recent findings suggest that A .hlp file starts with the magic number 3F 5F 03 00, followed by the position of its internal directory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I wanted Paperback to be able to open some old WinHelp .hlp files I had laying around, so I wrote libhlp, a pure-Rust reader for them. I had my wisdom teeth out on a Friday morning, spent the rest of that day completely out of it, and then woke up Saturday and did this instead of resting like a normal person. Recovering patients make great decisions.

Microsoft never documented the format, but Manfred Winterhoff did, in helpfile.txt, which ships alongside his decompiler, helpdeco. Between those and poking at real files, I worked out the format, and Claude wrote a lot of the actual Rust.

Recent findings suggest that A .hlp file starts with the magic number 3F 5F 03 00, followed by the position of its internal directory. A help file is really an archive, and that directory lists the files inside it. Most of them have names starting with a pipe: |SYSTEM holds the title and settings, |TOPIC holds the text, |FONT holds the fonts, |CONTEXT holds the topic names, and pictures live in files like |bm0.

The directory is a B+ tree, and so is every other index in the file, all with the same page layout.

All the text lives in |TOPIC, which is cut into fixed-size blocks. Each block can be LZ77 compressed, and positions in the file count bytes of the decompressed text, not of the file itself. Every block also takes up the same amount of that address space whether it fills it or not. In a typical file, each block gets 16 KB of space and only decompresses to about 4 KB, so reading has to skip the gap to the next block.

Inside the blocks, the text is a linked list of records. Some records start a new topic, and the rest hold its paragraphs, each with a formatting part and a text part. The text part can be compressed a second time, which is where it gets fun.

WinHelp's LZ77 is about as simple as compression gets. The data comes in groups: one flag byte, then up to eight items. Each bit of the flag byte, lowest first, indicates whether its item is a literal byte or a back-reference. A back-reference is two bytes, with 12 bits of distance and 4 bits of length:.

Recent findings suggest that the length is stored minus 3, since anything shorter isn't worth a back-reference. A distance of 0 means "repeat the byte I just wrote", and since the copy can read bytes it's still writing, x followed by a back-reference of length 5 becomes xxxxxx.

One fun quirk: some real files have back-references that reach behind the start of the data, where there's nothing to copy yet. helpdeco keeps its 4 KB window in a buffer that starts out full of zeroes, so those references just copy zeroes, and the files come out right that way. libhlp starts its window out zeroed too, instead of treating it as an error or reading off the front of the buffer.

On top of LZ77, a help file can swap its most common phrases for short codes, and there are two versions of this.

WinHelp 3.1 keeps the table in |Phrases. In the text, any byte from 1 to 15 starts a two-byte code, and every other byte is just itself:.

The lowest bit of the code claims whether a space follows the phrase. Phrases usually end at a word, so that saves a byte most of the time.

The Windows 95 help compiler added a fancier scheme, called Hall compression, with the phrases split across |PhrIndex and |PhrImage. Here, the lowest bits of each byte say what kind of byte it is. If the lowest bit is clear, the rest of the byte picks one of the first 128 phrases, so the most common ones fit in a single byte. Ending in 01 starts a two-byte code for the rest of the table, 011 starts a run of literal bytes, 0111 means a run of spaces, and 1111 means a run of zero bytes. For the runs, the upper bits hold the length minus one, since a run of nothing would be a wasted byte.

|PhrIndex doesn't store where each phrase starts. It stores how long each one is, packed into as few bits as it can get away with. Each length is a unary count in steps of some power of two, followed by the remaining low bits to add on top. The step size is set once for the whole file.

My first version always read at least one remainder bit. That works until a file uses a step of one, where there's no remainder to store. Then every length reads one bit too many, and everything after the first phrase is garbage. The fix was a single bits > 0 check.

According to recent reports, when a help author wrote a topic, they gave it a context string, a name like SaveFile. You'd expect a link to store the position of the topic it points to, but it actually stores a hash of the target's name. To follow a link, you hash its target name the way WinHelp does and look the result up in |CONTEXT, which maps hashes to positions.

According to recent reports, each byte goes through a lookup table that gives uppercase and lowercase letters the same values, so links are case insensitive. The table's entries are signed, so anything at or above 0x80 subtracts instead of adding. Get that wrong and almost every hash still comes out right, so it's really easy to miss. Oh, and an empty name hashes to 1, not 0, because that's what WinHelp does.

Text doesn't store its own formatting. A paragraph states "switch to font 4", and |FONT says font 4 is the bold one. Links are drawn the same way. WinHelp underlines a link by switching to an underlined font, so libhlp has to tell that underline apart from underlining the author actually asked for.

WinHelp is older than Unicode, so text is stored in whatever Windows code page the author used, which might be a double-byte one for East Asian languages. Sometimes the file's language ID claims which one. When it doesn't and the text is mostly non-ASCII, libhlp guesses the code page from the text itself.

Recent findings suggest that then there's WinHelp 3.0, the version from Windows 3.0, which is different enough to almost be its own format. Its topic blocks are 2 KB and never compressed, its records give the distance to the next record instead of its position, its topic headers are 12 bytes instead of 28, and its links point at topic numbers instead of hashes. libhlp reads it, but it took its own commit.

And then there are the files that only share the extension. Borland's help compiler and MS-DOS QuickHelp both made .hlp files that have nothing else in common with WinHelp, so libhlp just turns those away.

It reads the text, titles, tables, emphasis, links and pictures of every WinHelp version I know of, from 3.0 to the Windows 95 compiler, and it bounds checks everything. Paperback uses it to open .hlp files, so if you've got an old one sitting around, now you can read it.

AI boom leaves network operators waiting up to 18 months for kit

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Optical equipment prices up around 50% this year as telcos compete with datacenters for components, states RETN.
  • The AI building boom is driving up optical networking equipment prices and stretching delivery times to as much as 18 months, according to network operator RETN.
  • RETN says that network operators and telcos are now directly competing with AI datacenters for chips and other components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Optical equipment prices up around 50% this year as telcos compete with datacenters for components, states RETN.

The AI building boom is driving up optical networking equipment prices and stretching delivery times to as much as 18 months, according to network operator RETN.

RETN says that network operators and telcos are now directly competing with AI datacenters for chips and other components.

In a recent development, as Reg readers will be aware, memory prices have soared by four or five times over the past year or so, but RETN indicates optical networking equipment prices have risen by around 50 percent since the start of 2026. Worse are the extended delivery times, with optical network kit that used to arrive within three months now taking 12 to 15, and some orders taking up to 18 months.

This is as bad as, if not worse than, the shortages during the pandemic, when chip supply problems left network vendors unable to fulfill orders. The matter now is that because of the AI boom, demand is outpacing supplies.

In its report, "AI, Connected," RETN says developers building outside established datacenter hubs may need to involve network carriers two to five years before opening.

It has been revealed that the sudden demand for network kit from hyperscalers and AI campuses is only one factor, RETN states. Raw material shortages, skilled labor shortages, energy constraints, geopolitical tensions, and logistical challenges are also compounding the glitch.

Recent findings suggest that however, it concedes that many carriers didn't help themselves by previously postponing network upgrades to cut expenditure. That work has now become unavoidable at the worst possible time.

According to recent reports, network diversity is now seen as a must-have, the report says. Where customers were once satisfied with two routes to long-haul destinations, they expect operators to provide four or more redundant routes now.

The aim is to prevent a single failure from taking down critical services. Multiple connections are only useful protection if they avoid shared physical failure points, such as the same ducts or cable routes. A diverse circuit might cost €1,800 ($1,975) a month instead of €600 ($658), it claims, but an outage could prove far more costly.

Sources indicate that RETN also claims AI datacenters are moving away from populated areas to remote locations, where access to suitable land, power and water may be easier to come by. Hyperscalers are building in the Nordics, where land is affordable, the climate is cooler, and plenty of renewable energy is available.

In a recent development, remote sites may lack the fiber infrastructure needed to connect them to other datacenters and customers. The Register reported on this problem earlier this year.

For sites close to cities, developers often fund the fiber themselves, which adds just a few percent to the total project cost. But over longer distances, the case becomes harder to make, and carriers are understandably reluctant to build a long-haul route to serve a single remote site.

Some developers are prepared to swallow the cost: RETN says a major cloud provider is exploring converting an abandoned factory in Central Europe into a large-scale server farm, despite little existing fiber in the area.

However, RETN's warning is that connectivity must be planned alongside power and construction, not left until the datacenter is nearly ready to open. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a significant part of that.
  • In a recent development, this is where we are right now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

According to recent reports, running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a significant part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:.

In a recent development, this is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.

Recent findings suggest that GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so owners can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

In a recent development, we want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:.

According to recent reports, we suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

According to recent reports, no extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:.

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:.

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

According to recent reports, llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:.

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):.

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

According to recent reports, transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

Recent findings suggest that we also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

According to recent reports, our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

Recent findings suggest that A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

Industry observers note that the kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

It has been revealed that the first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

Recent findings suggest that to show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):.

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

Industry observers note that the initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:.

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an matter with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News .NET MAUI 11 Makes CoreCLR the Default Runtime and Adds Incremental XAML Hot Reload.

Nov 26, 2026 3 min read.

Microsoft released .NET 11 on 10 November, and .NET MAUI in .NET 11 changes the default runtime from Mono to CoreCLR on all supported platforms. It also adds incremental XAML hot reload, implicit XAML namespaces and new test project templates. The work spanned seven previews and a release candidate, and the documentation describes product quality as the release's focus. Overall, this release consolidates more than it expands.

In a recent development, .NET MAUI (Multi-platform App UI) is Microsoft's cross-platform UI framework for Android, iOS, Mac Catalyst and Windows apps built from one C# and XAML codebase. .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support release with two years of support. Microsoft notes that MAUI follows its own support policy, separate from the runtime's STS and LTS lifecycle.

Sources indicate that the runtime switch is the most significant change. According to Microsoft, CoreCLR puts mobile and desktop apps on the same runtime as the other .NET workloads. Release builds use composite partial ReadyToRun by default. On Apple platforms, which disallow JIT compilation, code that isn't precompiled runs in the CoreCLR interpreter. Native AOT is an opt-in publishing option, and its Android support is still experimental. Microsoft recommends developers to test app libraries before choosing their deployment model.

XAML gets four main improvements. First, incremental hot reload, still in preview, patches live instances of pages and controls without recreating them. It is on by default in Debug builds, works with dotnet watch, and can be disabled with EnableMauiIncrementalHotReload. Second, implicit namespace declarations are now on by default, so the root xmlns and xmlns:x are optional. Third, lazy ResourceDictionary loading makes large dictionaries initialise up to roughly eight times faster when XAML source generation is used. Finally, RelativeSource bindings with a resolvable AncestorType now compile to trim-safe code.

Industry observers note that handlers keep replacing the legacy renderers with newer implementations. Windows uses the upcoming CollectionView2 handler by default, Android Shell is now handler-based, and iOS and Mac Catalyst now use handlers for NavigationPage, TabbedPage and FlyoutPage. The old renderers remain available as a manual fallback. On iOS, Appearing now fires before a page is pushed rather than after it becomes visible, and secondary toolbar items move into an overflow menu. Developers who depend on the old timing should switch to NavigatedTo.

Sources indicate that controls get smaller additions. Maps gain clustering and custom pin icons, plus an Azure Maps-backed implementation on Windows. TabbedPage gains badges, BoxView a Fill brush, and LongPressGestureRecognizer becomes configurable. Shell also supports route templates such as trip/{tripId}.

Sources indicate that animation methods now accept a CancellationToken, and their non-Async variants are obsolete. On the platform side, a new Passkeys class in Microsoft.Maui.Authentication wraps WebAuthn creation and assertion, while the server still has to validate challenges and attestation. Permissions.PostNotifications now works on iOS, and splash screens can have dark-mode variants.

According to recent reports, for Android, the minimum API level rises from 21 to 24, and x86 architecture is no longer supported. The release notes report shorter builds: an incremental build after a managed source change dropped from 68.3 to 52.3 seconds. They also report startup gains of 2.4 to 4.5 per cent from partial ReadyToRun, at the cost of a slightly larger package. Apple targets now require iOS, tvOS and Mac Catalyst 18.2 and macOS 15.2, with Xcode 26.4.

Several changes break existing code. The Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility package no longer ships, the Color record is now sealed, Java.Lang.Object.JavaFinalize() is obsolete, and non-font SwipeItem icons are no longer tinted automatically. When upgrading, Microsoft advises to focus on throughly testing navigation, custom handlers and trimmed publishing.

The full list of changes, including per-preview release notes, is in the .NET MAUI documentation. .NET MAUI ships as a workload with NuGet packages, so a project can pin specific versions.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • However, I’ve recently been seeing a few gemini:// links here and there as footers in hand-crafted blogs, and I nerd-snipped myself to export this blog as a Gemini capsule that you can find at gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On May 1st, 2020, Project Gemini made the rounds for the first time via a Hacker News discussion thread. I remember seeing the announcement back then, barely a month after the Covid 19 worldwide lockdown, and thinking it was a cool gimmick. But that was that.

However, I’ve recently been seeing a few gemini:// links here and there as footers in hand-crafted blogs, and I nerd-snipped myself to export this blog as a Gemini capsule that you can find at gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/. The process has been fun, and I actually quite like the extreme minimalism of the resulting site. So what else would you expect from me? I had to write about it—hence this post.

Today we’ll learn a little bit about what Gemini is, how I approached the blog export to its native gemtext format, and I’ll confess a couple of… sins I committed along the way.

Industry observers note that A blog on operating systems, programming languages, testing, build systems, my own software projects and even personal productivity. Specifics include FreeBSD, Linux, Rust, Bazel and EndBASIC.

In a recent development, A terrible name, that is. Looking for information about Gemini these days is extremely hard, thanks to Google polluting the namespace with its own AI offering. Of course that’s not Project Gemini’s fault because Google’s thing came after them, but still, good luck finding stuff about this network.

Joking aside, let’s look at Project Gemini’s barebones front page:.

… and break down the introductory and only paragraph:.

Gemini is a new internet technology supporting an electronic library of interconnected text documents.

You can think of Gemini as a way to access a bunch of text-only pages, with links among them, so you can find information and follow links to additional resources. Instead of using http:// or https:// URL prefixes, you use gemini:// instead.

That’s not a new idea, but it’s not old fashioned either.

It has been revealed that exactly. Gemini is like the WWW, or “the web” in more colloquial/modern parlance. In fact, Gemini is a parallel community to the web. Obviously, that’s not a new idea because the web dates back to 1989, and we are now 37 years after that.

The idea is not unique either because Gopher, a much lesser-known option, exists as well. Surprisingly to me, I realized that Gopher came after the web in 1991 while researching this article. I had always assumed Gopher was first and that the web came to replace it because of Gopher’s rigidness. But that’s not quite what happened.

It’s timeless, and deserves tools which treat it as a first class concept, not a vestigial corner case.

Industry observers note that humans have shared written documents since around 3400–3100 BCE (roughly 5,100–5,400 years ago) in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, and that’s probably (hopefully?) not going away. It’s true, though, that at this point, text sharing is not the primary thing that the web does, as you well know. We have morphed the web from a document distribution tool into an app platform, for better or worse.

Industry observers note that A little confession: I worked at Google for 12 years, starting right at the time they published Google Wave (2009), which to me marked the start of truly interactive web apps—more so than Gmail (2004) did. In the back of my mind, I knew I was helping turn the web into how we run apps, destroying the traditional desktop paradigm—a feeling I never liked. And… it happened. Obviously, it’d have happened without me, a little pawn in the game, but it bothered me regardless.

Gemini isn’t about innovation or disruption, it’s about providing some respite for those who feel the internet has been disrupted enough already.

In a recent development, (That comma splice hurts.) As we have established earlier, Gemini’s ideas are not latest, so it’s indeed not innovative. And seeing how little people read these days, or even how unable to pay attention to long-form text they are, it’s not going to disrupt anything either. But respite is key: having a separate place where you know you’ll only find some sort of counter-culture sounds entertaining.

Fun fact: I wasn’t quite sure what respite meant and originally took it to be similar to spite. That meaning would have worked equally well here, if not better?

Recent findings suggest that we’re not out to change the world or destroy other technologies. We are out to build a lightweight online space where documents are just documents, in the interests of every reader’s privacy, attention and bandwidth.

Here is the interesting thing. Gemini claims that it has been designed to minimize the chances of becoming bloated, and I’m not exactly sure how you can prevent that. For example: articles can provide links to images, but images are not auto-loaded. OK, indicates who? The auto-loading part is something the client browser controls, and it’d be trivial to create a Gemini browser, or modify an existing one, to auto-load and render images. That’d go against the spirit of Gemini, but if enough people wanted it, it’d happen. Same story as the browser wars.

Industry observers note that and that’s the key: “enough people”. As long as Gemini stays under the radar and only like-minded people gravitate towards it, these properties will be maintained. But if for any reason it becomes more mainstream… unwanted changes will happen.

Recent findings suggest that gemtext is the native format of documents stored in the Gemini network, with a MIME type of text/gemini and a .gmi extension. Gemtext documents are typically grouped in capsules—which is just another name for “website”.

The format itself is like a super-diluted version of Markdown, supporting just these features:.

According to recent reports, workable for sure, but weak. In my opinion, Gemini missed the boat of creating a truly semantical web, but for that you need additional primitives to represent more concepts. In any case, you can read through the long FAQ to know that this was discussed and eventually ruled against, so know that a lot of thought was put into its design.

Yet another fun fact: just two days ago, I stumbled upon “Good morning and welcome to my idea of a new web”: the proposal of a “browser” that just renders Markdown documents. This feels quite similar to the idea behind Gemini, but using a better (not a great) format with more markup abilities. And I say fun fact because, as I was learning about Gemini, I was imagining developing this exact alternate idea.

One curious bit is that Gemtext is also the format for subscription feeds. Sure, you can offer an RSS feed for your capsule, but RSS is a monster spec that feels out of place in a minimalistic network like Gemini’s. So you can abuse Gemtext to create a feed by creating a page that’s primarily links with a de-facto YYYY-MM-DD Title format. Again, it’s simple, and it works.

The major benefit of Gemtext’s simplicity is that clients can also be super-simple. You can rest assured that all clients will be able to display the same content, consistently. So far I’ve tried Elpher within Emacs, Lagrange on the desktop, and Buran on my Android phone. All are simple. All display text in the same way.

I definitely do not recommend using the Gemtext format to persist your original content, but that doesn’t mean you have to write in Gemtext. Which brings us to Markdown again.

It was at that point that I committed to converting my golden copies to Markdown even though authoring in Markdown was more inconvenient. And believe me: it is inconvenient, especially when having to insert images. But now I own my content in a format that’ll survive for years to come.

Which brings us back to Gemtext. The thought that crossed my mind when I stumbled upon Project Gemini again three weeks ago and that triggered this whole thing was: can I write a script to convert my Markdown docs into a capsule? And with “I” I really mean AI, because this is the kind of experiment I was not going to code myself.

And of course I could. After just one simple prompt, I had a converted site that I could browse. Granted: the conversion Python script was literally awful, and the converted format was not great either, but having something I could play with inspired me to try harder.

Sources indicate that so I threw everything away and started over, again with AI, to write a conversion tool for my blog (codenamed gengems for now) that takes the existing Hugo layout and spits out a capsule end-to-end in just 300 milliseconds while processing 1000 documents. The tool is obviously written in Rust, and by now supports enough configurable features that I’m increasingly tempted to throw Hugo away for the web version and create my own static site generator too. Because, you know, while Hugo works, it isn’t the greatest in usability and its recurrent incompatible changes are annoying. I’ll resist the urge to do that for now… I think.

Let’s dive a tiny bit into gengems. First of all, this second iteration is still entirely vibecoded. Oops, first sin. I have not looked at the code because it’s working for what I need it to do, it’s fast, and it’s not going to be used by anyone else… unless you want it, but then I’d probably rewrite it once more now that I know what the final feature set looks like.

Now, for this second iteration, I was so close to running out of my $20 weekly OpenAI quota that I pivoted from my favorite GPT 6.1 Sol model to GPT 6 Luna to see how far I could go. Luna is so cheap that you can do a ton with it, and I actually got gengems to work well enough within just a few iterations.

But oh dear. Luna is cheap, but it’s also kind of crap for coding. It stops half-way. It doesn’t think through enough corner cases. It doesn’t produce enough tests. The intends it produces are very vague. You have to be extremely prescriptive when asking it to do things and even that leads to mixed results. Out of curiosity, when my weekly cap was reset, I asked Sol to review what Luna did, and oh boy did it have things to say. From design problems to important missing tests, passing through outright bugs. I let it fix those challenges, and I continued building with Sol.

According to recent reports, right now, I’m actually pretty happy with the results of gengems. I can configure the mapping of pages to templates in a much more explicit way than in Hugo. I can use MiniJinja for templating. I can specify cross-site links. I can handle inline links, figures, and even tables. I can generate archives/feeds for the site, for each year, for each month. I can process blog posts, and also standalone pages. All in all, the results are very satisfactory given the close-to-zero effort I put into it.

With the site exported to Gemtext, I needed a server. There are a lot of options out there, but the one that piqued my interest was Agate: a minimalistic Gemini server written, of course, in Rust. You run the binary pointing it at the directory containing the generated site and, voila, it works. Agate even takes care of auto-generating SSL certificates because all Gemini traffic is TLS-protected, and the fact that it’s automated is a relief because dealing with certificates is a pain.

But running Agate once, interactively, and making it serve in the background are different stories. I am running FreeBSD on my server and I could have used the prebuilt agate package, but then I encountered a crashing bug and wanted to add a feature, so I had to pivot to building from source. And, as you can imagine, Cargo leaves a lot to be desired if you want to install the resulting product to a running system.

It has been revealed that now, of course you can copy the built binary to, say, /usr/local/bin/agate, but there is typically much more than a binary in a distribution: think about documents, examples and, for a server program in particular, startup scripts. Mind you, Agate’s source tree does include a FreeBSD rc.d script, but it was buggy, insufficient, and it also required manual copying. So I created a PR to revamp the installation system based on earlier experience with setting up similar infrastructure in other Rust services I run.

It has been revealed that I mentioned briefly above that I wanted to add a feature to Agate and that it was the reason I had to build from source. And that feature is… analytics, which are the second sin right there.

It has been revealed that “Oh no, ah-nah-ly-tics! Privacy enemy number one! How dare you add analytics to something in the Gemini network!?!”.

But wait a second. What are analytics? You do realize that Agate prints and saves a log of incoming connections (with IPs redacted by default), right? That’s par for the course for any Internet server out there, because in order to serve requests… well, the server actually needs to know what those requests are and where to send the responses to. So you can always analyze the log to gain some insights on traffic.

It has been revealed that and that’s pretty much what I did. I just wired this exact same information to my own analytics service for visualization. The only thing I see are the pages that are being downloaded, when they are downloaded, and the originating country (computed from the requester’s IP after truncating the last octet to mask it). Essentially… good old page counters from the 1990s.

It has been revealed that the way I implemented this is generic though: I extended Agate to add optional support for an SSI-style URL inclusion primitive and then added such a call to the capsule-wide footer template given to my Gemtext generator. As a high-level primitive, it can serve other purposes, like sourcing comments for each page by making the footer download a pre-rendered .gmi chunk. I haven’t implemented that yet in my comments service, but it should be pretty easy.

According to recent reports, sounds interesting? I might try to contribute this SSI feature upstream to Agate, but I predict that this collides with the goal of a lightweight server and that it’ll be rejected. But I’ll try anyway. I want to get the FreeBSD-related bug fixes and related improvements merged first, because those are helpful to everyone, I hope.

Recent findings suggest that that’s about it! If you are in the U.S. you are about to have 4 days off, so spend that time falling into the Gemini rathole. And if you are elsewhere, do the same! It’s entertaining.

It has been revealed that from now on, remember that you can also read this blog via gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/ if you want a super-fast, distraction-free experience. To get started, visit the Gemini software page for a long list of clients to choose from and install.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.
  • We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018.
  • Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. New contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...].

Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

Posted Nov 21, 2026 13:13 UTC (Sat) by coriordan (guest, #7544) [Link] (1 responses).

The LLVM exception: https://merlijn.sebrechts.be/blog/what-is-the-apache-2-ll... It indicates two things. (Based on my quick read; corrections welcome) 1. That Apache-2 licensed compilers (which insert some compiler code into the executables they create) don't create Apache-2 obligations for the programs they create. 2. It fixes incompatibility with GPLv2 by saying that, for a combined work of Apache-2 plus GPLv2 code, if an authority decides that any clause of Apache-2 is incompatible with GPLv2 then that clause of Apache-2 doesn't apply. (Which I guess they decided is fine because the places where there could be conflicts, such as patents, using the GPLv2 version isn't enough of a problem to be worth incompatibility.) So, the LLVM exception looks like a pretty good instrument.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Datacenter spending is booming but the models, the chips, and the clout all live in US and Asia.
  • Europe's IT spending is growing more slowly than the global average, according to Gartner, whose analysts warn that the region's push for tech sovereignty faces commercial and technological obstacles.
  • Gartner forecasts European IT spending of $1.57 trillion in 2027, up 9.9 percent from 2026, compared with worldwide growth of 15 percent to $7.35 trillion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Datacenter spending is booming but the models, the chips, and the clout all live in US and Asia.

Europe's IT spending is growing more slowly than the global average, according to Gartner, whose analysts warn that the region's push for tech sovereignty faces commercial and technological obstacles.

Gartner forecasts European IT spending of $1.57 trillion in 2027, up 9.9 percent from 2026, compared with worldwide growth of 15 percent to $7.35 trillion. For 2026, it estimates spending growth of 20.7 percent in North America and 13.7 percent in China.

"The world seems to be racing towards this AI goal of where the large language model provider is going to be, and the race seems to be between North American-based providers and some Asia Pacific providers," John-David Lovelock, Distinguished VP Analyst at Gartner, told The Register.

According to recent reports, he said Europe had traditionally trailed in IT uptake. "We saw that happen when global sourcing, cloud, and software as a service all came along. It's down to the pushback against the idea of creative destruction," where fresh technologies replace old ones.

Europe's fastest growing categories are datacenter systems, forecast to grow 29.7 percent in 2027, and infrastructure as a service, at 26.7 percent.

Even so, Lovelock does not expect Europe to compete with North America and China on AI investment.

Recent findings suggest that "For AI provision, Europe is going to be behind, and there won't be a way to catch up," he noted. "The AI datacenters, the large language models, the foundational models, the tools and techniques for building out AI are all being centered outside of Europe, but enterprises don't need to do that. So the question becomes: regardless of where the source of the AI is coming from, can the enterprises actually adopt and use it? In one sense, Europe will be behind in the provision of AI, but it need not be behind in the use.".

Sources indicate that the gap nonetheless complicates Europe's push to reduce its dependence on US technology suppliers. The European Union has introduced upcoming rules to encourage tech buyers to favor sovereign tech over the dominant tech vendors, but Lovelock doubts they will move spending much.

Sources indicate that "Sovereignty is a wonderful flag that we fly on the front of a building. IT is running in the basement. CIOs are not going to buy a second-best solution that costs more simply because it's sovereign.

"They are not going to break any laws, but they are not going to make a decision that puts their company in a worse position at a higher cost. While sovereignty gets [vendors] on the list, it doesn't assure that they get purchased," he told us.

Earlier this month, Gartner predicted that by 2029, more than 90 percent of EU organizations will have a digital sovereignty strategy, but argued that a fully sovereign technology stack remains out of reach.

"The global technology supply chain is too interconnected, and many critical dependencies cannot be replaced at a commercially viable scale," remarked Bettina Tratz-Ryan, VP analyst at Gartner. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.
  • It has been revealed that AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.
  • As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

It has been revealed that AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

According to recent reports, this builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

In a recent development, transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this newly introduced phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

Sources indicate that the EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

Sources indicate that the coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Recent findings suggest that once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.
